" r always trust a man that children like. For- give the impertinence of my question, but may I ask if you are in any profession " Well, no. I ant unfortunate in that respect, for I have always rather despised an idle man. 1 once tried to get into Parliament, but they wouldn't have time, and I ,have never tried again, for in my heart I prefer literature to politics, and I give a good deal of my time to writing. The rest of it is &VOW to an experiment I am try- ing. I have a fair sized place in Warwickshire, and I manage it myself." "That's right," replied Mr. Fitzgerald. " Too many of us shift our responsibilities on to the shoulders of :was. But I half thought you were a lawyer, I hardly know why. I suppose the wish was father to the thought." H 8 was evidently thinking of the threaktned 'proceedings his wife had menlioned in the Gal- lery, but be made • no definite allusion to it, and Mr. - Lascelles felt it would have beet an intrusimi on his part to have done so. They went into the drawing room, rind when Mrs. Fitzgerald retired, they went into time billiard-room, and at about mid- night they went to bed. The dinner had been light, and cooked to perfection ; the wine had . been of the best, and but little had been drunk ; neither the music nor the billiards 'could account for it, but as Mr. Laseelles sat before his cheery fire, he found himself growing strangely excited. Something- was going to happen. A conviction of this laid hold of him, and kept hint on the alert. He rose presently and opened his door. The passages was in absolute darkness, and he stood there listening, but not a sound was to be heard. He still had this feeling of vague ex- pectation but nothing happened. After a while he realised that he was tired and very sleepy, and muttering half aloud, • " What nonsense this he shut the door, and very 800 n he was in hal and fast asleep. Then something did happen, but it was only a dream, a vivid -but by 110 means an unpleasant dream. It was a patchwork of the day, with its various incidents absurdly enough distorted,' but still reproducing With sufficient accuracy his ar- rival at The Towers, his welcome, and his in- spection of the house and its contents. The con- versations were as calmly irrelevant as they usu- ally are in dreams, and a stranger was present, and rooms be had not seen, one especially, were lionised, and several things of that description kept him busily dreaming, till be woke with a start to find the morning sun streaming into the room. He smiled as lie recalled his uneasiness of the Previous evening, and the harmless dream which had been the only outcome of it. It as- suredly had not been worth worrying about, rind before he had finitshed dressing, he had almost, forgotten it.

But, as he was passing the open door of the library on his way to the dining-romn, it came back to him, down to its minutest detail, for be saw Mr. Fitzgerald standing by the window talking earnestly and with unmistakeable anxiety to the stranger of his dream. He recognised him at once, and the sight of his face arrested his steps, while lie suddenly became conscious of the same curious feeling of excitement, which had perplexed him the night before. Mr. Fitzgerald looked up, and called to him to conic in. He Seemed haggard and careworn as be addressed him, _

"good morning, Mr. Lanelles, though I am sort.; ta say that it is a vety bad morning for me. I will not trouble you with what affeatm only my family and myself. But 1 ant obliged to go to Dublin at once on business of the last impori - ante. This gentleman has brought me most un- pectedly bad Dews. I would ask you to go with me, only I should be such wretched company for any one. And besides,- it would Cut short your visit here. if you would do too a favour, stay till- I come back to-night, and try to prevent my wife from distressing herself before we know the worst. Of course there may be a best to it, but I am afraid it is not likely," turning- to the stranger who slook his bead thoughtfully. " She will tell you all about it. 1 can't rest. I have or- dered my dogcart, and I mu just off. Good-bye for the present." He held out Juts hand. Mr. Lascellos took it, but did not realise it. His dream was strong upon him.

"Mr. Fitzgerald," he exclaimed with ill•sup- pressed eagerness, "I can't tell you how sorry I am, whatever it may be that you fear. And I dare not yet tell you what ;is in my mind. You may think me mud—you may even think 1110 brutal. But there is one question I must ask you. Yesterday did you show me the whole of your house ?"
Mr. Fitzgerald made an impatient attempt to disengage hilt hand.

" Benny, he protested, •.‘ I did not expect this from you. Can't you see that I am not fit b, speak of anything but what is pressing on me so heavily just now 7" " Yes' I know. But, believe me, this concerns you, not me. Let me ask my question in another way,—ls there an octagon room in the house 7" " Octagon room ! Oh, you mean in the north wing. You noticed it from the out-,ide, no doubt. No, we didn't go there, but Mrs. Fitzgerald nih take you to see it.l Come, Cameron, we ought to be going," and he looked hurt, as he bowed cold- ly to Mr. Lascelles. But the latter had passed from excitement to actual elation, as he cried, "At the risk of offending you, I beg you to show me the octagon room before you start." Mr. Cameron, who had been eyeing Min keen- ly, stepped forward in time to prevent an indig- nant explosion. " The dog-cart is not at the door yet," he re- marked, "we still have a few minutes. If you will allow me I will be your friend's guide, while you finish those memoranda."

As soon as they were in the hall, Mr. Cameroi, whispered, "1 um a junior partner in the firm of Yr. Fitzgerald's solicitors. I grieve very much to say that 1 have brought him disastrous intelligence. X was struck with one thing in your interview ith him. What did you mean when you said that your seeing the octagon recurs concerned him and not your'

lam ashamed to tell you. I really am. There may be nothing in it. But I am quite willing to be thought a fool on the remote possibility of be- ing of use to him. Even one chance in ten thou- sand is not to be neglected as you very well know. Would you mind telling me if any papers are in question P' " One paper is, very vitally, in question. We save lost all trace o.f it I much doubt whether it has ever been in our possession. We have always understood that it was here but Ur. Fitzgerald knows nothing about it. HO thought we had it. If it is lost or destroyed, and it looks uncommonly like it, I dread to think what will become of the fatnily. But here is the stone staircase leading up to the octagon room. The door, I believe, is never locked. Will you go up by yourself, and—" " No, no, sir,, ' interrupted Ur. Lascelles, who could by this time hardly contain himself, " any cost you must come too. It was your face I saw. It was you who did it before. Oh, I'll ex.' plain it all to you directly. But you must come up, and you go first." Mr. Cameron did not altogether relish this. ID would have preferred to have this incoherent young man in front of him ; but, as there was no time to lose, he decided upon humoring him, and lie ran up the stairs, two steps at a time, with a quickly formed resolve not to be attacked at a disadvantage. As ho, breathlessly pushed open the door, however, Mr. Lascelles was at his shoulder, and his first words were not re-assur- ing-, " I knew it, I knew it," he gasped in a choked voice.

• Mr. Cameron glanced at hint suspiciously. They were on the threshold of an octago nroom with a pointed roof, forming one of the turrets visible from outside. The door by which they had entered occupied one bide ; against the other seven bung full length family portnits in various stages of dilapidation, evidently stowed away here, as being beyond the reach of the restorer's skill, The one opposite was in no way remark- able. The paint had peeled off in large patehes, mid what was left was very dirty :, but Mr. Las- cellos seemed fascinated ; his eyes were zivetted nrou it, as he repeated two or three times, in a dazed, mechanical way, '• The left hand bottom corner." He turned abruptly to Mr. Cameron. who an abruptly stepped back out of his reach, and cried, Yes, lam sure of it. The left-Land bottom corner, Mr. Cameron. I see you distrust me. But indeed I am as much astonished at what I see, as you are at me. I will znake it all clear to you in a moment. Go to that picture opposite, and pull out the left-hand bottom corner. Oh ! do go ; you will soon understand my impatience." Mr. Cameron hesitated, but he went to the picture, though lie -watched Mr. Lascelles nar- rowly all the time. The picture WIN a heavy one, and it needed an effort to do as he was bid- den.
" he said. "What next I" " Put your band against the wall behind the picture. Is there anything there "No, only a hole ; a brick must have fallen out."
That's it. I RM certain it's all right. Feel that hole. Push your hand in, farther, man, farther, as far as you can. Now P' " 1" grumbled Mr Catneron. " it's all

choked vath—Huilo : what's this? There ci smnething here. It crackles like—lt is paper." And with an agitation that egualled that of Mr. Laiwelles, he drew out, smothered in dust, a long folded paper, tied with tattered and decaying tape. Each of then forgot the other, as they tore the paper open. One look was ,enough for Mr. Cameron. " Good heavens !" be almost shouted. " It's the Lost Will. You've saved Mr. Fitzgerald. But how did it get there ? And how on earth did you know that it was there ?" The two men shook hands ‘varinly, and Mt Lascelles replied. " I am-indeed thankful. But come along ; Mr. Fitzgerald ought to know at once. I will explain my share in this extraordinary business when you are together." _
Thewi, found him in the ball, drawing on his gloves, and loole,ig miserable. He stared in amazement as they rushed up to him; Mr. Camer- on waving the recovered document wildly above his head.

Sb IS, tie erica. - zoom rne aog•eart away. Mr. Laseellett has found the Missing Will. I wish you joy with all my heart." Mr. Fitzgerald turned horn one to the other with a bewildered expression on his face. " I don't understand," he sta 1111 l tered. "No more do I," laughed Cameron, "but here's the Will. I uniterstand that." .
" Thank God," answered Mr. Fitzgerald with emotion. " But • how did you find out where it was, Mr. Lascelle6 ?"

"I confess I understand it as little as you do. But everything that has happened today I dreamed last night. The sight of Mr. Cameron's face brought my whole dream back to me.; and. though I fancy you both thought I had taken leave of my senses, I felt it would have been cruel to have raised false hopes, • if nothing bad come of it. Mr. -Cameron will tell you you how capriciously thought I behaved. That was because I wanted to stick to oven time smallest features in the dream, and give, it e very chance of coming true. Silly of me, wasn't it ? But it did come true."

" Well it is the strangest thing. Come and tell my wife. She wil thank you better than I can. I am longing for tho details." Then in the low measured tones of a solemn 'conviction, lie faded, " Mr. Lascelles, in entertaining you, I have been entertaining an angel unaware."

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Our Friends and Neighbours.—lt is exactly fifty years ago that our late Sovereign receivPd in London the Emperor Napoleon HI, and his young and lovely Queen—the Empress Engenie—Queen Victoria's sympathies were then entirelyvvith the deposed Orleans family, and her diary records how greatly she was impressed with the dynastic changes in France "How strange," she wrote, "to think that I, the grand- daughter of George 111. should dance with the Emperor Napoleon, nephew of England's great enemy," the dance referred to moreover taking place in the Waterloo Room at Windsor Castle. One is reminded of these circum- stances by the happy change that has taken place in French feeling towards us in the past two or three years, and the forthcoming visit to London of the French naval officers, will show how entirely se have forgotten the time %%ben Paris delighted—only a few years sincP, in unflattering cartoons of our Royal Family. The French visit will rank as one of the chief events of the London season, and Society hostesses intend to leave nothing undone to do honour to our visitors.

Related to the ex-Empress Eugenie.—Mr. Arthur Devereux, whose name is prominently before the public in connection with a sensational crime, is said to be related to the ex-Empress Eugenie, and if that is so, the terrible tragedy of the death of Mrs. Devereux and her twin children, will have a distressing interest for one -whose cup of sorrow is already full to overflowing. The ex-Empress is a dauguter of a Spanish Duke, and -was born in Granada in Spain, on May sth, 1826. Her smother, before her marriage, was a Miss Kirkpatrick, who bailed from Closeburn in Scotland, and it is stated that Mr. Devereux's maternal grandmother was a sister of this Miss Kirkpatrick. If that is the case, as is asserted by a member of the family, the ex-Empress Eugenie is greataunt to the man who has been :arrested /or the murder of his wife and twin children.

The Osborne Family.—ThelDuchess of Leeds has been -spending the spring in Italy where she usually resides for about half the year. This season she is bringing "out her young daughters and will therefore be much in London after Easter, but her tastes are more for things intellectual than forth° ordinary attractions of Society. She is sister to Lord Durhani,and her marriage with the Duke of Leeds—then Lord Carmarthen—took place in February 1884. The Duke has not, as many suppose,any 'titular associations with the great Yorkshire city. Be takes his title from the small country village of Leeds, in Kent, though curiously enough the fortunes of the Osborne family were closely connected with the woollen trade, which is one of the staple industries of the Yorkshire city. An old world Romance.—The founder of the Osborne family was one Edward Osborne of whom an ideal story of old world romance is told. HQ was apprenticed to Sir William Hewett, a famous clothworker,whose house and place of business stood on old London Bridge. One day it was young Osborne's good fortune to save the clothworker's pretty daughter who had fallen into the river, and he was eventually awarded with her hand. In due time he succeeded to the business and fortune of his father-in-law, and in 1582 Sir Edward Osborne was Lord Mayor of London. Since then the Osborne family have prospered 'fiexceedingly, and the Duke of Leeds, besides other sources of wealth, owns some five and twenty thousand acres in his native country.

Some Grand Old Ladies.—The death of the Dowager Duchess of Abercorn has removed the most venerable of our grand old ladies. but there are still several others who should be included in this catejory, foremost amongst whom is the Baroness Burdett Coutts. She is the best known,and one of the oldest of living peeresses being but a little younger than the Dowager Lady Clancarty, who is ninety-two. The Dowager Duchess of Somerset is full of years and honours, and so also is Lady Caroline Duncombe who held the train of the Duchess cf Cambridge at the Coronation of Queen Victoria. Lady Mary Farquhar has turned ninety, but the woman with the widest and most intimate know- ledge of Society for the latter half of the past century is probably Lady Cork who was married in 1854, and is n granddaughter of George Canning, the famous states- man.

Our Treacherous Spring.—The vagaries of our spring weather are a never failing subject of comment but then they involve us in vexing problems which are snore or less a trouble to all of us. The woman who puts away her furs and wraps with the first few days of warmth and sunshine, is very much like the housewife who begins her spring "earthquake" on a certain early date,after which there can be no more flres.Both are des- tined to do a lot of shivering before some summer really c omes, or perforce have to return again to winter habits. The cuckoo is supposed to be a silly bird but its very late arrival this spring is said by many people to indicate a belated summer. In spite however of all warnings, the line days always tempt a great many women and girls to try and meet summer more than half way, but though the morning may seem to warrant the sunshade and' pneumonia" blouse, the wise know that the day may close with keen blasts, and everthing unpleasant in the way of weather. Braids Fashionable.—Braid is enjoying a great vogue and not only in the adornment of cloth, serge, cashmere and similar fabrics, but is appearing upon voiles, nun's veiling, crepe de chine, silk mousseline, etc. In the latter instance, the braids match the fabrics perfectly in colour, and are mostly of the variety known as " silk diamond," but tailors are still permitting lighter or darker tones of braid,and are even sanctioning contrasts. A new trimming for airy-fairy evening gowns, consists of narrow soft taffetas ribbon, bordered with tiny flowers and foliage, carried out also in ribbon. For edging the sash, trimming the waistband, or finishing off flounces, this is an ideal trimming, moreover it can be had in a wide variety of colours, and is by no means as expensive as it leoks. Easter Eggs.—Many Easter "eggs" this year are taking the form of the motor car—miniature automobiles, perfect in every detail are filled with chocolates or candies, and there are wicker cars, fitted with tin or glass receptacles for holding flowers or I.he tiny orange trees, which everyone is trying to secure just now. Tiny azalia and rose trees, are also being offered by up-to-date florists, audit is now even possible to secure, at a somewhat fabulous price, the miniature almond tree. Jewellers are showing many new motor designs, which mostly take the form of brooches, or charms, and the latest trinket boxes are perfect little automobiles, the seats of which lift up, and disclose velvet-lined receptacles for trinkets. French dolls dressed in motoring attire, and looking very much more fascinating than the real motorist, when attired for a "run," are filled with sweetmeats, and these particular "eggs" are being well patronised by the little folks. The Appointments of the Writing Table.—Tinted notepaper is in vogue, palest lavender holding a fore- most place in our affections. And to be correct all letters must be sealed with one's own seal, a charming silver wax being. the most approved. Another old fashion revived is that of the quill pen, which all fashionable women are attempting to wield now-a-days. So far fashion has not decided that we shall scent our paper and envelopes, in old-world style, but the all-per- vading sachet finds a place in the drawers of the writing table, and affords to its contents a faint suggestion of the fragranoe of one's favourite perfume.

div.head: DRESS-FASIIION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASIIION-HOME.
MART LADY LONDONDIMRY.

Mary Lady Londonderry is slowly recovering from the shock caused by the painfully sudden death of her second son, Lord Henry Vane Tempest, and has gone back to her place in Wales, Plas Machynlleth, where she will stay for some weeks. This property belongs to the Dowager, as it came to her from her father, Sir John Edwards. For many years Lady Londonderry enjoyed the unique position of being a churchwarden to the little church close to the place. She is a grand dame of the old 'school, musical, accomplished, and with great charm of manner that endears her to all who come in contactovith her. Considering her advanced age she is now in wonderful health and spirits.

div.head: AN AFTERNOON FROCK.
div.p: AN AFTERNOON FROCK.

Our illustration shews an afternoon frock realised in golden-brown taffetas. The bodice is draped to the figure, and opens over a vest of Alencon lace. The stoles, of drawn chiffon, are edged with fun frills of the lace, and fasten down the front with bows of dark-brown velvet. A distinct novelty M the shape of the sleeve, which is formed of a short full puff of the taffetas, terminating at the

elbow in a narrow shaped band of drawn chiffon, with two frills of the Alencon lace on each side of it. Gathered Mosey round the top, the skirt is of generous width at the feet, and is quite plain, with the exception of three wide "virgin" tucks above the hem. A shaped belt of brown velvet, beauti- fully cut and fitted, laces down the front and holds in the vest,while leaving the ends of the stoles free.*

div.head: WOMEN AND STAGE PLAYS.
div.p: WOMEN AND STAGE PLAYS.

It has been generally understood that the first woman to take part in a play on the English stage was Mrs. Coleman in 1666. This, however, says Household Words, on the authority of Dr. C. F. Forshaw, is not correct. Dr. Forshaw, from a 1663 play-bill, and a further reference thereto which he possesses, finds that a Mrs. Marshall took the part of "Celia" in that year at Drury Lane.

div.head: Mn. BARRIN AND Miss VANBRUGH.
div.p: Mn. BARRIN AND Miss VANBRUGH.

There is a fact of more than ordinary interest in Miss Irene Vanbrugh's appearance in "Alice Sit-by- the-Fire," says the Sketch. She forms the connect- ing link between Mr. Barrie's first appearance as a dramatist and his most recent. It was in "Walker, London," at Toole's Theatre, where Mr. Barrie's first play was produced, that Miss Vanbrugh took a prominent part as Bell Golightly.
GIRL'S COAT AND SKIRT.

The sketch shews a neat coat and skirt for a young girl, which would serve for cooler days through the summer. A colour should be chosen that will go well with any coloured blouse. Navy serge is always useful, but the pale shades of grey or biscuit colour are more fashionable, and lighter for spring wear. This particular example was carried out in a pale biscuit-coloured home-spun mixture of open texture, the shaped collar being of line faced cloth in the same shade. The coat was only slightly shaped to the figure at the sides,

and is outlined by a stitched strap and taos or cloth. The leg-of-mutton sleeves are finished with a pointed cuff and cloth strap. The sides of the skirt are arranged in inverted pleats, and are stitched down to about the knees, and the hem trimmed with strappings of cloth. The owner of this costume was wearing a shirt blouse of cream delaine with a scarlet belt and tie, and a simple straw hat, round the crown of which was tied a scarf of red and white spotted ribbon.

div.head: FOR THE CHILDREN'S WELFARE.
div.p: FOR THE CHILDREN'S WELFARE.

An International Congress on the Protection and Education of Children will be held in connection with the Exhibition at Liege in September next, and will extend over three days. The programme will comprise four sections. As it is hoped that those bodies which are interested in the subjects under discussion may be able to send delegates and to furnish papers, setting forth their views, the National Union of Women Workers, 9, Southamp- ton-street, High Holborn, London, W.C., has formed a special committee, under the chairmanship of Miss Maitland, Somerville College, to arrange for a representative attendance of delegates from i the numerous societies with i which t is n touch. All papers will be read in French. Further informa- tion may be obtained froin the Secretary, Rue Rubens, 44, Brussels, or from the Secretary of the National Union of Women Workers.

Two tablespoonfuls of milk may be used if required. Well butter four saucers, and nearly fill with the mixture; put them into a good oven for twenty minutes. Take them out and set them on a dish, screen them with castor sugar. and hold over tnem a not salamander; send them to tante with half lemons, or a dish of greengage jam, or a dish of any jelly to fancy. The batter must bis allowed to stand two hours before being put lute thu saucers.

div.head: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.
div.p: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.

Successful anniversary servicvs were held in the above place of worship on Sunday. The preacher at the morning service was Mr. W. Light. and in the afternoon an address was given by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. The choir sang the anthem "0, Praise the Lord, all ye nations." The Rev. J. Manning was the preacher in the evening and delivered an excellent discourse upon "The trial of Jesus." Mr. P. L. Richardson gave an impres,/ sive rendering of "Rock of Ages," and the anthem " How excellent "was sung by the choir. On Monday evening a service of song was given, entitled "The Fireman's Lily." The connective parts were read by Mrs. Pattison and Mr. J. B. Isaac presided.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was again a most interesting meeting of this Society on Sunday. Mr. A. Healey presided and spoke upon the uncertainty of life. Many familiar faces of those who used to attend those meetings, he said,'lwere now missing. Their friends were now in the enjoy- ment of the bliss of the Better Land. Mr. W. Hind- marsh, of Manchester, was the speaker, and his subject was" Whosoever compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." These words were, he said, very applic- able to the time of our Lord,but had seemiegly no such meaning in a literal sense for the present, yet in the moral and spiritual sense they had a great meaning, Masters would pay tchat they were compelled to pay. Servants would put as much work in as they were com- pelled to. There was a compelled service all round,and also a voluntary service. Said he, "I would rather be a good workman than a bad Christian ; let us not be afraid of going one mile with our fellows but many miles of service and help. Let us go out of our way to help to remove the causes of wrong doing." Mrs. Ellis of Halifax, sang sweetly "Divine Redeemer" and "Hear ye, Israel." Mr. J. Owen and the Secretary took part in the meeting. Three new members were heartily welcomed, 444 having been now enrolled. Appropriate hymns were sung,Mr. W. H. Payton Mus. Bac. presiding at the organ.

. . Both speakera smiled. Geoffrey taseettea tins riding. It was his first visit to Ireland, an& while waiting for a friend who was to join him in Dublin, be amused himself by hiring a horse, and xploring the country. The people, .71til their quaint humour, were a continual reve/ation In him, and durints his excursions be never missed an opportunity of'culering into conversation with the peasants. Ile had 'ken inclined to doubt, bare lie knew them, whether they were as ready as they wore said to be, until one day, he sprang a test upon the ostler et the livery stables, by asking him unexpectedly, " If the devil bad to chose between you and me, Pal,whim would he choose P"- ." Me, your honour, me," came the answer wthiinteven a semblance of hesitation. •Why " Ikea:lse he is sure of your honour at any tune." This put his doubts to flight. He cultivated the natives assiduously, and was rewarded by many funny, shrewd sayings, which in the even- jugs he would enter ill, bin notebook. His first. remark, as most likely to lead to further talk, was generally some reference to any big house that could he seen from the road, and he WAS "nly pursuing his usual tactics on this occasion. It was a lovely morning, Ho had ridden eighteen mileq, and was thinking of a halt, and a bite fot himself and his horse at the first farm he came to, when a turn in the road led him to, what was evi- dently the ledgit of an imposing looking country house, part of which was visible through the trees that 'surrounded it. A gentleman, with two terriers at his heels, ' was standing lighting a cigar, as Mr. Imseelles rode up, and it was to him that he put his invariable question ; but under the circumstances, noting the cigar, the terriers, and the unmistakeable bearing of the person he addressed, be raised his hat courteously, without any trace of the easy familiarity which he had found most successful with the horny handed PODS of the soil. The smile was encouraging, so he continued, " Thank you, very much. I feel I ought to know whose the place is, since you have been so good as •to tell me, but, as a matter of fact, I gon't. My name is Lascelles." This time the other laughed, and said, " Even, an Irishman couldn't beat that. I'm afraid I haven't a card with me,. but my name is Fitzgerald. Now tell me why you want to know."

"Well, I am afraid I am only a sort of thirsty vagOond. But I must apologise for trespassing on you in this way. If I had known, I should never have attempted to quench my thirst at the fountain head."

_ "Mr. Laseelles, I am a plain man, and lam not. good at riddles. What is it you mean 2" "1 mean that I am a stranger in a strange land. I have run over for a holiday. A friend I was to meet has been unexpectedly detained, so I am filling in the time by making acquaintance with the country. Mounted on my hired steed I go to end fro learning much and enjoying it im- mensely. The thirst that is on me is a thirst for information nothing- more questionable than that; and I am very much obliged to you for ac good-naturedly telling me whose this beautiful house is. Good-day, and thank you again. I must pursue my researches further." ITe bowed, and was riding on, when Mr. Fitz- gerahl said, " Stay a moment, Mr. Lascelles. If you have come from Dublin, your horse will need a rest. Let me offer both you and him hospitality. As you are not pressed for time, you will find your- self repaid by a nearer inspection of my old house. I must confess to being as proud as I am fond of it, and I shall be very glad to take von over it. It is quite the show place of the neighbourhood, and as a rule tourists are rather a nuisance to us. But a vagabond's pathetic thirst is a different thing, and I invite you to drink, metaphorically of course, nothing more questionable than that." " You are most kind. I shall be delighted. But a metaphor, as a rule, only holds good up to a certain point. Beyond that point it is apt to leave something to be desired : after a eighteen mile ride, to be very much desired," and Mr. Dandles looked whimsically at his companion, /is they turned in at the gate together. The latter's eyes twinkled with amusement, as he answered gravely, "Yes, I know, metaphors must not be over- strained," and then with apparent inconsequence, " It is very warm for the time of year." "Very," assented Mr. Lascelles, and the two understood one another perfectly. When they reached the stable yard, a groom took charge of the horse, and Ur. Fitzgerald led the way into the)house. It was an old building that had been added to by successive generations of Fitzgeralds, the more modern portions being saved from offending the eye by a profusion of creepers, which lent their mellowing harmony to the whole. There were turrets and gables, sug- gesting ideal nooks and cosy retreats; and, built as it was, round three sides of a spacious quad- rangle. The Towers as the house was called. was a fine example of what one sees only now and then, a faultless and picturesque exterior with no distinctive style of architecture. 'Welcome, thirsty vagabond," Mr. Fitzger- ald began, as they stood at the open, front door, waving his band, with a humorous affectation of pompousness; then with a hurried change of manner, as a lady crossed the hall, he added. "My dear, let me introduce Mr. Laseelles, whom good fortune has brought us as our guest. Mr. Laseelles, my wife." She greeted him with frank cordiality, and be- fore luncheon was over, he was as much at home with them, as they were with him. Given a cer- tain subtle sympathy, friendships soon ripen, and it was not long before they were all on excellent terms. The children claimed him for an hour to show him their ponies, and rabbits, and 'general- ly to do the honours of their department, and then the inspection of the house took up the rest of the afternoon. In the course of it, while his host was called away for a few minutes, Mr. Las. miles WWI standing with Mrs. Fitzgerald in front of a picture, one amongst many in the Gallery, when she said, _ _

" There is some sort of mystery connected with this Hugh Fitzgerald. He was of the elder branch. But the estate is not entailed, and my husband's father came in by Will. An odd re- port is going about that some person is claiming to he the direct descendant of Hugh," (pointing to the picture), " and occasionally we hear of it from our lawyers, but until lately my husband has made light of it. I don't mean that he is at all anxious now, but it appears that the lawyers find it necessary to put all the papers in order, so as to be ready should any real attack be made. Of course it would be a very serious thing for Us, and for the poor children, if anything did go wrong, as I am told that this person is thorough- ly unscrupulous, and has degenerated into a mer• adventurer ; who would not hesitate to take ad- vantage of any legal technicality." Mr. Lascelles murmured SOlllO words of sym• pathy; when she resumed, " What a shame to bother you with all this. I always think of it ~lien I pass this picture, but I ought not to have spoken of it. Come and see something pleasantev." They strolled on, sometimes to look out of a window at some effective point in the landscape, sometimes to bend over a case of miniatures or enamels or dainty china. The Gallery was it veritable museum of treasures, and Mr. Las- cellos, who was an ardent lover of art, was be- ginning to appreciate what strange good luck had befallen him, when Ur. Fitzgerald came back and said, looking at his watch, - _

" Ur. LAS-c'elles, it is getting late, and it is a long way to llubiin. From what you lot fall as to your movements, I gather that nothing im- peratively compels you to be there to-night. Let us persuade you to waive all ceremony, and stay here. It will be a great pleasuro to us, and I daresay we can find something more to show you to-morrow before you g 0.".. _ _

div.head: EALL RIGHTS IlEfilliVED.) ATHLETICS ANT) HEALTH
div.p: EALL RIGHTS IlEfilliVED.) ATHLETICS ANT) HEALTH
W. BEACH THOMAS (Author of the Isthmian " Athletics," dc.).

There is a class of person who has a whole- some horror of all athletics. We hear much about " the brutal athlete." as if be were a creature who only enjoyed kicking his neighbour's shins and had no share in the usual amenities of po- lite life. Again we are told that athletics are the ruin of health as well as of manners, that Athletes in their later years find themselves less capable of violent exertion fitful their unathletic brethren, that; heart and lungs and legs are all injured by great indulgence on the path, or field or river. In each of these accusations :there is a rudiment of truth ; some athletes ere brutal, some, damage their internal organs and their limbs ' • • but that athletics in the gen- eral way are at all inimical to health, mind or morals is a contention we wish to combat. It would be possible to talk at large on the, subject to any extent. Anyone could write a vague puff of the athletic spirit; we can argue—and truly—that the Anglo-Saxon must have his games, .that exercised violent exercise, is a safety valve, leVing off the steam that else might pro- duce all manner of explosions. Again we can go back and quote the Duke of -Wellington to prove how courage is formed by the Mimic fights of football, and endurance by races on path end river. Doubtless also it ,is true that our battles have been won on the school " playing fields," that discipline, self-reliance, acquaintance with danger, are fostered by all branches of ath- letics. . Yeti again—intellectually we can point to the past athletic pro Ness of many of our most uominanding intellects. Four of His • Majesty's judges, for instance, were in the • University boat ; a a umber of the Bishops have been, dis- tinguished athletes. The Attorney-General de- feated Lord Jersey in the earliest • days of the Inter-'Varsity .sports. The subject is long and interesting, and abstract talking "in the air " could make out a very pretty case. But in this article we propose to stick rigidly to facts, the facts furnished by carefully gathered statistics, and by the physiological investigations of well- known 1)hysic:1111M

div.head: .AILE ATHLETES HEALTHY?
div.p: .AILE ATHLETES HEALTHY?

It happens from time to time that a well known athlete dies suddenly. The world, genuinely sorry for the mishap, . is too ready to attribute the calamity to the violence of past exertion. One such death was an, 'Jounced in '9B, when the American Myers, per- haps the finest quarter-miler of all time, suc- cumbed to rapid, heart disease. As, long ago as '67, public attention was largely directed to the subject of the effeat •Of athletics on the health by. the collapse of a great'sculler and also of a famous prize fighter. The -consequent outcry against the excessive indulgence in games in- duced Dr. Morgan, a great physician -and'a con- siderable athlete; thoroughly to investigate the statistics of the subject. He started, it is true, with the a priOri notion that exercise must be a good thing, but it is impossible for anyone to say that his prejudices had even the slightest effect on his scientific investigations. His plan was to inquire as to the health and life of every sit.gle • Man who had rowed in the Inter-Uni- versity race since 1829, " and to compare the body of facts thus collected with the life and health tables of the insurance -companies. So thorough were his inquiries that he succeeded in getting, either from their friends or the ac- tual athletes, full accounts of all but three of the competitors in the races between '29 and '65. The results of his search were published in '69, -a number of the letters from the ' old blues " being given in full. His conclusions. based on facts tested by extreme scientific ac- curacy, were beyond all exiiectation favourable to the cause of athletics. Out of nearly three hundred instances, only seventeen confessed, or were said by their friends, to have suffered ill- effects and even of this small number Dr. Mor- gan shows that a majority indulged hi the race at a time when their health was in a precariow state.

Dr. Morgan applied also another test, that. ot longevity, and again in this direction be found his statistics all in favour of the oarsmen. His calculations tend to show that the aggregate lives of a crew of eight rowers totalled fifty years in excess of the average life. Yet again, Dr. Morgan went into the question of heart and long • troubles, as it is supposed that these two organs are specially liable to the ill effects of over exertion., The athlete once again came out successfully. For whereas some 46 per cent. of grown men die on the average from diseases of the heart and lungs, among the old University oars only an average of 37 per cent, succumbed to affections of these organs. Now these statistics refer primarily to oarsmen, but if they be considered in relation to the truths of physi- ology Underlying them their conclusions will apply with equal truth to any form of violent exertion, athletics proper, football or cycling. We will, then, endeavour—with as little use of technical terms as possible, to expose the actual effects produced on the organs of the body, principally the heart and lungs, by sudden and maintained athletic exertion.

div.head: EXERCISE : ITS ADVANTAGES.
div.p: EXERCISE : ITS ADVANTAGES.

In the first place it is indisputable that cer- tain forms of exceeding effort may so affect the body as to produce death. Skilled veterinary surgeons, whom we have consulted, say that I racing greyhounds very frequently die of sudden I heart disease. The same disease is found in an I acute form also in racing horses, and every year ' many hundreds of draught horses suddenly col- lapse from a similar cause. Doctors, again, .whose practice lies among operatives, among men whose daily task is to lift and carry heavy sacks and weights of all sorts, report numerous cases of men who about middle life suddenly lose health and vigour from the giving way of blood vessels of the heart. We have elsewhere quoted the instance of one prize fighter and one sculler who both met sudden death. The pro- blem is how to snake this extensive group of facts tally with the statistics above quoted from , Dr. Morgan. For the moment we have statis- tics cutting statistics—two bundles of facts mu- tually antagonistic. The studies of yet an- other doctor who has taken special interest in the subject will help us to escape from the ap- parent dilemma. In a general way we are apt to consider the internal orgasms as quite separate in kind from the constitution of the limbs and muscles. We divide training under two heads,— studying separately exercise and ; ailments as ' though thee xercise did not affect the inner mail nor the food the outer. Facts do not favour this view. It must be remembered that the I heart itself is Composed almost entirely of mus- cular tissue, and that the exercise which hardens the muscles, say of the thigh, has exactly the same sort of effect on the muscles of the heart. The more quickly the heart beats, the more rapidly is the blood pumped and the more vio- lently isitthrown against the walls of the principal bloodvessels (the Aorta). The result of this fre- quency and violence of the heart action enlarges I and strengthens the muscles of the organ ex- actly as the movement of the leg increases the I strength of the leg muscles. The result is that I the athlete at the end of the course of training possesses a heart, and lungs also, which have reached a state of development that ought to be of the utmost benefit ,to health. Of all consti- tutional advantages the possession of a power- ful heart and lungs is perhaps the most vain. able. So far then the athlete, especially if be was orignilaly rather weak in these respects, hal reaped nothing but advvantage for himself.
EXERCISTI-ITS DANGERS.

However, pail passe with the beneficial . de- velopment has grown up a corresponding risk, or to use a more accurate word, responsibility. The comparison with the muscles of the limbs now no longer holds good ; for while a man runs no particular risk by letting his once large thigh muscles degenerate, the shrinkage in the muscles of the heart entails a very serious danger. The athlete, We' will suppose, after several years' constant exercise.. has suddenly to adopt a more ,r less sedentary mode or file ; ass time goes on he will take less and less exercise and in copse- pence, though without necessarily incurring bad effects, he will have lost the constitutional bene- fits that his athletics once brought him. In the meanwhile, however, his desire for such bouts as he enjoyed in the past will come upon him, when opportunity offers, with not less than their for- mer force. In consequence, by a race or a long cycle ride or even an excessive walk he will call upon his muscles (of heart as well as leg) to do in a day the work that should have been ex- tended over several weeks. His subsequent stiffness of limb will soon make him realise how great the effort has been, but the stiffness, or, technically, the over-dilation, of the muscles of the heart and Aorta will not give the same in- formation to his senses. Nevertheless that one day's bout of exercise may have set up the be- ginning , of the disease though the day previously there did not even exist the germs of

sum a wediciess. Ti sum up the conciusion—. what happens is this, that the athlete who trains carefully and not too •quieldy benefits his con- stitution immensely, but at the season when he allows himsdf to run down, he incurs greater risk than other people from sudden strain. His or- gans are more elastic, and if you stretch • lactic too far it tends to lose its native resilience.

There is one more point to which the athlete must pay close attention. The study of . the heart makes ,it clear that exertion extended over a long period of years produces much the same effect as an excessive and sudden strain.. The .men whom . Dr. Morgan studied owed their salva- tion and the accruing benefit to the fact that their athletie career, that is their violent ath- letie career, was not continued past the age of 24, or so. Unless man is ot exceptional phy • sique, and takes infinite care of himself, it is ai-• twist certain that his health in later life will suffer, supposing be has continued to appear in the competitive arena up till the age of, say, thirty. , It is a very different thine' ' to be an, athlete and a competitive athlete. We believe that the Maintenance of vigorous exercise lip till the threshold of old age is the first secret of health. of keeping a sound mind in a sound body; but limb racing, exercising, against some One else de- mands a very much mare trying and exacting form of energy.
A GYMNASTIC COPING-STONE.

If we may take it as accepted that the athlete must take more care of himself then other peo- ple, the centre of the problem all lies in the, difficulty of maintaining the career he has be- gun. " He has begun by putting himself on a higher plane, hygienically, than the rest of the world, how is he to prevent his fall being of sunder dimensions to his rise Is it possible for a clerk or anyone engaged in sedentary and office work to keep up his athletics ? There- is, of 'course, the•bicycle to help him, to take hum out of town, out of himself .and out of his leth- argy ; but on the body the bicycle has and not always beneficial effect. .To us the so- lution seems to lie in it greater cultivation . of gymnastics. Anyone can practice. gymnastics, and that without the need of a gymnasium or even of any gymnastic parnibernaha more ex- pensive than dumbbells. Eveu a dumbbell is not necessary. The immense ,effect produced by any regular daily movements on both Mns- cle and health' will seem incredible to those, who have not made practice of • such. Any man who by indulgence in athletics has properly developed his physique can maintain (not pro- duce) that physique by as little as ten minute's- careftil gesticulation in his bedroom. A gym- nasium, paraphernslia, the study of gymnastic manual will assist him, and will render his ex- ercises less appallingly dull, but necessary they are not. Personally we are convinecd both from a priori reasoning, from surgical investi- gations, from experienced fact, that in the im- position on himself of some regular gymnastic exercise lies ~the first secret of sound health.

We have spoken largely of rowing, and from, what we have seen, we believe rowing to be Vie most exhausting of all sports,—and for fins reason ; that the continuance of seven other oars in the boat makes shirking or withdrawal from the race an absolute impossibility. if therefore, men may row the Imrdez,t race in the world— from Putney to Mortlake—Mal afterwards con-- triye to enjoy e:zceptioutil health, we may con- cluds that other 'forms of exercise are at least not less conducive ,to the general health of the- body. 13,4 let it be again said : The athlete both bt the domain of muscles and morals must td-- W...ys take the trouble to con lune and maintain: t‘a3 good scate he has acquirer/

Cheshire Lines Platelayers' and Workmen's Provident Society. The 30th annual meeting of the Cheshire Linea Platelayers' and Workmen's Provident Society, which consists of workmen employed in the Engineers' Department of the Cheshire Lines Railway, was held at the works, Battersby-lie, Warrington, on Wednes- day. The chair was taken by Mi. Harry Blundell, M. Inst., CE,, the chief engineer of the Company, and the meeting was largely attended 'by the officials and delegates front Lancashire and Cheshire. The secretary submitted the annual report, which stated that the number of members was 1221. A large sum had been expended in aid of 316 sick members, who had received assistance from the funds of the society, and 23 death claims had also been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed, Mr. Thomas Pratt was re-elected secretary for the ensuing year, and Messrs. George Walker and It. Jones were re-elected auditors.

div.p: 71113 BLACK MOTOR CAR.
By J. B. BARRIS BURLAND.

CHAPTER iv.—(Continued.) The only sister of Mrs. Porteous was pre -sent at the funeral. Her husband, who held -a small living in Essex, had conducted the burial service. Both were staying the nsght in London. On the way back from the cerne- -tery the Rev. George Behag suggested that the -widowerand his child should return with them to his vicarage and spend a week in the coun try. The change would do both of them ,good, and would help in some way to take them out of their grief. Mrs. Behag warmly seconded the proposal: In appearance she was a plain hard-featured woman; and her general manner was a little forbidding to those -who did not know the kindness of heart that lay _under the somewhat rough , exterior. _ _ .

-She had no children of her own, and this had soured her life. But all her maternal instincts were roused on ,behalf of the mother- less child, who sat beside her in the dark carriage, silent, with wide open eyes, wonder- ing where his mother had gone to, yet not daring to ask his father for a solution of the problem that puzzled his little brain. John Porteous, in spite of the mist of bitter and vain regret which clouded his thoughts, saw his way clear before him. He replied -that business- would unfortunately keep him in town, but that he would be very grate- ful if they would take charge of his child for a few days. As a matter of fact the offer only anticipated his own wishes in the matter. He could secretly leave England while his son was away, and write a short note imploring Mrs. Behag to take the lad under her charge, bring him up as her own son, and never let him know his father's name.

When he went to bed that night, he fell on his knees and grayed. It was many years -since he had asked anything of his God, but that night he besought forgiveness for his sins, and prayed that the punishment might not 'fall on the head of his innocent child.

The next morning the Rev. George Behag and his wife• arranged to leave Liverpool 'Street by the 11.40. John Porteous did not 'go to the Bank that morning. He wanted to lative the last few hours with • the child, whom, in all probability, he would never see again. After breakfast he took the little lad into his study. The child was excited at the idea of leaving London, and his father was loth to damp ,his jubilant spirits. However, Porteous found it impossible to smile in that room. He tad purposely chosen it as the place to say '' good-bye." There, at any rate, his purpose would not be likely to falter. The dark -shadow that lay upon his face did not escape the keen observation of the large childish eyes. After a while the two talked and played together as if nothing out of the common were about to happen. But by degrees the laugh- ing smile died from the child's face. He Threw down his jumping dog, the wonderful black animal that reared impulsively on its hind legs at the mere pressure of the thumb on indiarubber ball, and came up to his father's Side.
"Where's mummy? " he said plaintively. "She's gone away, Dickie," the wretched man replied. "When will she come back, papa ? " "She is_not_coming_back, Dickie."
, The child clapped his hands. ' " Mimmy's gone to the country," he cried joyfully. I will see her to-day? " The man did not answer.

"To-day, perhaps," the child repeated, a little doubtfully. "Not to - day, Dickie, but some day. Mamma has gone on a long journey. I told you so before, Dickie." " Yes, yes, papa, but Uncle George lives an awful way off, miles and miles and miles. Perhaps— , "Not to-day, Dickie. see her, if you are good." "But, papa—" The man seized the child and kissed him . . passionately, stifling the question on his lips. Then he took him on his knee and talked to him about the strange and beautiful things he would see in the country—the cows, the horses, the pigs. " Pigs," the child asked excitedly. "R 1 pigs? "Yes, Dickie, real pigs that grunt, so," and he imitated the animal to the best of his ability. The child's mind was wholly occupied in listening to the delightful sound'. The pig represented to him the highest form of animal' existence. But even the pig palled at last. He called for other animals, and Porteous ..gave each of them in turn, running through the whole gamut of the farm-yard. He was imitating the quack of a duck, when there was a knock at the door and a servant entered.
Some day you will

"Two gentlemen to see you, sir." "I cannot see anyone now, Mary," he replied. "Ask them to look in again. Who are they ? " "They gave no name, sir, but they said -their business was important." " Please ask them who they are and what they want. I cannot see anyone unless it is on a very urgent matter." The servant left the room. Porteous walked over to the wim:ow and stared idly into the street. Then he suddenly started, and his face grew very white. Two policemen were standing at the corner half a dozen yards to the , right of him. There. was nothing unusual in that. But a, hundred yards further down the street to the left there was another policeman, and his eyes were fixed on the window. John Porteous moved quickly away and glanced at his child. Then he laughed. " Conscience makes cowards of US all." It was only a mere coincidence. It is not unusual to see policemen in a London street. It is not extraordinary for one of them to be looking at a window. " Quack, quack," said the child in a piping voice, and waited anxiously for his father to resume the pleasing sound. The "maid re- entered the room. .
" The --gentlemen say they must see you, sir," she said, " they have come on business from the Bank." • "Their names ? " he asked.

Before the servant could reply, two men pushed past him into the room. They were both strangers. One ,of them kept his hands ' in his pockets. "We -should like a word with you, Mr. Porteous," said one of them, and then looked at triC bet v "and

_ "You cam go, Mary," he replied, take Master Dick with you." "No, no, papa," yelled the child. He was Picked up kicking and screaming,. and carried forcibly from the room. Porteous went to his desk and half opened one drawer, as though he intended to look for something. Then he turned round to the two men.

" Well, gentlemen ? " he said. One of them stepped forward and produced a paper. " John Porteous," he said, " I arrest you in the name of the King, on a charge of em- bezzlement and forgery. Do you wish the warrant read to you? "You need not trouble," Porteous replied, I have no doubt that it is in order, and that you have the authority to act on it. Unless. inderxl,you are playing 'a practical joke on me. Doubtless, there has been some mistake."

"We have a cab outside the door," the other man said, jingling something in his pocket, " will you come quietly, or must—" Porteous stealthily moved his hand to- wards the half open drawer, but before he could slip his fingers into it, he found himself covered by a revolver. " Close that drawer," the man said sharply, " the game is up. Edwards, put on the -hand-cuffs." Porteous closed the drawer, and buried his face in his hands. Resistance was useless. He knew now why there were three policemen in the street below him. Edwards advanced towards him, the handcuffs clinking as he Walked. Porteous raised his head. ', I will come quietly," he said. "My wife was buried yesterday. My little boy is going away with some relatives to-day. I expect them here every minute. Let there be no scene. See here." He locked the drawer and threw the key in the fireplace. f' Very well, sir," the man replied. He hai wife and child of his own. He realised the ~pathos of the scene, the arrest of the man the clay after his wife's funeral.
" May I write a line, to my brother-iu-law r " Certaint„ but I must read it." "You can read it."

"Very well, sir, -3-r.ou can write." John Porteous took a sheet of paper and hurriedly wrote a few lines to the Rev. George Behag. " Dear George, I am called away on urgent business. Please take Dickia away with you. Will write later. Jack Porteous."
The sergeant read it and smiled. "Urgent business," he repeated, "Ha I ha! very good." "My child," said Porteous in a low voice, "may I see him ? "

"certainly. Edwards, ring the bell." A minute or two later the servant entered. Porteous told her to bring the child down again. When the boy came, his father took him on his knee and kissed him. The men turned their back i and examined the pictures on the walls.

" Dickie-," said the wretched man, "you will have to go in a few minittes. You will be a good boy with your Uncle ? " "Yes, papa," the child answered, " and when will you come ? " " Later on, Dickie, later on." "In a few days'?"
" Perhaps, Ijickie. Good-bye, my boy." "Good-bye, papa." Porteous clasped ihe little child in his arms, kissed him passionate- ly,. and set him down on the floor.
"Now run along,: laddie," he said. The boy trotted across the floor, then turned as he reached the door.
"What do the fowls say, papa; I'ze for- gotten." , " Cluck, cluck, cluck, cluck," Porteous replied, "and cock-a-doodle-do. Good-bye, Dickie."
The boy laughed and clapped his hands. Then he vanished.
" Are you ready, sir? " said Sergeant Scott. " I am ready." * * *

Three weeks later John Porteous wag sentenced to fourteen years , penal servitude. The . judge found no extenuating circum- stances. A man of high position had abused the confidence Placed in him. The prisoner could not Mien plead poverty as an excuse. The money had not been taken to save a home from ruin, nor to replace losses incurred in a moment of reckless speculation. It had been taken, deliberately' and Consistently for some •purpose which the prisoner declined to dis- close. ,The judge had no doubt but that the nrisoner had been keeping up a second estab- Eshment. He laid particular stress on the fact that the anonymous letter which' had put the bank on the scent of the fraud was in a woman's handwriting. All attempts to dis- cover the writer had failed. This was clearly a Case where a man's own sin had found him out, and where the woman for some unknown motive had perpetrated a swift' and terrible revenge. Through all the summing up, John Por- teous stood white and silent with his-hands on the .rail of the dock. He alone knew who had written the letter, Which had brought all: his plans crashing clown about his. head. ,He did not with the world to know.- From false motives of honour he hugged the secret to his hreast. He -did not then 'realise how in the long years to come that secret .would eat away the best part of. his soid and heart and brain, and leave an empty house- for, all the devils that come up to earth from hell.
CHAPI'I7_P, V.
NEATIIEP:STONE !ALL.

• HVATIIETIS'ONE HALL, the seat of the Rte Hon. Earl of Heatherstone,. G.C.8., G.C.5.1., Privy Councillor, and one time Minister at the Court of Rome, is, as most tourists know, one of the show places of Essex. It stands on the summit of a small hill, and its great west front, 000 feet in length, looks over a finely timbeted park and across several miies Of undulating ,and wooded country. Pullin(' it the ground sloped, gently down to a high wall stone. Leyord that lay the man toad running northwards into Suffolk, and beyond that a creek, and 'beyond that again, a ‘i•iste of marsh land stretching to the sea. Ileatherstone Hall • itself was • built by the first Lord • Heatherstene in uso, and 'replaced a smaller, but more picturesque building of red brick, which had served as, a home for the family since the days of Queen Elizabeth. It was of white stone and shone as a land mark for miles around, and even far out at sea the sailars on the small vessels that passed up and down the coast Could see the light of the rising sun on its long line of windows. Inside everything was on the grand scale. The first earl had spent most of his life in a royal palace, where he had discovered many ways of making money; and his views of a house, suitable far a private gentleman, had been modelled on the ideas, of kings. The reception rooms were enormous, and so numerous that half of them were only used once or twice a year. The visitor. v.'ho was allowed to wander through them an payment of Is. when the family were away, grew heartily sick of look- ing at pictures and objects of art. It was almost as bad as a day at the Louvre. One room, a huge chamber of gold and Marble, was styled " the throne room." George I. once held a court in this regal apartment. But the, name was a standing jest .with the Hen therstone's neighbours, who lost no oppor- tunity of poking fun at the family's preten- sions to almost royal. state. Everything was in keeping with the splendour of the house. The steward would' have 'Made an excellent Lord High Chamberlain. There was a Ma.s- terOf the Horse, and a Mistress of the Robe's— a young' acting manager, invited 'to bring 'his Whole company down to the private theatre, had irreverently styled her, "the wardrobe mistress." • .

Such was the home of the Heatherstones. A family of great wealth, but of pride out of all proportion to their greatness. For if the truth be told, the family intellect never a.gain came tip to the high standard set by the first fad_ His successors were men of position and importance. Many of them held high offices of state, . but they held them • more by virtue ,of, their great wealth and influence than through any great personal talent. There were ,no fools or spendthrifts in the 'family. They v ere all 'English gentlemen ot culture and sound common sense, but they never rose to the height of genius. They were solid and hard-hcaded,• but.. common-place. Such men are.the ballast of the Empire, but it is left to men of a different breed to steer it through :the stormy seas of foreign politics.

One glorious summer's day, 20 years after ;he events narrated in the last chapter, Lord eatherstone was giving one of his three annual garden parties. Lady Heatherstone was a confirmed invalid, and had not left her 'coin for two years, and the duties of hostess devolved on I.ady Agnes Cliff e, Lord Heather- stone's only daughter. by a former wife. The party was, as Lord Barry Quy drily observed to Miss Cynthia Vox-Stanton, only a semi- state function, and Lord Harry had come .in a 4annel suit and panama hat. Yet it was no ordinary entertainment. It was, in fact, semi-political in character. A bye-election of unusual importance was agi- tating the whole of the Eastern part of the county. Lord Heatherstone represented Tory- ism in its most solid and uncompromising as- pect. Itis true that his great ancestor had been a. Whig, hut as he explained to his friends, a Whig in the time of George I. was a power in the land, and the Cause was worthy of the attention of a gentleman. Only two classes of people had been asked to the party, those whose views were un- mistakably of the right sort, and those 'who had no views at all. The latter were, of course, open to reasonable argument. Lord Harry Quy, the young man who refused to take the garden party seriously, had been chosen by Lord Heatherstone to represent the Conservative hopes of the district. He was a younger son of the Marquis of Gorehavon, whose estates joined the north side of the Heatherstone property, and was a general favpurite in the county. & genial, careless young sportsman was Lord Harry Quy, and tus chief recommendation to *parliamentary honours lay in the fact that he was not likely to do anything startling, and that he was a scratch golfer at St. Andrews. His career at Oxford had been a brilliant one. He had been President of the Union and _President of the 0.11.D.5. He had rowed 4 in the eight, and lad got his Nue at Rugger, as a smart and

powerful forward. Incidentally he had taken a 4th in Law. It was one of the traditions of his family that they should study the laws of their country. His father had taken a second, but then Lord Gorehaven had been no athlete, and apart from the exigencies of the hunting season, he had been able to devote his time to solid reading. There were over Soo people at the garden party, and before 4.30 it was felt that speeches were in the atmosphere. The tennis and croquet languished. Groups of budding poli- ticians conversed earnestly in shady corners. Lord Heatherstone had been seen to glanee at some notes in his pocket, and one of his two secretaries was surreptitiously consulting a large book tinder the shade of a rhododendron. Lord Harry Quy was nervous and irritable, and looked furtively rolind as ,though study- ing a safe line of retreat. Finally, he retired to the extreme edge of the lawn and pretended to look for lost tennis balls.

While he was engaged in this engrossing occupation, a shadow fell on the flower bed he had chosen for the scene of his operations, and he turned eharply. round on his knees. "Hallo, Lady Agnes," he cried cheerfully, ,‘ have you come to lend a hand ? " Lady Agnes laughed, and looked at her frock. _
"I am not dressed for gardening," she said," and why 'Lady Agnes this afternoon, 'sir?"

"I am such a stranger," he replied, "I do not think I have seen you more than once since you received me— receive' is, I think, the right phrase for a Court function, is it not ? " Don't be idiotic, Harry." "How many have kissed your hand since then," he said, rising to his feet and brushing some of the earth from his trousers. " I suppose you kiss duchesses on the cheek. I believe that is Court etiquette ? " "That is so," she replied, gaily, " don't you wish you were a duchess ? "‘ Lord Harry's face grew grave, and he turned slightly away from her. Then he looked her/in the face and laughed. "You are a child, Agnes," he said. "Thank you, and what are you—an M.P. ? Ha I ha I but you won't get in. And what are you then ? " "A fool, perhaps, Agnes; I know you think me one.'
The girl laughed and patted him on the back.

She was only seventeen, and very beau- tifuL She and Lord Harry Quy had been corn- paniqns from childhood. She regarded him as on of her best friends. But on his side the friendship had ripened into love,. The girl as yet guessed nothing of the tiuth, for the young man had carefully concealed it from her. Her manner towards him was that of an old playmate. As she touched him, he imperceptibly shrank from her. Poor old Harry," she said mockingly, "don't mind me. Father's going to make a speech about you in a . few minutes. You had better come and listen. It will be an antidote to my valuable opinions: You will learn that you are one of the pillars of the Empire, the friend and leader of the people, a great legis- lator—you did get honours in law, didn't you ? ' Lord Harry winced. "That's enough, Agnes," he said, with a forced smile, I daresay I scan hold my own, if it comes to a fight," and lie unconsciously squared his broad shoulders and tightened the muscles ol his hands.

"I am afraid you won't be able to fight the other candidate in the prize ring," she said, with a provoking smile. "Stacey Clarke would not be worth fighting anywhere," he replied, "and if it were not for Arthur Holme he would not get too votes. He is a fine fellow that Holme, a big strong chap, hard as nails, and a good worker. I wish we could have got him to work on our side. Do you know him ? " "No." she said," and no one seems to know much about him ; but all the fisher folks swear by him, and you know they form a large part of your electorate." "Yes, worse luck. There is no feudal hold pri these fisher chaps. They don't cafe a hang for land-owners. In most cases they own their own cottages, and they think more of a mate with a first-class certificate than an earl who does not know a main halliard from a jib sheet."

_ "Mr. Holme has the pull of you there, Harry. You ought to buy a yacht." " I hate the sea," he replied. "I should certainly make a fool of myself. This fellow plays the game well. He has bought a 15.t0n oyster smack and lives in it. No fancy yachts for him with varnished decks and a crew to do the work. He sails the boat himself, with a fisher chap that he treats as a pal. He dodges about these creeks all day -long, lives and dresses like a common fisherman. Does his electioneering for Clarke on the water and gets right to the heart of all the men. He is a clever fellow. I daresay it's all humbug, but he makes them think he is a son of the sea, and that he does not care a rap for land-lubbers. But I know something about Stacey Clarke that I intend to let out before the election." " Not a scandal, I trust," Lady Agnes replied, with a laugh. "Really you candi- dates are almost as bad as old women round a tea-table. You revel in raking up your opponent's past, and construct conclusive evidence of a fearful crime out of shreds of gossip." " No, it is not exactly a scandal, but it will knock off about to per cent. of his votes." " Tell me, if I ouglit to listen to it." "Well, he's got a motor car." Lady Agnes burst out laughing. "What a terrible thing," she said, " I hope you will reveal his secret as soon as possible." " I can tell you it is a serious matter, Agnes," the young man replied. You know the Liberals are dead against motor cars. They are one of the vices of the rich.' This is not a toy thing with bicycle wheels and a rattle that sounds as if it were going to drop to pieces, but a 24-h.p. Mercedes, an 'infernal machine.' 'An infringement of the liberty of the subject.' An old rattlebox that crawls along at eight miles an hour and stops at every hill, might be tolerated. But this swift, smoothly-running monster is an insult to all peace-loving citizens. It is a point in my favour." "1 thought you intended to buy a motor car for yourself," queried Lady Agnes. " I do," he replied, " but not till after the election. lam going to buy a car compared to which Stacey Clarke's Mercedes will be a mere toy. But at present I mean to let out about the Liberal candidate's motor. He has been trying to keep it rather quiet. It has not been out for weeks. It would not be mean to do this, eh, Agnes ? " " Certainly not," she replied, with a laugh, "but you must remember that sailors are not likely to be troubled much by the motor nuisance."

" Hum l Well, I will see about it. What on earth's that ? " A loud burst of cheering suddenly burst upon their ears. A crowd was ' gathering round Lord Heatherstone. One of his secretaries flew across the lawn to where the two young people were standing. "We must go, Agnes," Lord Harry said calmly.' "Let me see you after all t his busi- ness is over. I have something rather im- portant to discuss with you." " More important than politics? " . Yes," he replied. "In about an hour's time. Your 'father won't speak for more than that, and I can promise you that five minutes will exhaust all I have to say. I will be down by the old cottage near the East wall. You know it ? We used to pretend it was a castle on the .border, and that all the land be- yond the wall was inhabited by the enemy." " Of course I know it. Harry," she replied, "hut why walk all that way? It is half a mile, and besides, I am the hostess and cannot be rude." . .

"Oh, most of the people will go before your father's finished. And you can make some excuse to the rest. I want to get away front them all, and talk with you. I haven't had a good chat all day. If we stay here some idiot is bound to come up and ask for my news on Russia in the far East." "Well, I will bethere if I can," said the giri, with a laugh. "We must go now. I can see ' that father has started his speech. Mr,. Nlaxwell-Frinton is sidling off towards tht Aouse under the cover of the audience."
They strolled up to the crowds of people that had gathered round the great Lord Heatherstone, and separated. is Jo be continued.:
The Examiner, Thursday, April 20, 1905.
