div.head: NORTHERN UNION CUP.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION CUP.
THE SEMI-FINALS,
Warrington Conquer Bradford Again.

The utmost enthusiasm prevailed in Warrington over the semi-final tie between Warrington and Bradford at Rochdale on Saturday, and h Tea ran high that history would repeat itself, for Warrington knocked the crack Yorkshire team out a year ago. The confidence placed in the local team proved amply justified and Warring- ton qualified for the final by a very meritorious win. Glorious weather favoured the fixture and there was a fine crowd of 17,000 on the Rochdale Athletic Ground, the gate receipts being .£650. Warrington supporters assembled in strong force, and the various special trains probably conveyed not less than 3,000 people from the town of tan and wire. Biadford supporters were not so numerous, 500 being the estimate. Both teams suffered from a prominent absentee, Warrington being short of Hockenhall, and Bradford of Dechan, but the, sides were representative of the playing strength of the two clubs. Teams : Bradford.—Gunn, back; Connell. Mosby, Eae•'ers, and Dunbaviu, three-quarter backs: Marsden and Surman half backs ; Laidlaw, Greenwood, Sherratt, Thresh Barker, Turner, Smales and Rees, forwards, Warrington.—Hallam, back ; Fish,. Isherwood, Dickin- son, and Kenyon, three-quarter backs ; Davies and Brooks, half backs; Boardman, Thomas, Belton, Naylor, Shugars, Preston, Swift and Jolley, forwards. Referee.—Mr. A. Smith, Halifax. Touch judges, Messrs. W. Lancaster, Rochdale, and R. H. Moore, Oldham. Warrington lost the toss, which was not of much importance, as they had a strong sun behind them and a light breeze only, against them. Preston started with a huge kick into the Bradford quarter which was mulled by Mosby, and the speedy Warrington vanguard looked i like taking the ball over n the first minute. Gunn managed to save, however, at the expense of a scrum- mage on the line. ' Bradford got possession and a strong rush removed play to safer quarters. Play had not been in progress more than seven minutes when a sensational incident occurred. The Bradford backs got possession and passed across to the right wing. Connell was right on the touch-line and attempted to pass back to Mosby. Like a flash,Fish :lumped forward and intercepted the ball, and a second later heemerged behind the Bradfordbacks at top speed. I There was a roar of delight and excitement from the crowd, which increased as the Warrington crack out- I paced his pursuers, eluded Gunn with ease, and finally completed a great individual effort with a try behind the posts. Preston added a goal, and with a five points' lead Warrington appeared certain winners. Bradford made great efforts and frequently beat the Warrington forwards for possession., butt the backs were spotted with a certainty which destroyed all attempts at com- bined attack. There were numerous stoppages for injuries, Barker of Bradford having to come to the touch-line to have a broken finger attended to, but the Warrington men seemed to be getting the hardest knocks. A penalty against Warrington put Bradford on the attack, Surman making a poor attempt , to drop a goal. The Warrington forwards took the ball to the other end by a good dribble headed by Preston, i only to be penalised and sent back by one of Mosby's ponderous kicks. Marsden got away at centre and passed to Eagers, but the latter was promptly grassed by Brooks. Again, the ball came out on Fish's wing, and by a speedy run he secured, only to aecidentally kick' the ball in touch when picking up. Off-side play by the Bradford forwards resulted in the capture of Hallam, and Warrington were hard pressed. Marsden attempted to rush over, but was smothered, and just when the tension was greatest a timely pass from Davies and Fish enabled the latter to kick sway to the quarter line. Bradford kept up the attack, and a weik punt by Naylor was responded to by Eagers,who dropped a fine goal man unexpected sort of way. The success encouraged Bradford and Warrington had a very warm five minutes. Marsden was well watched, but he should have scored once easily. Kenyon accounted for Dunbavin who pissed back to his captain, the latter knocking-on badly a yard from the line. Warrington appreciated the let-off and Fish changed the venue with a brilliant run into the Bradford half. A high punt by Isherwood gave Dunbavin anxious moments, Dickinson grassing him near the line. Kenyon got the ball at his toes, but lost possession. and Dunbavin dribbled splendidly right to the Warring- ton line, Hallam saving the situation by inches only. Right to the interval Warringt an had to defend, Dicken- son once breaking up a passing bout in wonderful fashion, while Kenyon safely negotiated a nasty cross- kick.Finally a penalty drove Bradford back, and at half- time Warrington were leading by 5 points to 2. The Bradford forwards startel the sesond half well and Warrington for a tithe were obliged to adopt the safety game. They had to play, too, for all they were worth to cope with the desperate rushes of the Brad-, ford forwards, of whom Barker and Greenwood were very conspicuous at this particular period and Fish was temporarily disabled in a tackle by Marsden. It was ' not long however, before the Warrington forwards, roused and inspired by the desperate work of the oppos- ing pack, began to put more fire into their play, and then the game developed into a keen tussle. The War- ringtonians adopted bustling tactics, which kept Brad- ford off their usual passing game, Thomas being ever on the ball. Brooks pluckily stopped a rush and was kicked by Rees, who came under the ban of the referee, but escaped with a caution. Warrington were persistent and a penalty kick was taken by Preston at long range, The burly forward made a fine kick and landed the ball well over the bar amid great cheering. Bradford res- ponded well, and raised hopes when Dunbavin was seen careering down the left-wing. Hallam safely held him, however. Davies got away cleverly from the scrum with Fish in attendance but he failed to pass and a great opportunity was lost. Warrington were now going strongly and they drove Bradford to the line. Dickin- son ran cleverly and kicked across, Fish beating Connell and scoring as smart a try as any- one could wish to see. The referee disallowed the point amid much hooting from the c rowd. Bradford again rushed the ball down, Fish having difficulty in getting rid of it behind the goal-line. There was a scrummage close in, Davies smartly punting into touch, while two fine clearances by Hallam put Warrington on the offensive again. Kenyon ran well on the right, and Warrington were again dangerously near the Bradford lino. There was some hot work, and five minutes from time Dickenson limped off the field. In the closing stages a little unsteadiness by Warrington backs nearly cost them dear. A couple of Bradford forwards had a clear field when one of them knocked-on. Hallam again sent the ball half-way, and time was called with War- rington winners by 2 goals I try (7 points) to Bradford one goal (2 points). THE ROVERS BEAT THE RINGERS.

The other semi-final between, Hull Kingston Rovers and Broughton Rangers was played at Wakefield before 12,700 people, the receipts being £i9G. Both teams were well represented as followS: Hnil Kingston Rovers—H. Sinclair, back; W.Madley, A. W. Robinson, W. Phipps, and G. IL West, three- quarter backs; J. Gordon and J. Barry, half-backs; A. Starks, J. Kemp, A. Spackman, M. Osborne. A. Windle, F. Gorman, R.Townsley, and G. Ellis, forwards. Broughton Rangers—Poole, back; Harris, Hogg, Wilson, and tlampson, three-quarter backs; S. James and Woodward, half-backs; Trotter, Smith, Preston, Benn, Beetham, Ruddick, Whithead, and Templeton, forwards.

Referee, Mr. W. McCutcheon (Oldham). Touch judges, Messrs. F. Asquith (Wakefield) and F. W. Tattersall (Normanton). The Broughtonians won the toss, and elected to play with a light breeze and a strong sun at their backs. The Rangers backs straight away began to make good use of the advantage, and from the opening bout of kicking exchanges Sinclair, with the dun in his eyes, misflelded the ball, his side haVing to defend as a consequence. Broughton were very aggressive, and the ball was passed from Woodward to James, Wilson, and Hogg, and after the last-named bad cleared West he passed to Harris, who scored a fine try. The position was a difficult one, and the try-getter failed with the goal kick. With this three points lead the Rangers played up well, and the game improved. Starks had a shot at goal for obstruction, which proved abortive. Then Aladley broke away cleverly, only to be circumvented by a magviflcent kick on the part of Poole, who found touch well inside the Rovers' half. This was followed by Sinclair having a punt charged, but the rush of the Broughton forwards was finely checked by Phipps. Hogg tried hardato get over,but was "floored," by West. If the Broughton centre had passed to Harris a score could scarcely have been prevented. Half-time arrived with the Lancastrians leading by a try (3 points) to nil. The Rangers attacked strongly for the first few minutes .after the resumption, and Wilson was only collared inches short of the line after sprinting welL

The genie was waged in mid-field for some time, and then the Rovers got on terms through a cleverly executed movement. Gordon got the ball from a scrummxge,and passed to Medley. The wing man beat two opponents, but then found himself surrounded. Without hesitation. however, he slung the ball twenty yards across the field to Robinson, and the oval then going from Robinson to Phipps, the last-named made a splendid opening for West, who ran over with a brilliant try. Medley's goal kick was a failure. The cheers which greeted this exciting bit of combination had scarcely ceased ere they were renewed through a further success for the Rovers. A scrummage was formed near the Rangers' posts, from which the ball rolled to Phipps. Without attempting to pick it up, the Rovers' centre took a flying kick, and landed the ball over the bar,thus scoring a goal. Straight- way the Rangers worked their way to mid-field. Hampson here broke through, and after jumping over Medley, i who had fallen n an attempt to tackle him, he passed to Hogg, and the latter to Wilson,who scored a brilliant try, to the huge delight of his supporters. Harris failed at goal, but the Rangers were now leadiag by a point. Naturally the game became intensely exciting. Each side attacked in turn, but the kicking of the two full- backs, Sinclair and Poole—the latter's was, if anything, the better—nullified all efforts to score. Five minutes from the finish the last points were, however, recorded. Barry got the ball from a pack,and it went in a brilliant passing movement to West. who went over with a magnificent try. Medley kicked a goal. The Rangers tried hard to reduce the deficit, but were prevented by the clever work of Barry, Gordon Robinson, and Sinclair. Thus a brilliant game ended in a victory for the Rovers by 2 goals and 2 tries (10 points), to 2 tries (6 points).

div.head: NORTHERN LEAGUE.
div.p: THE NORTHERN LEAGUE.
First Division.
RESULTS OF SATURDAY'S MATCHES.

G. T. P. G. T.P. *Wigan -20 Oldham ...... 1 0— 2 Halifax -14 *Hunslet 1 1— 5 *Swinton -10 Runcorn Leeds -10 *St. Helens 1 1— 5 *Salford -21 Wakefield 0 0— 0 *Batley -14 Hull Leigh - 2 Played on the ground of the clubs marked WARRINGTON SWAMP BROUGHTON RANGERS.

Broughton Rangers paid their postponed visit to War- rington on Monday evening to play a League match which had an important bearing on the championship. Neither tam was quite at full strength, but Warrington were weakened the most, no less than six" " team mencoming in. There was a gate of about 3,000, Mr. J. Smith, Widnes, being the referee, and the teams were as follows :

Warrington, Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Berry and Kenyon,threequarters ; Brooks and J. Davies, half-backs ; Thomas, Preston, Cook. Belton, Forster, Harmer, Ashton, and Morrison, forwards. Broughton Rangers : Poole, full back ; Harris, Wilson, Barlow, and Hampson, three-quarters; S. James and Kiloy, half backs; Trotter, Bann, Templeton Ruddick, \Vhitehead, Cornthwaite, Thompson, and Smith, forwards.

Broughton had the advantage of the breeze, and magnificent kicking by Wilson put IVarrington on the defensive. 'lsherwood spoiled James when well on his mutating, but faulty fielding by Isherwood almost let in Wilson. Hallam, however, cleared effectively, and the home forwards forcing the ',pace Broughton were com- pelled to take up a defensive position. A magnificent run between Berry and Isherwood looked omnious until Poole stepped in and saved the situation. Berry again broke away, but Harris intercepted, and kicking over Hallam's head the ball went dead. Warrington again took tip the attack. Wilson in turn checking Isherwood and Kenyon. Fish recovered the ground splendidly, and another hot raid on the Rangers' goal almost ended in Brooks scoring, that player being forced into touch at the corner. Berry effected a magnificent run being overtaken by Wilson Hampson ran effectively, nnd placed the visitors in an attacking position, which cul- minated in Kiley scoring an unconverted try after smart passing. Interval score—Broughton Rangers, 1 try ; , Warrington, nil. Warrington were inn very aggressive mood on resuming and Fish nearly got in at the corner. S. James relieved with a fine rue to centre, where Brooks brought him down, and then the home forwards asserted themselves. They rushed the game to tbe line where Preston broke through a scrummage and grounded near the corner, the scorer failirg at goal. With the scores equal, some exceedingly fast play was witnessed, and the Rangers' line had narrow escapes, Wilson once saving gallantly when Poole had been beaten. A long kick by Fish was only poorly responded to by Poole, and Berry securing ran and passed to Hallam, who had followed up and who scored a try which hugely pleased the crowd. Warrington continued to show brilliant form, and after a superb dribble by Preston, Berry scored. The Rangers were given no rest and Brooks dashed over from a pack near the line, Fish goaling. In the last few minutes, Kenyon out-paced everyone in a long race for the ball and scored near the posts, Fish kicking another goal. The rout of Bronghton was complete. Final : Warrington, 2 goals 5 tries (19 points); Broughton Rangers, 1 try (3 points).

div.head: DISAPPEARANCE OF A ST. HELENS
div.p: DISAPPEARANCE OF A ST. HELENS
MINISTER.
A Sad Story.

Great sorrow was expressed in St. Helens on Sunday I when it became known that a message had been received from Cornwall reporting the disappearance of the Rev. Stanley Osborne, a newly-appointed Wesleyan minister in the town. Mr. Osborne was appointed as fifth minister in the circuit, immediately after last year's Conference, , and came straight from college to take up this, his first charge. He soon made himself known as a capable and ; earnest young pastor, the congregations at various churches on the circuit evidently holding him in high regard. Evidently his devotion to work was greater than his strength to bear his burdens, and about a month I ago he suffered a severe breakdown. He obtained leave I , from the superintendent minister of the circuit,the Rev. I Thomas Hollis, and at once went off to Padstow, Corn- ' , wall, where his mother and sisters reside, it being , anticipated that he would have sufficiently recuperated within a fortnight to permit of his return to duty. This wAs not so, however, and during the past fortnight Mr. Hollis received one or two very strangely-worded letters. Nevertheless, he was expected back on Saturday in order to take the service at Sutton-road on Sunday morning and the evening service at Wesley Chapel. In the meantime Mr. Hollis received a tele- I grain on Friday and a letter on Saturday, from which it. was very evident that the mind of the unfortunate I young man—be was hut twenty-four years of age- was very considerably deranged. This naturally upset the superintendent minister, and he feared that Mr. Osborne was in a most grave state. That this anxiety was justified only too fully appeared yesterday on the receipt of a message that Mr. Osborne had disappeared. On Saturday morning he went out with the intention of calling on his doctor, and as he did not return either that night or Sunday morning a search party set out to look for him, it being feared that some serious accident had befallen the young , , minister. Finally his hat and umbrella were discovered I on the edge of the cliffs, while pinned down by a stone I to keep it from being blown away was a sheet of paper, , on which was written the following words:— ; "My dear Mother and Sisters.—Pray forgive me. ' The Lord has heard my cry. He knows T have not been accountable for my doings recently. When left alone I am simply mad; but I am forgiven, and lam now simply raving and am going over." " Going over" too evidently referred to the cliffs. i , and the mother of Mr. Osborne is prostrated with the• f thought that her son has been driven by his sufferings to put an end to them in that terrible fashion. Search is being made for any further sign of the missing minister, but the worst fears are generally entertaine,

div.head: Warrington Man's Singular Death.
div.p: Warrington Man's Singular Death.

On Monday there was reported to the Liverpool city coroner the death of Charles Parry, 08, Tiber- street. The deceased was a lodger, and was forty-one years of age. He was discovered lying at the bottom of the stairs. The horse ambulance was called, and the deceased was removed to the Royal Southern Hcrspital,, where it was found life was extinct. Deceased had been employed by Messrs. Crosfiela, soap manu- facturers, and bad a wife and three children living in Warrington. He had been separated from his wife for some time.

div.head: RADIUM AND SNAKE POISONS.
div.p: RADIUM AND SNAKE POISONS.

Professor ciaaveau announced in a communication to the Parisian Academy of Sciences that radium emanations have the property of destroying the toxicity of serpent venom. Viper and cobra poison, if sabmitted to the action of radium, is said tc lose its virulence after fifty or sixty hours of exposure.

div.head: CHILDREN'S MENTAL ACTIVITY.
div.p: CHILDREN'S MENTAL ACTIVITY.

The mathematical aptitude of boys and girls of eight to fifteen has been compared, by Professor V. Mercante, of Buenos Ayres, by tests of quickness in reading numbers and in arithmetical operations. A curious discovery is that an abnormal activity of memory exists at about thirteen, followed by a period of intellectual depression, and at fourteen by a sudden leap in creative imagination and reasoning power.

div.head: NEW ADHESIVE.
div.p: A NEW ADHESIVE.

A new adhesive that has gained popularity in France is a mixture of caseine and tannate of lime. In preparing it, a solution of tannin is precipitated with milk of lime, the liquid is poured off, and the precipitate is slowly dried. This dry calcium tannate is then ground in a mill with dry caseine in the proportion of one to ten times its weight, according to the use to be made of the adhesive. The compound dissolves in water, petroleum oils, and carbon bisulphide, adheres very strongly, and is applied as a paste with water.

div.head: SUN SPOTS.
div.p: SUN SPOTS.

The Abb6 Morena:, in a paper to the Academy of Sciences, Paris, on the constitution of sun spots, propounds.a theory of the phenomenon. Ile regards a spot as a superheated region of the sun, where the phenomena of radiation no longer exist, because the intense heat favours dissociation of the chemi- cal matter. If the surface layer of the photosphere is alone affected we have "veiled spots." If the dissociation is deeper there are layers of clouds one over the other, containing new chemical com- binations, as in the penumbral rays.

div.head: DARKNFRS OF OCEAN DEPTHS.
div.p: DARKNFRS OF OCEAN DEPTHS.

How far does sunlight penetrate beneath the sur- face of the sea? has been asked many times, and now the camera has answered the question. By exposing the tnost sensitive photographic plates at varfous depths it has been ascertained with definite- ness how much sunlight there is in the water with eaehl descending foot. There is a point at which no action of light is found, and that point is 600 ft. under the surface. Below that is absolute dark- ness, and the only way in which the most delicate plate can be affected in that black abyss is to send down an electric light with it.

div.head: MODERN\ PROSPECTOR.
div.p: THE MODERN\ PROSPECTOR.

The old prospectors or "metal hunters" of America, armed with pick, shovel, and pan, are now succeeded by regular parties with pack mules, a geologist, a chemist, maps, and scientific ap- paratus. The old "pocket bunter" and ordinary prospector dug the soil of a mountain side, or gathered the sand of a stream and washed it in his pan to find the yellow streak of gold. The modern prospector drills the rock and sinks a shaft by ex- plosive cartridges ignited by electricity from a chemical battery, which also serves to separate the precious metal from the dross by electrolysis. A chemical laboratory for analyses, and mercury for amalgamation, are part of the outfit.

div.head: CONTENTS OF MAN-OSTRICH'S STOMACH.
div.p: CONTENTS OF MAN-OSTRICH'S STOMACH.

Dr. Warbasse, of the German Hospital, New York, in the "Annals of Surgery," describes a "man-ostrich" operated on for tetanus caused by foreign bodies in the stomach. He gained his living by swallowing nails, penknives, &c. In 1900 he was seized with convulsions, and two keys, two chains, fourteen nails five hair-pins, and over 120 ordinary pins were taken from his stomach. He continued his calling, and in 1904 entered the German Hospital for tetanic convulsions. The radiograph shewed a body like a nest in him, and on opening the stomach it was found to consist of seven keys, seven penknives, twenty nails, a little spoon, a button-hook, an ordinary pin, and two watch chains. The penknives had been swallowed five and the button-hook ten months before. Two months after the operation the "man-ostrich" left the hospital cured, but whether be resumed his gastronomic feats is not stated.

div.head: WITY WE FAINT AND ANIMALS DO NOT.
div.p: WITY WE FAINT AND ANIMALS DO NOT.

The most probable reason, said Dr. Lockhart Mummery in the course of a lecture, why syncope or fainting is peculiar to the human subject is that the nervous system of man is much more highly developed and, more delicately balanced than is the case in animals, and also that man owing to his upright position has his circulation more under the influence of gravity, and so has to depend almost entirely upon his nervous system for the proper maintenance of cerebral circulation. In man any sudden disturbance of the higher vaso-motor centres which puts them even momentarily into abeyance allows gravity to act upon the circulation, and as we should expect is followed by a sudden fall in the cerebral blood pressure, resulting in anemia of the brain and syncope. In animals, how- ever, we should not expect this to happen, as their horizontal position does not give gravity the same advantage in respect of their cerebral circulation.

div.head: SEEN OR HEARD BEFORE.
div.p: SEEN OR HEARD BEFORE.

"Seen before" is the name given to a curious mental impression some feel of being in precisely the same circumstances before, although that is not the case. An instance of the phenomenon was brought before the Society of Neurology, Paris, by M. Ballet. A woman, on going into a room, before she has time to examine persons or articles in detail, feels sure that she recognises some of them; in other words, that she has seen them before. The "heard before" is another variety of the phenomenon, which, according to Ballet, implies a state of psych-asthenia, or cerebral in- sufficiency, and is not an exaggeration of memory. It may, however, be a defect of perception rather than of memory. Perhaps, after all, remarks the Globe, it is nothing more than imperfect or partial suggeztion. We mean that something in the thing seen or heard awakens or suggests an old recol- lection of something like it, and so gives a momentary impression that it has been seen or heard before. The phenomenon does not seem very uncommon, and if we are not in error Christopher North once threw out the explanation that it might be caused by one hemisphere of the brain acting a little behind the other so as to produce a sort of double consciousness. Wigan drew attention to it as far back as 1844.

div.head: TEE "BILIOUS TEMPERAMENT."
div.p: TEE "BILIOUS TEMPERAMENT."

A "bilious temperament" is supposed to be irritable, brusque, choleric, or, as Hamlet said, "splenetic and rash." The Journal de Physiotherapie has published results of experiments made to trace the source of this temperament. Frogs were inocu- lated with bile, and their muscles excited by elec- tricity. It appears that small doses of bile, or constituents of bile, in the blood excite the muscles, but large doses have rather the contrary effect, as in the case of paralysing poisons. A small proportion of bile in the blood makes the muscles contract suddenly and intensely when electrically excited. A strong dose makes them act rapidly, but not so energetically, and these effects seem due to bilirubine in the bile. Its action on the heart requires more investigation, but the motor nerves are also excited by it. It appears, moreover, that the bilious and cholemic are subject to hyper-excitability of the brain and hyper-activity of the mind when the cholemia is weak and recent; but when. the

cholemia is of old standing and intense, especially if the nervous system was already enfeebled, the contrary effects of depression, asthenia, intellectual and moral uneasiness, dysphoria, lassitude, tend- ency to melancholy and sadness, are observed. There are thus two sorts of "bilious subject," one produced by feeble cholemia or small doses of one, and characterised by hyper-excitability and hyper-activity; the other owing to larger doses of bile, and characterised by melancholy, asthenia, sad general depression.

div.head: EXAMINEE.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE.
APRIL 20th. 1905.
Jr would seem that UNIONISTS' th e much-desired
PATCHED-UP TRUCE. unity of the Unionist

party is to be re- stored by a familiar piece of conjuring. Mr. i CHAMBERLAIN, at all events, retains a touching faith in his capacity to make things quite different from their real nature by calling them convenient names. For instance, the taxation of food is to be relieved of all obnoxious elements by the simple device of assertiug that it is not protective taxa- tion. On the celebrated half sheet of notepaper, Mr. BALFOUR declared that he was not in favour of raising home prices. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is de- lighted with the idea. Sreither is he in favour of raising home prices. On referring again to that half sheet, he finds that Mr. BALFOUR is in favour of closer commercial union with the Colonies and of a Conference to consider what shape the union ought to take. Then, why all this misunderstanding, dear friends ? M. CHAMBERLAIN and Mr. BALFOUR are aiming at the same objects. They have not the smallest desire to impose Protection duties. Their duties ' will be retaliatory and preferential, but never never will they protect anything or anybody. We have had all this pretty game before, but Mr. CHAMBERLAIN seems to have just discovered it. He had a long conference with Mr. BALFOUR the other day, and propounded this notable scheme as a brand new idea. Something at all events must be done to reconcile the Tariff Reforms, with the rest of the party, so as to present a united front at the General Election whenever Mr. BALFouR finds that he can really keep this Parlia- ment going no longer. There have been rumours that Mr. B&Lroua cherished the hope of turning the Duke of DEVON- SHIRE into this policy of taxation, which is to be not for revenue, and yet not protective. Elowevec, the manner of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S attack on the Duke scarcely points a reconciliation. He and Mr. BALFOUR may persuade each other that foreign I

imports can be chscked without any return to IProtection, but the Duke is not a good subject for conjuring tricks. It is made a grievance that he stayed so long in the Cabinet when the two wizards had got to work. He is reminded that he said our system of Free Trade was not as free as it ought to be; but the Duke had his eyes opened at last to what was really meant by Mr. BALFOIJR'S "economic notes" and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S juggling with the corn duty. He came to the conclusion that althouh it would be well if it were possible to make foreign countries lower their tariffs, there was no machinery for such an enterprise which would not land this country in Protection. The conjurors want us to believe that some economic system can be devised which would have all the advantages of Protection, and Free Trade, too, without being in the least protective. It will be even better than Free Trade. It will be Freer Trade as time goes on. It will even develop into Freest Trade. The conjurer will first produce cabbages out of the hat, and then pineapples. All this make-believe may be good enough:to patch up an electioneering truce between the " whole-hoggers " and tho "little piggers," but it cannot take in anybody who lies grasped the simple economic elements of the coatroversy. As we look abroad we see Protection in various "degrees, but it is always the same in kind. It is extravagant in Russia and moderate in Belgium, but no foreign Protectionist has ever pretended that th 3 system is Protection in one country and not in another. If Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S policy were to succeed the whole world would recognise that we had become Protectionist, and would take its measures aczordingly.

A keen contest for the chairmanship invested the annual meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians with particular interest. The candi- dates nominated were Mr. William • Hickman and Mr. Jacob Billingo and the last-named was elected by a majority of three votes. From the standpoint of length of service both members had practically equal claims, but there were one or two points which, in our view, told strongly in Mr. Hickman's favour and would have justified the Board in con- , ferring the nonour upon him. In the first place he has already rendered good service in the vice-chair, and there is every reason to believe that he would have applied himself diligently to the duties of the higher office. It should also be borne in mind that a country guardian has occupied the chair during the past year, and Warrington, as the most important part of the Union, might well have considered itself ' entitled to a turn on this occasion. In view of Mr. Hickman's opposition to the Workhouse extension sciietne his election would no doubt have given general satisfaction to the Warrington rate- payers.

The touch of romance which attached to high- way robberies in the past does not give an attrac- tion to the attack on the North Mail driver near Newcastle. The Dick Turpiffs of the old days were not only chivalrous towards women,they were gentle towards men, in so much that they did not excercise superfluous force. The unhappy New- castle driver was clouted on tue head with a stick when his assailants clearly had him at their mercy, and altogether he seems to have had a very bad time. There was a brutality about the perform- ance, se far as can be learnt, which is likely to make it serious for the assailants if they can be arrested and convicted. Moreover, it is a particularly bad offence to steal his Majesty's mails, for no one can tell how far-reaching the mischief may be. The discomfiture and disarrange- ment of plans, the false judgements and the :suspicions, that may arise from the failure of correspondence mean a lot of trouble. It is for this reason that post-office officials, when they lapse under temptation,are so sharply punished.

In this, Nelson's centenary year, special interest attaches to any remarks on the subject which one so intimately acquainted with the modern Navy as Lieutenant Carlyon BeHairs has to make. Addre3s- ing a company of Nelson's own county men, Lieutenant Bellairs said that if to Blake is due the 3reation of the regular Navy, it is to Nelson that we owe the creation of the soul of that Navy. ,The true inwardness of this saying only a Navy man knows. For the civilian,however, the Nelson monu- ment in St. Pant's and the Museums at Greenwich provide eloquent commentary. The monument gives Britannia, like a lecture in the naval schools, pointing young midshipmen to the old sea hero ; and that is precisely what Britannia, as the Trafalgar models, relics, and paintings at Green- wich suggest, is doing to-day, and will continue to do as long Hs the British Navy lasts. Nelson is the soul and spirit of that .Navy. He created its comradeship. Invited to choose his officers, he could reply with confidence "Choose yourself, my Lord ; the same spirit animates the whole profession." He possessed, too, that quality of great leaders, fear- lessness of responsibility—dangerous, indeed, where orders are ignored and matters political undertaken, but, with Nelson's brain and dash, providing the classic argument for initiative. Before the Japanese, he had weighed the tempera- ment and character of adversaries, and his rule for meeting Russians—to attack the head of the lino —was the plan which won Togo his victory on August 10th. A French historian has said that a 1 nation is safe in its greatest crisis if it can but remember its own history. Lieltenant Belliars would paraphrase this dictum, and say we are safe so long as we can really and truly say, " We always remembered Nelson."

* * * We hear that the Progressive Labour League is making arrangements for a series of public meetings to be held early in May. The principal speakers will be Mr. H. Vivian and Mr. Fred Maddison who created such a favourable impression by their stirring and well-reasoned addresses at the ward meetings last week. Mr. A.H.Crosfield is also expected to be present. * * * Our readers' attention is especially drawn to Mr. Henry Whitham's article in another column on " The Beef Trust," the article being another of the series headed" Frenzied Finance.' Mr. Whitham's story of the way capital is banded together, and employed to plunder the small trader and the consumer is a remarkable revelation of the corruption existing in America's inner commercial circles.

* * * Speaking at Southport on Monday night,' Mr. Marshall Hall, M.P., Conservative member for the seaside town, perpetrated a couple of bulls which deserve to be recorded. Referring to the Unionist Party, he said: "Our object is to unite it into the one cohesive mass it always has been!" Another " bull " was: If I had two houses equally good, and one was a little better than the other! "

* * * There was such a marked absence of opposition at last evening's debate in connection with the Social Service league that Mr. Lloyd Jones for the time being "turned Tory" and made quite a touching appeal on behalf of the Government which was being so unsparingly criticised. His Conservative con- victions (?) however, were apparently very unsettled, as he voted both for and against a continuance in office of the present Government.

** * •• A striking example of the value of trade unions to the worker is afforded by the Amalgamated Society of Engineers which has 90,000 members and an income of nearly S.:400,000 per year. During the year 1904, no less a sum than £127,000 was paid in assisting unemployed members, while sick pay and superannua- tion, absorbed £53,097 and .9.,111,307, respectively. The engineer who is not a member of this Society must be as blind as the mole to his own interests.

* * * Manchester is this year receiving £50,000 from the Gas profits and £46,000 from the Tramways profits, in relief of the rates. What a vast undertaking the Manchester tramways have developed into. The weekly income is over £12,000, and the number of passengers about 2,000,000. There is no comparing these figures with the statistics in Warrington, but A is getting about time the tramways earned something for the ratepayers. As a luxury they are at present, somewhat expensive. . .

* * * Lady Warwick is a socialist. The baptism of the infant daughter of Viscount and Viscountess Helmsley took place at the St. James's on Monday. Her Royal Highness, the Princess of Wales,the Hon. Mrs. Gervase Beckett, and Lord Brooke were the sponsors, and tho child received the names of Mary Diana. Mary Diana is the grand-daughter of Lady Warwick. There are ; tpany barriers to break away before the childreu of the poor people can have the same privileges as those of the wealthy socialists. Socialism !!!

* * * Evan Roberts, the Welsh 'revivalist has beea examined by four medical men. Their certificate reads as follows :—" We have examined Mr. Evan Roberts. We find him mentally and physically quite sound. He is suffering from the effects of overwork. We consider it advisable that he should have a period of rest." We wonder why it was thought necessary to have him medically examined. Surely, there has been nothing unseemly about his conduct in Liverpool? However, a rest may do him good—and will:do the converts no harm.

* * * Mr. J. C. Sutton, the esteemed clerk to the Warrington Board of Guardians, possesses a long and worthy record of public service. For thirty-seven years in succession, he informed the Board on 'Wed- nesday, he has fulfilled the duty of presiding at the annual meeting, pending the election of Chairman. His has been an active career and he recalls with pardonable pride that it is sixty years since he first became a junior clerk. The Board has in him a highly valued official whose knowledge of the Poor Law is perhaps second to none.

'Warrington Volunteers are to renew their acquaint- ance with Salisbury Plain this year, it having been decided that the battalion shall encamp there from July 29th to August 13th. It may not be generally known that" pay "in camp, which will be the same as last year, has always been a gratuity and not a payment that can be demanded. Deductions may be made at the discretion of the Commanding Officer for misconduct and neglect of duty, and all fines and de- ductions are handed over to the general committee of regimental institutes.

* * * The new Vicar of Daresbury, the Rev. T. T. Lee- Jones, who has just taken up his duties in the Ches- hire parish, is an enthusiastic sportsman. At Gains- borough, where he has held the honoured post of headmaster of the Grammar School, he has been an active member of the cricket and golf clubs, and, says a local paper, " A more popular clergyman has never worn the cloth in Cleveland." Prior to leaving for Daresbury the rev. gentleman was the recipient of handsome gifts from the athletic organizations and also of a cheque from the governors, students at the Grammar School, the parents, and inhabitants of the town.

* * * The "Young Woman" for February contained an interesting interview with We. Crooks, the wife of Mr. Will Crooks, M.P. She has been and still is a worker. After leaving school she became a domestic servant, then a housekeeper, afterwards a nurse in the Poplar Infirmary and finally the wife of the " poplar "Member of Parliament. Not being able to afford a servant she does all her own work but finds time however "to play a friend in need to any of her neighbours who want help and sympathy, and does much to make Poplar tolerable." Would that we had more Members of Parliament who could boast of such democratic and willing help-meets. , * * When a railway guard gets 3,600 invitations to "have a drink " in the course of It months, he stands in need of the help of such an organization as the United Kingdom Railway Temperance Union, vihich has just held its annual meeting in London. There is no branch of employment in which sobriety is more essential than on the railway, and it will be a source of gratification to all reformers to know that the Union has 22,615 members. There is a scarcity of funds, however, and if the travelling public would devote some of its spare cash to the Railway Temperanca Union instead of making thousands of offers of "a drink" to the drivers and guards it would be doing an excellent service and insuring itslown safety at the same time.

Farewell Supper. There was a pleasant gathering at the Old Coffee House, Horsemarket-street, on Monday evening, when about thirty members of the Warrington branch of Wheelwrights and Smiths assembled to bid farewell to two of their comrades (Bros. Withenlisaw and Dale) who are leaving for Canada. Supper was served, and the after proceedings were presided over by Bro. Weaver who gave the toast "Success to the Warrington Branch," the Secretary (Bro. Lewis) responding. The toast " Our departing brothers" was also honoured and a musical programme was then submitted. Songs were given in credible style by Bros. McGarty, -Berney, Foster, Unsworth, Meacock and Bibby, several of the items being of a humorous description. Bro. Withenshaw acted as accompanist. The toast of "The hostess" (urs. Brown) having been honoured, Bro. liVithenshaw returned thanks to the company for their good wishes. He would remember the Warrington branch with feelings of pride and pleasure when he reached far- away Canada. The singing of "Auld Lang Syne " brought an enjoyable evening to a close. * * Doe the octopus like plums, and have plums got feelings? These are not the problems of an artful Government Inspector of Education designed to. puzzle I the elementary school child's brain, but merely ques- tions which naturally arise from Mr. H. J. Westbrook's spmewhat mixed metaphor at the Stockton Heath Parish Council meeting on Monday. Mr. Westbrook likened the Village—pardon! *e should say townlet— ,to a "comely plum" and Wtirrington to a rapacious monster with octopus hands ready to pluck the plum, which. is alleged to hold strong objections. We really don't know which is in the worst plight—the plum waiting to be seized, the monster confronted with au attractive but indigestible repast, or the metaphorical Mr. Westbrook.

The annual report of the Independent Labour Party states that the committee look forward with confidenc( to the result of the General Election, believing thal the. .most important result will be a new party .ir British politics destined to play a great and increasu4 part in controlling the affairs of the nation.

* * Mr- Winston-Churchill, * M.P., when talking to Mr. Herbert Vivian, on the terrace at the House of Commons as reported in the "Pall Mall Magazine" said "If I had my way, I would abolish all this nossens. The House of Commons should be a place • of business not a place, of entertainment. Many members make this the one resort for their hospitality —Tea on the Terrace ! "

* * * Alderman Bennett is rapidly accustoming himself to the duties of chairman of the Education Com- mittee and on Monday be conducted the meeting of • the authority with a much firmer hand. The mem- bers, too, did not show that disposition to "all talk at once" which marked the annual meeting, and the Proceedings passed off in quite a dignified way. o 4:4 o A resident of Penketh seems rather hurt that the -ancient custom of "walking the boundary" has been • abandoned of Late years. The Parish Council has to solemnly consider the advisability of revising the : practice so that before long we may hope to see a :Procession of councillors endeavouring to maintain its ''llignity while negotiating the obstacles of a varied nature which may present themselves on the boundary. * * * • "If you have got nothing else from this Govern- ment you have got two taps !" said Mr. Howes at the 'meeting of the Social Service League on Thursday. He Was referring to the meddling with army headgear Which has occupied the attention of the War Office, Whilst less trivial matters have been neglected. Tommy Atkins' opinions on the " Broderick ' and other innovations of headgear, are, we understand, not fit for i.ublication.

* * The Museum and Library Committee can hardly avoid taking some steps in regard to the nuisance at the public - reading room caused by the betting fraternity, now that the Pre° Church Council has forwarded a solemn resolution thereon. The practice of blacking out the betting news from papers in the Public reading-room ought to be general. It is no Part of a municipal authority's business to provide facilities which only tend to an increase of the betting evil.

* * * The days of chivalry are not ended ! Last week, as We had occassion to note, the Mayor laid himself open to the grave charge of slighting the ladies. As if to dissociate himself from his worship's expression, Mr. -May has taken up the cudgels on behalf of the fair sex and at Monday's meeting of the Education Committee was anxious to declare that "he hoped he was a friend of all the lady teachers" and promised to do his utmost to secure just treatment for them. With such a staunch champion the lady teachers " may " feel cr.l 'oven greater sense of security. * * * Mr. F. Fearneley,speaking at a meeting held under 'the auspices of the Conservative Labour Party the other evening, concluded by saying that ' the Govern- ment had done ntuch!not only for the working classes, but for the honour ancKintegrityof the British Empire." Eancy that —"the honour and integrity of the British Empire." Mr. Fearaeley is fond of joking, but to be oontinually at it is bad for the party he represents. We wonder whether he has ever heard of Chinese slavers, in South Africa. He may not. Would some kind, benevolent, Conservative friend waken him! He is getting hypnotised by his own verbosity. *s* The Junior Conservatives are evidently not enamoured with the prospect of debating the interest- -313g topic: "Should the Government resign," seeing that they have declined to meet the Social Service League for the purpose. Any excuse being better than none, the immature disciples of Protection have fallen back upon the old device of abusing the other isicle. They could not see their way to attend the debate because "it appears the League is not the "a-political organisation which it originally professed 10 be." As the Rev. H. Dannico remarked, they artist be "either ashamed of their principles or of their party," or they would be prepared to defend both under any circumstances.

div.p: Burning Fatality. Charles Davies, 4, Anderson's Cottages, Penketh, died at the Warrington Infirmary on Wednesday from burns accidentally received on the same day.
• PUBLIC BEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASIIIRE:AdVt. St. Austin's Ward. .

The vacancy in this Ward, occasioned by the elevation of Councillor Tinnion to an aldermanic seat, has not yet been formally declared. The Conserva- tives have selected Dr. Joseph as their candidate, but up to the present no opponent has been decided upon. Music Licenses for Easter. At the Warrington Police Court on Monday the magistrates granted the following applications for temporary music licenses :—David Walsh, Crown and Sceptre; R. Perdu, Higher Angel; Thomas Potter, King's Anna; John C. Rigby, Queen's Hotel; Thomas Cooper, Blue Bell; George Lang, Rose and Crown. H. M. AsmoN's Lire TONIC is the KING or TONICS.-63, SANKEY Sr., WARRINGTON.—Advt. An Easter Attraction Placed high in the list of Easter attractions are the entertainments which will next week be "give R in the Parr Hall by the New Century animated picture com- pany. This is the company the visit of which to Warrington a short time ago was attended with such success. Amongst the many excellent pictures which will he shoun is a (series of animated views depicting the chief incidents in the war in the far East, and a novel item "Every cloud has a silver lining." After- noon performances will be given on Monday, Thursday and Saturday. "PREMIER" CYCLES at 9 guineas for Best Grade, unsurpassed.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. A Hardened Offender. • At the Police Court to-day Patrick Burke, 3,Fennell street, was sent to gaol for six months for exposing his children.—Mr. Browne on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., stated that Burke had been previously before the court on a similar charge. On Monday he set fire to the bed in which his wife and children were sleeping, and then turned them out of the house. The case was a bad one and it was hopless to expect Burke to re- form.

Death of Mrs. KelsalL The death occurred at her residence, Queen street, Warrington, on Saturday, of Mrs Kelsall (widow of the late Mr. Richard Kelsall, formerly of Boggart House Farm,Burtonwood).The deceased lady,who was 78 years of age and widely respected had been in a delicate state of health for some time. The funeral took place in the churchyard at Burtonwood on Monday, when there was a good attendance ot relatives and friends which spoke highly of the esteem in which Mr. Kel- sall was held. The Rey. A. M. Mitchell, vicar, officiated. '

The Allegation of Corruption. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee on Monday, Aldermen Pierpoint and Sinethurst, and Councillors Ashcroft, Lord, Stott, Clegg, and Craik were appointed a sub-committee " to investigate the charge made by Alderman Tinnion at a recent meeting in reference to a member of the C nporation attempt- ing to induce an, individual to adopt a course by which that individual could make a sum of money out of the Corporation and the councillor to be benefited thereby to the extent of £100."

Advt. - - The New Assistant Markets Inspector. A special meeting of the Markets Committee was held on Monday afterooon at the Town Hall, under the presidency of Alderman Hutchinson, to consider the appointment of an assistant Markets Inspector to I fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. C. E. Place. There were numerous applications for the position and the following candidates were selected to I appear hefore the committee on Monday : Messrs. I Percy C. Bailey, Joseph Massey, Alfred Rogers,George Rushton, J. H. Wildman and Harold Brtzell. The choice of the committee fell upon Mr. Wildman. All the six candidates are Warrington; ans. "PREMIER" CYCLES at 12 guineas with change ! spot.... gear &0., mequalled.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 1 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. 1 Breakfastless School Children. I There is no falling off in attendance at the Ragged School breakfast table. On Monday, 58' were present, Tuesday 62, Wednesday 69, Thursday 64. Only five fresh children have been for the first time this week,the rest presented themselves more or less regularly each morning of the preceding fortnight. The Executive thankfully acknnidledge a donation of six loaves from Mrs. Lawrence,Willis-street.No further donations have been received, and unless there is some response this week-end, the Ragged School workers (who have all willingly given their services) will have to cease their efforts. This will mean about 60 known cases of ' children going to school each morning without a meal or with an insufficient one. The expenses of the breakfasts (with the exception of the donations already , acknowledged) have bean defrayed by coppers collected in other localities. Pusmc BENEFIT. UNDER VIE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASFURE.—AdVI. Drowning Fatality at Lymm. An inquest was held at the Court House, Lymin, on Monday on the body of Esther Turner (8), daughter of Walter Turner, mariner, Croady's-cottages, Canal- side, Lymrn, whci was drowned in the canal on April 15th.—Robert Littler, labourer, said deceased was his niece.. About six o'clock on Saturday, he sent her to the village for some cigarettes and told her to be sharp back. lie waited hall an hour and then went along the canal to meet her, but heard that her cape had seen picked up by her sister, who had found it in the water. With the assistance of P.C. Hughes dragging opera- tions were commenced and continued until midnight. I Early in the morning, witness again commenced dragging with the help of Samuel Ogden and recovered the body at s.4o.—.There was no evidence to show how the child got into the water, and the jury returned an open verdict of "Found drowned."

UNDER THE CLOCK for Good Booxs.—Advt. Good Friday Services. Good Friday observance at Warrington will be on much the usual lines. By the Anglican and Roman Catholic churches thb day is looked upon as the most solemn of the year and there will be numerous services. At Wycliffe Congregational Church the occasion will also be fittingly observed by the holding ,of d special service in the morning. The Rev. John Yonge will preach. In accordance with a well-estab- lished custom the members of Bold-street Wesleyan Church will celebrate their foreign missionary anniversary. The Rev. M. F. Crewdson (late mission- ary in India and Africa) will preach at a service in the , morning, and in the evening the annual public meet- ing will be held. Mr. J. Upson will preside and the Ispeakers will be the Rev. M. F. Crewdson and the Rev. Marshall Simon (late missionary in Africa). The lhree hours service will be the chief feature at several of the Anglican Churches, and from 12 to 3 there will be addresses on the seven last words from the Cross. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS 111LNERAL A SRS,—Advt. Church of England Temperance Society. The operations of the Dioceson Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society having been extended in many directions, it has been decided to raise a large sum of money to help the work. It is therefore pro- posed to hold a grand Diocesan Bazaar in St. George'S Hall, Liverpool, on Novemeer 21st, 22nd and 23rd, in aid of all the departments of the work. There will probably be fourteen i stalls managed by about one hundred ladies, connected with Liverpool, Bootle, Southport, Birkdale, St. Helens, Huyton, Roby, Ormskirk, Warrington &c. The president of the local stall is Mrs. John Fairclough and associated with her are Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Peter Rylands, Mrs. Morley Stevenson, Mrs. Carleton, Miss Bessie Dutton, Mrs. Ralph Johnson, Miss Massy, the Misses Tinsley and Miss Alice Daunt, secretary. The society has many claims on the liberality of Warrington and district, as it provides Mr. Henry Taylor our Police Court Missiohary in connection with its Police Court and Prison Gate Mission. The society's Women's Tem per an co Home in Liverpool , has taken from Mr. Taylor many women from War- rington for periods of six months each. The day school lecturer of the society visits all the Warrington schools—Church of England, Roman Catholic, &c:, the arrangements for winch are made by the Director of Education, Mr. Moore Murray. The town also has the benefit of other branches of the society's work.

div.head: Examiner, Thursday, April 20,1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Thursday, April 20,1905.
SHOULD THE GOVERNMENT RESIGN?
JUNIOR CONSERVATIVES DECLINE TO DISCUSS THE QUESTION.
" Either Ashamed of Their Principles or of Their Party."

Through Mr. Herbert Hayes the members of the War- rington Junior Conservative Association were recently invited by the Rev. H. Dunnico to join with the mem- bers of the Warrington Social Service League In a debate upon the question as to whether the present Government is or is not worthy of the confidence of 1 the people. The debate was held in the Golborne-street schoolroom last night but before any discussion was I entered upon the Rev. H. Dunnico read the following letter which he had received from Mr. Herbert Hayes: —"With regard to our conversation at Orford-lane on Wednesday evening last, I have carefully considered the question of attending with a few friends your debate on the Social Service League at Golborne-street chapel. From information which I have gathered, however, it appears to me that your i league s not the non-political organization which it originally professed to be, but that it is being utilized to further the interests of the Radical candidate for the borough, while the methods of working the Warrington branch of the Social Service League are also not free from suspicion in this respect. On these grounds and after careful consideration—what- ever my sympathies may be with respect to the real object of the League—l cannot myself attend or recommend any of my friends to\ be present at your debate." "As president oi this League" said Mr. Dunnico having concluded the rending of the latter, "I cannot permit this letter of Mr. Hayes' to pass without comment. The interests of the National Service League may be safely left to those who are rdsponsible for its proceedings. I can only say that so far as the refer- ence to our League is concerned it is one I deeply resent. We have never contended that this League was non-political in fact

div.head: WE ARE INTENSELY POLITICAL
div.p: WE ARE INTENSELY POLITICAL

I and we exist for the sole purpose of educating the people in the science of politics. What we do contend is that we are non-party political. To demonstrate that ' we haveprovided an open platform for the free expression of opinion of men of every shade of opinion.' We have had Alderman Bennett amongst us, Mr. H. P. Hughes and others. I have myself invited Mr. Hayes and his party to come and take • part in our debate but they have refused. In view of this it is unfair and dishonest to write such a letter as the one just received. Again and again the vote of this class has gone against the convictions of the league but that has not effected us in the least. If I were dis- posed to adopt the attitude of Mr. Hayes I should say that tho reason they are not here is because they have no opinions to express or such as they will not bear the light of day. It seems as though the Warrington Con- servatives were ASHAMED EITFIER OF THEIR PREICIPLES OR THEIR PARTY

if not both. In order to show that we are not such as we are supposed to be we are quite willing to meet the Conservative•party on their own grounds and will dis- cuss this question under discussion or any other." (Applause.) Mr. ELWELL was extremely brief in introducing the question of the debate, contenting himself by merely moving the question "Id the present Government worthy of the confidence of the country? If not, ought it to resign?" Mr. E. WYNNE-JONES seconded, and stated at once that he did not think the present Government was worthy of the confidence of the country, and that he considered Mr. Balfour's continuance in office was a grave and National peril. Mr. Jones proceeded to con- demn the Government for their inefficiency in Army matters. Mr. Broderick was doing a great deal of harm to the auxiliary forces—forces which were the only means of preventing

div.head: Tro EVIL TYRANY OF .CONSCRIPTION,
div.p: Tro EVIL TYRANY OF .CONSCRIPTION,

and which ought to be encouraged. The Government ought to resign because of their tampering with our Free Trade. He was glad to believe that when a Liberal Government was returned to power it would not simply maintain Free Trade , but would free the land as well. The present Government ought to resign and give the Liberals a chance of improving our land laws. (Hear. hear.) Mr. T. TROWE expressed himself in opposition to the question. The state of the country to-day, he said, was due as much to Liberal as to Conservative Governments. To-day there were more; rich people and more poor people, and the poverty was more acute. Even with Lord Resebery and H. Sir Campbell Bannerman we could not expect legislation for the workingmen. If we had men in Parliament like General Booth, who would work in the interests of the working classes, we could expect legis- lation in the interests of the masses. He did not believe that the Liberal Government would tackle the land laws. Did they mean to tell him that Lord Rosebery and his class would do that? It ws all nonsense to say so. He had met many I.Aberals who regarded Lord Rosebery as the prospective leader of the Liberal Government. Mr. JOSEPH HOWES addressed the meeting and at once dealt with the last point raised by Mr. Trowe. He had never met one Liberal, he said, who wanted Lord Rosehery to be the leader, and he was quite certain that Lord Rosebery would not be the leader of the Liberal Government. Mr. TROWE would recommend them to have A GOVERNMENT OF GENERAL 1300T1I'S,

- - - but that would not be possible. General Booth's primary aim was to make people in a fit condition to enjoy the future lite. What he did for the people in this world, he said, was very secondary. If they were going to build up a Parliament in heaven, General Booth would be, an excellent Prime Minister. (Laughter.) He would ask the 'meeting to bear in mind that Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman had distinctly pledged himself to tackle the land question. The Tories were the most consistent politicians in the world. They had one unbroken record of opposition to all great, useful measures. (Laughter.) The Government had plundered the poor for the sake of the rich—that was what the Tories had always done. We would not get the reforms we wanted till we roused the workingmen. It was a lamentable thing that the Tories ran away from the House of Commons the other night to avoid discussing the fiscal question, but it was worse in Warrington when their leaders ran away and would not support them. Mr. Howes entered upon a satirical criticism of the conduct of the Primo Minister and other members of the Government. • He alluded to the treaty with Japan and said he did not see what advantage it was to this country. The one advantage of the present Govern- ment MS that we had "touched bottom" and could not get any lower. Whether the next Government did all we wanted or not, it could not possibly do worse than the present Government. It had a good chance of doing better mid therefore it would be wise to return the Liberals to power. Mr. MYLES and Mr. Corrnsua both agreed that the Governnient ought to resign. The latter went so far as to suggest that the King ought to step in and make the Government appeal to the country. With tae object of creating a discussion Mr. J. H. Morton moved AN AMENDMENT that in view of the fact that the Government was interesting itself in social reform, to demand its resig- nation at the present time was unjustifiable. Mr. E. LLOYD JONES formally seconded and to arouse greater interest in the discussion argued from the Tory point of view. Being aware of Mr. Jones's staunch Liberal principles the meeting,after recovering from the surprise at first occasioned by his attitude, was con- siderably amused. Mr. E. PLINsToN warmly took the Government to task for its legislation on the education and licensing questions and said he was convinced that under a Liberal Government the question of trade disputes would be satisfactorily settled. The Chinese Labour question ought to have been dealt with and hounded down from every pulpit. Mr. Heywood, Mr. S. Wright, J.P., and Mr. G Walker followed in a similar strain. Mr. WALKErs said he viewed the Aliens Bill as the Government's death-sad repentance rather than as an earnest desire to deal with what was undoubtedly an objectionable feature—the importatipn of destitute and diseased aliens. What degree of honesty was there in a Government which professed to deal with aliens imported into Great Britain but which imported Chinese into South Africa? Mr. S. WRIGHT was strongly in favour of Labour representation but under present conditions he said until the workingmen took a greater interest in politics they would not get a Labour Government. Would the workingmen of Warrington be prepared to incur the expense of maintaining a Labour member in Parliament ? Mr. HOWES, in a second speech, dealt with TIIE ALIEN AND THE UNEMPLOYED DILLS which he described as utter frauds. The Liberals were prepared to support the Government in a measure to keep out diseased and criminal aliens, but the present Bill was not a real endeavour to grapple with the ques- tion. The provisions of the Unemployed Bill were only optional as far as the provinces were concerned, and even in London the authorities could only incur expense to the extent of a penny rate, the Government not making any grant. As the method pro- posed of detain with the problem was the establish- ment of farm colonies, artisans and other classes of workers would have no opportunity of being employed. On a vote being taken a resolution expressing the view thatthe continuance in power of the Government was detrimental to the best interests of the country and to the honour of publio life, was carried practically unanimously.

Just tell him that." Mr. Urion left. Mr. bristles,and bone'proclucts. It owns steam and electric Davies has neve: paid the charges, and since that day railroads ; it owns the entire trolley-car service in ihe has never been able to do any business over that several cities. It owns factories, shops, stock-yards, ' line' , -la 1

! tnill .a, land and land companies, plants, warehouses, politicians, legislators, and Congressmen. It defies Wall-street, and terrorizes great railroad corporations. It compels the railroad to dismiss its manager, and then blacklists and ruins some small commission agent. It fixes the price the farmer shall receive for his cattle and pigs, and the price the butcher shall receive for his meat. It fixes the price the California fruit grower shall receive for his fruit, and claims a share of the proceeds from the cotton-grower of Georgia. There is scarcely' a limit to its power in fixing the price of all kinds of grain, and it is now seeking to control the price of bread. Its operations have impoverished or ruined farmers and stockmen, destroyed millions of investments, caused banks to break and men to commit suicide, precipitated strikes and annihilated industries. So great is the terror it inspires in some quarters that citizens under the constitutional guarantees of freedom do not dare even in the privacy of their offices or homes, to speak a word that this power would not approve of, and multi-millionaires, railroad magnates, and captains of industry quail before it. It has been declared by federal and 'State courts to be an outlaw and to have no right to exist. Of course it will be asked, " How can this thing be inn democratic nation, in a free Republic ?" The -answer is a long one. It is complicated, and is intricate beyond all conception. Discrimininating rates and advantages for the big house against the little. That is the . source of the Beef Trust's power. It was so with the Standard Oil rebates. All Special advantages, all concessions, reductions, and variations from published tariff rates, all preferences of one shipper over another, are condemned and distinctly forbidden by the Inter- State Commerce LaWof the United States, but then, if the Legislature has its price, and the Judge knows he must make hay while the sun shines, the rest is easy. It is written that probably the railroads of the United States will pay this year to the American Beef Trust 25,000,000d015. in rebates that are prohibited by law. There is no attempt to disguise the thieving procress, other than juggling with. names. The rebates are not called rebates ;they are called private ear charges. They remain rebates all the Salim. Before 1874 the popula- tion centres in the United States were supplied with fresh Meat, vegetables and fruit from their own immediate' neiglibouthocids. This restricted the variety and seasons of production, and often the supply. Thirty years ago a very able man invented and perfected • a freight car, that could be used as a travelling refrigeratir ; that is, one having unusually thick Or double sides, bottom and top, and supplied with ventilators and in tanks. So soon as this invention was found to be practicable, an enormous change took place in the most important national industry. Fresh meat began to be transported to great distances, fruit was brought in perfect condi- tion across the continent, vegetables were carried from the South to the North in the middle of winter; all 'differences of climate ceased to exist. Households in New York were as well supplied with sub-tropical products as households in New Orleans. A new in- dustry, that of, handling :and distributing these pro- ducts, came into being.: millions of dollars, and millions of men are now engaged in it. The most pro- found development was, in the meat industry. Originally the local butcher supplied the fresh meat, or, when the supply was deficient, cattle were shipped alive, on the hoof, in cattle Cars. The refrigerator car chanAed all this. With a capacity of 60,000 lbs. these cars can move a , tremendous amount of stuff. From extreme north to south, and from east to west, they are owned by the Beef Trust, and they monopolise the whole of the carrying of the chief portion of the world's food products, and fix the priees. It is estimated by two of the ablest men who have made a study of the question that the net profits from carrying alone amount that least 72,000c1015. a day. Added to the land carrying business we have the steamship with its refrigerator compartments all aiding to swell the revenue of this mighty octopus. Most wonderful of all, this millionaire making thing, with its mighty tentacles, does not rest satisfied* with , the mere profits arising from the carrying charges It has an ice business that simply coins money and to which I will refer further on. Let us see from it few examples what its freight traffic is in the shipping line. The Trust is the largest shipper in the world. From Chicago the annual shipments of dressed beef are about 1,500,000,000 pounds, of barreled pork about 175,000 barrels, of other pork products about 600,000,000 lbs., and of lard 375,000,000 lbs. Kansas City slaughters at least 1,000,000 hogs a year, South Omaha a little less, St. Louis 500,000, St. Joseph about the same, Sioux City about half as much, St. Paul a little more than Sioux City. Consider the . enormous shipments of dairy products East and West; • 57,000,000 lbs. of cheese, 197,000,000 lbs. of butter, , inure than 1,000,000 cases of -egm from Chicago alone in 1903. Also the vast shipments of dressed poultry, cduntry produce, fruits of all kinds, the great trade in fertilizers and offal, the canned goods and soap that are shipped by the Trust, and the salt and other supplies that are shipped in, and it may be seen at once how it is that the Beef Trust can dictate its own terms to the railroad President. He dare not, by refusing to obey the Trust's demands, raise a disturb- ance. A swarm of furious stockholders, directors, lbankers, investors and Speculators would be howling ! after him, and he dare net Say he was fighting for a I principle. Big tonnage and dividends stand a long : way ahead of principle. Take the following statement made by an. able lawyer before the inteiStitte. Commission as • an example of what the money mania will do with a man's conscience. The lawyer's client was. called upon to answer a t ertain question touching rebates. The !lawyer interfering said :—" Suppose the company did make an allowance ton Shipper. The shipper is not a. ' railroad. This Commission has to do with common carriers, and if shippers, by means of the use of these !cars, get some payments —assume they do—that is not prohibited by law, directly or indirectly, and what this company does every private car-line . does, no matter • what witnesses may testify, and no matter what their disregard for their oath may be." 'When general managers, auditors, and other general officers of great railroads are willing to rm on the witness stand and swear to statements absolutely untrue, and proved to be untrue from their own records, what can we ex- pect from their subordinates? The above refers chiefly to the Trust's doings with the railroad companies. Let us lool.c. what its work is with the shippers. Of course it is the ice business that makes the refrigerator to he in such demand, and many an uncomfortable hour have I spent in them. I give one saninle case. Mr. Davies is a commission merchant of Chicago. He is a Welshman, and happens to have sonic old world potions about justice and right. His business is to receive fruit as a con- signee, and to sell it. All the stuff he handles must be carried in refrigerators. When be began business.

Now note what followed: On October Ist of last , year he received a car-load of fruit from Lawton, I Michigan, on another line in an Armour car. On ! this the "icing charges" were 2200. dols. • But he I. had a letter from the shipper saying the cars had not. been iced at all. The charge was a robbery. Naturally Davies refused to be plundered. Three days later his Ishipper at Lawton sent word that he had been notified !by the Armour agent there that no cars could ko to Davies unless the charges were prepaid. In other Words the Trust was carrying out it word to ruin him. But about that time Mr. Davies made one or two moves on his own account, and laid the whole matter before the commerce commission. Publicity was'gained,but the boycott still stands on his shipments: 1 Another instance as an example of the ' Trust's ' methods of getting all the traffic will bear; and robbing the consumers all round. On August 11th, 1904 Coyne Bros. received a car loaded with lemons from Epwortb, Indiana. It came, to Chicago by the Chicago and Illinois. On the original bill was the regular Louisville and Nashville " icing charge " of I4dols, Epworth to Chicago, But in Chicago someone added the Trust's " icing charge" of 45d015. from Epworth anal the railroad Company presented the bill with both amounts on it. Coyne Bros. demanded to know if they were expected to pay both " icing charges." The billwas withdrawn and returned with the I4dols. charge erased. Of course this demon- strated that if the Trust were not empowered to play the bandit, the charge ,would have been 14do1s. and do more. Coyne Bro. refused to pay the 45d015.' and the Chicago and Illinois applied' the boycott —that is, it took them off the credit list. The time was the height of the. fruit season, car-loads of fruit for the firm were lying rotting in the sun to the heavy loss of jaw:swat shippers, but the railroad company refused to handle it until the firm deposited a certified check to prepay the charges. Coyne Bros. persistently refused to pay the Trust's extortions,' and in the end the agent of the Trust appeared at their office. "I have come to tell you," lie said, "that you will have to pay that charge or else everything that goes into an Armour car for you will have to be prepaid before it ,can start." The manager for Coyne Bros. shoved paper and pencil upon the attorney and said: "Will you put that in writing for me?" "I will not, you understand plain English,don't you ?" saying this he left. In the next few days the firm found that its shipments from the Michigan grape region were cut off. It sent one of its own men there to load cars, but the railroad refused to bill them. All the company would say was, "They had their instractions from Armour's and must follow them." Complete evidence that the Beef Trust was dominating the railroad. • One more instance. On August 15th, 1904, a firm in Chicago received a car load of melons from Carlisle, Indiana. The freight charges were 35•50d015. and the icing charges 50•63d015. Distance from Carlisle to Chicago, 216 miles, time consumed, about eighteen hours. According to the icing bill there must have been consumed about twenty tons of ice. Here was a clear fraud to the amount of .35d015. on the cost of fourteen tons of ice. I shall weary the reader with all these details, and must stop. Think of the fraud and the robbery that is going on, and who but the consumer has to pay , it? With over 40,000 of these cars operating in the country, no wonder we have the swelling millionaires who are astonishing the world with their boundless . wealth. We have in California a sort of local Trust.l A Mr. Seyner, a butcher of this city, having stood its i ' exactions as long as he could, has taken it into Court, , and I give a part of his evidence. ' Seyner mentions names and dates to back up his assertions. According to him he waS tined and paid 50dols. in March, 1903, for buying a bill of meats from the Western Meat Company, because that con- cern was not in the ring ; he was caught again dis- regarding the combine's mandate in January, 1904, and paid another 50do1s. into the treasury of the i board ; for selling meat to the California Co-operative , Meat Company in September, 1004,. he was fined 250d015. In January of the present year he was again j fined 250d015. for buying from the outside firm of , Wicker & Zahn. I The Armour Beef Truit is now before the Court and this is how it respects the law. The accused packers have a formidable corps of detectives'and guards, with . are busy spying upon witnesses 'and officials. Eight I, witnesses, several from distant points, appeared at the i States Attorney's rooms to-day, escorted and closely watched by agents of the packers, who sat with them, took them out to dinner and escorted them away with- out allowing them to so much as give their names to outsiders. Of course the names appearing as the heads of the various Trusts may be bunched together and then we • find some half-dozen men who are in effect the ruling power of the' United States. Feeling throughout the States is getting-very strong. Of course the Standard . Oil, as yet, stand at the port. The popular dislike of the Standard Oil group of capitalists is not the result of evidently unreasonable prices of oil products, but from the company's ruthless and illegitimate methods of competition, and a realization of the actual social danger involved in the control of these enormous accumnlations of ready cash by a small number jof rich men. This feeling is illuS rated by I the protest of a number of Eastern lergymen against the acceptance of 100,000 do . offered by John D. Rockefeller for certain religious work. It is not necessary to consider the wisdom of the protest. ! It is sufficient to recognize the feeling which it expresses and which is almost uni.ersal. The thought . of the better minded people is that benevolent societies ' have no right to take Rockefeller's money. The great dividends regularly received foam Standard Oil for ' many years have given this group of capitalists control, I not only, of their own money, but of the people's money deposited in banks, trust companies, and insur- ance companies in which they are directors.
