[By Mr. H. Whitham].
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Ovalist.")

"That the third time pays for all "is one of the axioms we learnt in our school-days, and when it suits us to do so we fervently believe in it. Just now there is no more p polar phrase in Warringtan, for the simple reason that the Warrington team have won their way intci the final round of the Northern Union Cup Com- petition for the third time, and as success has so far been denied them it is hoped and expected that tbe "third time" will make amends for all previous disappointments..

Warrington certainly ought to win the Cup this time—but then I said the same thing last year! The task will probably be no easier,for Hull Kingston Rovers are a sturdy lot, but experience should certainly stand the Warrington men in good stead and enable them to produce that form which we all know would win them the cup against any and all corners. They have proved themselves admirable cup-fighters ever since the Northern Union Competition was introduced, but they have been equally bad finishers. Four thnes in ' the semi-final, and three times in the final, and no cup, ! is a recofd lamentably dificient in one particular. That that deficiency will -be made up on the 29th inst firmly believe.

Warrington are entitled to the warmest praise for their achievement last Saturday in conquering Brad- ford. There was no secret made of the opinion outside Warrington that the Yorkshiremea would win this time and the shock of some of the knowing ones must have been great ! The Warrington men never doubted their ability to beat their burly foes once more, and they never once lost the whip hand during the struggle. Bradford were over-played by a cleverer and more resolute team and the temper shown before the close of hostilities proclaimed the fact that they knew it. Warrington's "winning way" was once more apparent, and apart from merit, luck again favoured them. I must explain how. At the end of five minutes they were five points up. How much such an asset can be valued at, only those who have played in a serious cup-tie can realise. The reason is easily explained. Mosby once more paid , the penalty of entering the lion's den. In the County match at Oldham, Fish taught him a lesson, but he apparently forgot. At any rate, he and Connell made a great blunder when they tried juggling with the ball on Fish's wing. The master juggler was on the spot, and the way he snapped up the ball and left the Bradford team standing in his run behind the posts was a eye-opener. It was perhaps the greatest effort of Fish's brilliant career, and there is no doubt that it won the match. Just note what other scribes say of it.

This is what the " Manchester Guardian" says "The Bradford forwards WOll a pack well in the Warrington half, and the ball was handed out to the three-quarters ; there were some exchanges, ending in a rather long throw out to the right winger, But the ball never reached him. Fish was expect- ing, and with abound he took the pass andlappeared 311 ofla sudden behind the whole Bradford three- quarter line, and with only Gunn, the full back, in front of him, There was a yell of triumph from I'` Warrington. Fish was off at' top speed instantly, and making two or three subtle feints, quite with- out slackening pace, he beat Gunn so utterly that he did not, even feel his touch. He then flew with splendid boldness right across the ground for the posts. There was a grand race between him and a Bradford three-quarter, who made pursuit straight down the middle of the field and so on a shorter course to cut him off. but Fish's pace was superb, and he grounded the ball plump between the posts i a yard n front of his pursuer, having run fully two- thirds the length of the field." Then the "Yorkshire Post"also gives honour where honour is due. Perpend : "If a certain M.P., had been at Rochdale on Saturday for the semi-final tie between Warrington and Bradford he would have found no difficulty in " crystallising " the game in a sentence. It was simply, the tale of a stolen pass. Before the con- test was five minutes old,and while warrin,gtoa were defending on their own quarter-line, Fish flashed in, in the way which has made him famous, and stole a pass intended by Connell for Mosby. The move- ment was so sudden in design, and so brilliant in execution, that Fish left the whole of the Bradford team, except the full back, looking at his heels. Of Gunn'; opposition the Warrington crack made small account, and running inside he scored a magnificent try under the posts. It was the effort of a great individualist, aud deserved all the cheers that greeted it."

The gnus after this electrifying start was a grini struggle in which neither side gained much advantage. Warrington had the worst of matters forward for a long time, but the backs were superb and broke up the Bradford combination in a fashion which has rarely been equalled. It was pace which told the tale, and the superior speed and alertness of the lighter Warrington men enabled them to keep the foe in check. Bradford had chances, certainly, and once Marsden missed a pass right on the line, but all they got was a dropped goal from the erratic foot of Eagers.

In the second half Warrington were even more plainly the superior side. The forwards lasted well and gave the Yorkshire pack a lively time. Preston kicked his second goal, a magnificent bog-range penalty shot, and the Bradford defence was completely beaten once by a grand cross-kick from Dickinson who left Fish with a clear field. The left-winger made no mistake, bait the referee did, and the try— as fair a one as ever the team got—was disallowed, presumably for an imaginary off-side. The refereeing of Mr. A. Smith, was, throughout, the subject of unfavourable comment. He all)wed the Bradford men too much latitude altogether, and certainly proved more than once anything but a friend to Warrington.

" Free Lance " iii the " Athletic:News" says, on the question of:refereeing: It is significant, too, that no fewer than five of the Bradford forwards at different periods were spoken to by the referee—two were at the instiga- gation of one of the touch judges. But what was the outcome? Simply a warning, and the offending player allowed to resume. The result was that towards the close it was a case of hammer and tongs, and the weak display of refereeing only excited the derision of the spectators. If the men were guilty of rough play they should have been ordered off, if innocent they ought not to he inter- fered with. Mr. A. Smith by no means increased his reputation as a strong referee."

" Impressionist" in the" Umpire" kas also some interesting comments on the snatch, with a portion of which Warrington men will not agree. Ho says : " Will history repeat itself, or will the Warring- tonians this time,make amends for previous failures. That the team is capable of such a task goes with- out saying. Their methods are not such as would appeal to a stylist. They are totally incapable of giving a " class " display such as we have seen from say, Broughton Rangers and Bradford on occasion. But, on the other hand, I know no team of recent years so likely to turn to account the momentary weakness of their opponents, no team more dogged- ly tenacious to keep a lead, no team with more dangerous individuals. These three points were all in evidence of Rochdale. As to whether they will be in the ascendant a fortnight hence is quite another story."
The italicsare mine, and I would just refer the reader 0 an account of the Broughton Rangers match lower down.

It is hardly possible to single out any of the War- rington men for praise, without doing an injustice to the rest. All played a great game, but • apart from Fish's brilliance, it was Dickinson's day! The right centre showed better form than he has for two seasons, and his aggressive tactics well earned for him the title of "the dashing Dickinson." Mosby and Eagers will have lively recollections of his vigorous tackling and indomitable pluck. Brooks and Kenyon, the two . juniors of the team, again distinguishect. themselves, and there is every confidence in their future behaviour. There were a lot of hard knocks received, but every , man stuck manfully to his work. I never remember a ' game in which there were so many stoppages for injuries, and the Lancashire lads were the chief sufferers. The referee's want of firmness in checking undue roughness spoiled the game as a spectacle. It might, under good management, have reached a high class.
The final will be once more at Leas, and all Warrington seems to be going. "Hope lives eternal," &e., and Warrington are certain of great backing from the good- old town.

Nine special tmins have already been arrangedfor to take Warrington enthusiasts to the final at Meadingley by the Midland and London and North- : Wtestern The former line has made a great effort to compete with its powerful neighbour and will run right through via the new Chinley and Doe line. lam informed that both companies will see that their patrons get to Leeds before the match, and not after this time! •

The following officials have been appointed for the. final tie between Warrington and Hull Kingston Rovers, at Leeds, on Saturday, April 29th :—Referee, Mr. J. Bruckshaw (Stockport); touch judges, Messrs. W. Robinson (Bradford), and J. A. Smith (Widnes).

Warrington supporters are requested t 3 note that should Warrington manage to lift the cup on the 29th inst., the" Examiner" of the following Friday will contain an art-paper supplement with portrait of the cup-holders. Bear this in mind and tell your friends.

There was a League game at Wilderspool on Monday, when Broughton Rangers came to see if they could not make amends for cup-tie failure by annexing the League Championship. Vain how,! Though short of six of the cup team, Warrington showed magnificent form, and literally made rings round the Rangers, who sustained their heaviest defeat of the season. At half-time th 7 were a try to the good, but the locals ran up 19 points in record time on resuming, and no one would have thought the opposition was furnished by one of the crack teams of the Union. What about "classy exhibitions " now, was the gloat of the local enthusiasts. Both forwards and backs were brilliant in the open. The two great feats in any opinion wem Preston's masterly dribble, and Kenyon's single-handed try.

_ -- Warrington have surpassed all their previou records in League football, and their play of late proves that it was no idle boast when it was said six months ago that they could win the c'aampionship if they set about it.
The South-West Lancashire League up-to-date is an follows :
For Warrington to be in the running again, Leigh and Wigan %rill require to draw to-morrow (Good Friday). Warrington, of course, are expected to beat St. Helens on the same day.

A strong team has been selected, as follows :—Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Berry, and Kenyon, threequarters ; Brooks, and J. Davies, half-backs; Boardman,Thomas, Preston. Cricket. The Stretton arid Appleton Cricket Club is making preparations for a sawed:ll sesson. At the annual meeting on Monday the following officers were elected: —Mr. T. H. Lyon, president ; Mr. C. Hallows, captain; Mr. J. R. Moordeld, sub-capts.in Mr. Isaac Broady, treasurer : Mr. J. G. Hatton, secretary. A good list of fixtures has been arranged and the opening game will be played on Saturday the 29th April.
s -- Warrington commence the season on Saturday with 0. match at Bolton, while the second eleven try conclu— sions with Bolton second at Arpley.

Bowling. Bowling commences in real earnest this week end. On Monday an open main will be held on the King and Queen Hotel green and a close contest should result, a large number of entries having already been received. The opening main on the Cemetery Hotel green will be played on Monday and on several greens players will compete for prizes.

Nothing has as yet been done with regard to the opening of the Corporation green in Victoria Park, though no doubt the responsible committee of the Council will take the matter into consideration at their next meeting. The question of the fee to be charged for use of the green will also be taken into considera- tion and we would again urge the establishment of a small charge which will not in any way be a hardship.
ME
Cycling.

- The football match between Warrington and Bradford naturally affected the number of members of local cycling clubs who turned out for club runs on Saturday, many wheelers preferring to follow ‘Varrington's fortunes. Haif-a-dozen members of the Warrington Cycling Club made the journey to liels:2y on Satarday, and spent an enjoyable time., The cold east winds which have prevailed during the past Week have had a deterrent effect upon cyclists and unless the weather improves in this respect the wheelers will not be so greatly in evidence this week-end. Tours to Llangollen and Llanfairfechan have been arranged by the Warrington Cycling Club and many have signified their intention of making one or the other of the tours.

A Clarion Cycling Club has been formed in Warring- ton and already the membership has exceeded all ex- pectations. An attractive programme has been arranged and promise is given of a successful and enjoyable season. A united meet of English Clarion Cycling Clubs will be held in the Dukeries this week end and many ‘Varrington cyclists are looking forward to join- ing in the meet.

div.head: The" Kitties " Band at Warrington.
div.p: The" Kitties " Band at Warrington.

The visit of the famous Scotch Canadian band to Warrington aroused considerable interest on Monday, and there were fair audiences at the two performances given in Parr Hall, the entertainment being generally voted excellent. Clad in the brilliant uniform of the Gordon Highlanders, the " Kilties " present a- mo:st attractive spectacle on the Platform. Their playing of Scottish airs and marches,too, left little to be desired while the ordinary band programme Was pleasingly varied with unique 'features. Honorary pipe Major Johnstone favoured the audience with a stirring bag- pipe solo, and the Clan Johnstone troupe of dancers gave such popular items as a Scotch reel, Irish jig,ancl sailors' hornpipe as well as we ever saw this class of , dancing performed. Mr. Tom Johnstone danced the sword dance, displaying exceptional nimbleness and • grace. Then there was a part song, " The Boys of the - Old Brigade," by the " Kilties " choir, but this only served to convince us that the members of the " choir" can render better music with their cornets and clarionets than with theit vocal organs. Probably the best band selections were the overture to "Williana Tell," " Scotland's Pride," and- ballet music: from " Sylvia." Finally, hearty praise must be given to Mr. John S. Leick, who proved himself to be a cornet soloist of remarkable power and expression. His- International Fantasia " was very deservedly- encored.

div.head: WORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: WORE THE MAGISTRATES.

YOUTFIFIJL MOTOR DRIVERS' RECICLESSNESS. At the Warrington Police Court on Monday John Isherwood (17), London-road, Stockton Heath, was charged with driving a motor car at a dangerous speed, on Warrington Bridge on the 10th inst.—He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said that on the date in question P.C. (36) Cooper was on point duty at Bridge- foot when he saw the defendant driving a motor car at a most furious rate down Bridge-street. Cooper held up his hand for the defendant to stop,but the youth took no notice,ani drove over the bridge. He was travelling at Seventeen miles an hour and even had he been only going five miles an hour he would have been travelling at a dangerous pace. He bad however got the machine under controll as in Knutsford-road be got caught in the traffic and pulled up. Defendant was employed by Mr. W. H. Bellian and was taking the car to the gentle- manwho owned it.—PC. Cooper, Mr. George Osborne. Knutsford-road, Mr. Samuel Cross, butcher, and Inspector Flood, gave evidenceas to the speed at which the car was travelling, all saying that it was between 17 and 18 miles an hour.—The Chief Constable remarked that the defendant, when spoken to said that he lost his bead for the minute.—Defendant was fined in the costs (245. 6d.) his license being endorsed.

div.head: DECLINE IN THE NUMBER OF INMATES.
div.p: DECLINE IN THE NUMBER OF INMATES.

Mr. Spruce remarked that the numb<r of inmates of the House was steadily declinilig and was now 122 as against 140 twelve months ago. Mr. Roylance asked whether anything had been done in regard to the application of the Ladies Visiting Committee with reference to the provision of couches for elderly inmates. Mr. Spruce said the House Committee could not see their way to provide couches as suggested. They had, however, decided to purchase two dozen cushions for the use of aged people.

div.head: EARLESTONVN COLLIER'S DEATH.
div.p: EARLESTONVN COLLIER'S DEATH.

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an i quest on Saturday, on the body of John Hopwood, aged thirty-four, of 86, Legh-street, Earlestown, who was killed at the Wood Pit, Haydock, on Wednesday night by a stone falling from the roof. The evidence showed that a large fall of roof had taken place in the roadway and this man with four others Nns putting it right again, when the stone fell and killed the deceased, Thomas Rafferty, of Haydock, having a very narrow escape. The Alines Inspector said this roof was usually hard rock, but it had been shaken by something or other. There was no blame attached to the workmen. A verdict of" Acci- dental death" was returned.

div.head: PENNY BANKS.
div.p: PENNY BANKS.

A summary of the information with reference to penny savings banks which had been obtained from the schools at which such banks are conducted was sub- mitted to the School Management Committee, and it was resolved: That a copy of the circular upon the subject from the Board of Education be jorwarded to the managers of those schools at which sifch banks are not carried on, in the hope that the managers may be able to see their way to their institution." The minutes of the School Management Committee were approved in their entirety. THE ATTENDANCE OF CHILDREN AT CHURCH. The School Attendance Committee reported that a letter was submitted from the managers of the Heath- side National School, intimating that the usual annual service commencing at 8.15 a.m., will be held on Ascension Day in the St. Paul's Church, that the scholars will be back at school by 9.30 a.m., and that as usual, arrangements will he made whereby any chil- dren whose parents may prefer it will receive secular

instruction in the school whilst the others are at church After some discussion it was resolved : " That the managers of the school be informed that the committee have noted this intimation, and that they be reminded that permission should be obtained from the Education Committee when it is desired that a school should not be opened until a later hour than usual." . _ .
Tle action of the Rota in asking for information to be obtained as to the schools from which children attended church on Ash Wednesday was confirmed.

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
MR. H. ROBERTS'S ONLY PLEDGE.
The Demand for Secondary School Teachers,
THE SALARY OF HOLY TRINITY SCHOOL HEADMISTRESS.

Although not of long duration, there were discus- sions on several matters of considerable public interest at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee which was held at the Town Hall on Mon- day evening. Alderman Bennett presided and there were also present :—Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Wilkinson, Ellison, Barton, Wright, Burton; Fulton Smith,l and Evans; the Revs. John Yonge and Father Wilson, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, H. Roberts, C. H. Unsworth,H, Kingdom,R. T. Fairclough, J: D. Buckton, T. May, G. Walker J. Upson. E. Plinston and J. Moore Murry (director Walker,
NEW MEMBERS OF THE SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

Mr. UPSON said he had been asked to move the election upon the school management committee, of Councillor Brough and Mr. Henry Roberts, to fill the vacancies caused by the death of Alderman Sutton and the elevation of Alderman Pierpoint to the vice-chair- manship of the committee. Councillor Brough they all knew. Mr. Henry Roberts wasa representative governor of the Grammar school, a representative on the Council of the Liverpool University, and therefore had con- siderable knowledge of higher education and would be of valuable assistance to the committee.
Councillor WILKINSON seconded.

Mr. R. T. PAIRCLOIJGII said he spoke about the matter at the last meeting of the Education Committee when it was understood that Mr. J. D. Buckton should have the first vacancy on the School Management Com- mittee. There were two representatives of Church of England schools on the Education Committee and he would like to point out that the actual attendance at Church schools was 6,976 as against all other sections in town. He failed to see why representatives of Church schools should be debarred from serving upon the School Management Committee. He proposed the election of Mr. J. D. Buckton.

Mr. PLINSTON seconded. Councillor Brough and he were very good friends, but he thought the seats upon committees should be fairly divided and for that reason and for the reason of Mr. Buckton's ability he seconded the nomination.

In answer to Councillor Burton, the DIRECTOR said the Committee was composed as follows :—Councillor Craik, Councillor Fulton-Smith, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, C. E. Parker, C. H. Unsworth, J. Upson, the Revs. Morley Stevenson, E. J. Wilcocks, N. Wilson, and John Yonge. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH Every other denomination in the town is represented on the committee.

Councillor BARTON: I think the Church of England is fairly well represented. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : The Church of England is not represented at all. It was proposed by Councillor BARTON, seconded by Councillor ELLISON, that all three gentlemen be placed upon the School Management Committee.
Councillor WimuNsiiN : 1 think Counaillor Brough is already on a sufficient number of committees.

After g brief discussion it was decided not r:o increase the size of the committee and on a vote being taken Mr. Henry Roberts and Mr. J. D. Buckton were elected to fill the vacancies. MR. HENRY ROBERTS'S ONLY PLEDGE.

Mr. HENRY ROBERTS said he desired to thank very sincerely the members of the committee for their recommendation of himself for appointment on the committee, He did not seek the position but must confess it was a position he would like to have occupied since the formation of the Education Committee. The question of education was one of great interest to him and he hoped he would be able to render some service in the carrying out of the very important duties which devolved upon the Committee. "I come here," he said, "absolutely unpledged except to this—and I will give no pledge except this—that so far as in me lies I will endeavour to apply the knowledge and experience that I have to the proper, fair. and catholic administration of the Education Act," (Hear, hear).
THE HEADMISTRESS OF HOLY TRINITY SCHOOLS. THE QUESTION AGAIN RAISED. _ . .

At a meeting of the Finance Committee it was noted that the resolution of the committee with reference to the salary of the head mistress of the mixed department of the Trinity National school, had not been approved and adopted by the Education Committee at their last meeting. The confirmation of the minutes was moved by Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, seconded by Councillor WILKINSON. Mr. PLINSTON said he had tried to understand Mr. Jolley for some time but up to the present he had been unable to make anything of him. There were upon that committee one or two men who had upon a certain matter defied the comrittee. He had reason to believe that in regard to the headmistress of Holy Trinity schools the Finance Committee had found they had been doing what they ought not to have done in interfering in that question, and it was now left for the School Management Committee to do something in the matter. In his opinion it was absolutely unfair to that mistress that that matter should be played shuttle-cock with for so long. If she was entitled to the increase in her salary by all means she should have it. If she was not entitled to the increment the committee should have a proper resolution brought before them upon which they could divide. Ho thought Mr. Jolley slaould have stated some reason why that matter had been left alone. It was too late when he got his agenda paper for him to give notice of motion or he should have done so and appealed to the committee to give that teacher the increment to which he thought she was justly entitled. The Rev. JOHN YoVoK asked whether it was too late for Mr. Plinston to move a resolution on the lines ho had suggested. Alderman BENNETT : lam afraid it cannot be done. Mr. Plinston can move that this paragraph be not approved, and the matter can be brought forward at a subsequent meeting. Mr. PuNsToR : What is there to disapprove of? (Laughter.) If the Chairman will give an explanation it will perhaps got us out of the difficulty. Mr. WALKER felt that after the last direct expression of opinion which was given by the committee the matter should have received more definite attention at the hands of the Finance Committee. He thought they were generally agreell that the lady teacher who was affected was suffering a hardship. The matter had been referred back twice and he thought something definite should have been done. It was now too late to do any- thing at that meeting hut he thought the matter would eventually have to be dealt with by a direct and special resolution.

Councillor EVANS WAS also of the opinion that some- one would have to give notice of a direct resolution in opposition to the Finance Committee. He would be sorry to see such a thing done but so far as he was con- cerned there had to his mind been no reason given to justify the action which had been taken. If they got nothing more than was contained in; the minutes he was prepared to move a direct resolution. He would like to know whether the Finance committee was going to dominate the position or whether the Education Committee was going to do so. Alderman BENNETT : I don't think there is any desire on the part of tbe Finance committee to dominate. Councillor EVANS : Perhaps Mr. Jolley has some conclusive evidence which he has not given upon the question as to why that particular course should be taken. If he has, this committee should have known of it long since. Mr. UNSWORTII thought some of the speakers had been a little previous. He took it that it would now be the duty of the School Management Committee to con- sider the question of the teacher's salary and fix it according to scale. Councillor EVANS : The salary is already fixed according to scale. The resolution has been twice referred back and still the increase is withheld.

Councillor /FULTON SMITH said that evidently the lady affected was supposed to have friends on that com- mittee. When the question first came up the School Manacement Committee decided that the lady's name should be withheld out of consideration for her. Those who had opposed the original resolution had made her name public with the remit that if she tried to get another situation she would have to face considerable
difficulty. He hardly thought that was evidence of friendship for the lady. The sub-committee might be relied upon to do no injustice either to the teacher or to the Education Committee.

- The Rev. JOHN YONGE said he had from the first taken up a strong position on that question, but there was no reason for him to be considered a friend of Miss Davies; and all he had said and done had been on a question of principle. It had appeared to him from the first that there had been no satisfactory evidence given to them, either on the School Management Committee or the Education Committee, to justify the procedure of the Finance Committee. If it were true that there had been some little peccadillos—they were not much larger— with regard to some matters of minor detail in the keep- ing of accounts, the punishment which had been meted out to the mistress was a travesty of justice. The CHAIRMAN: I don't think we ought to go back lon the general question. It is a matter of procedure. There is no desire to go against the decision of the General Committee. The Rev. .1. YONGE : I wish to assure Councillor Fulton Smith that some of us who take the position we now take have no claim to the friendship of the teacher. Mr. MAY remarked that there seemed to him to be several objectionable features in the mode of procedure in regard to this case of discipline. Did the sub-com- mitlee propose to proceed with such a drastic measure without obtaining the sanction of the General Com- mittee'? That was one question he should like to ask. Another was—Why should these important minutes be constantly submitted in a formal manner? The expen- diture was increasing, and large sums were being paid, and yet there was no explanation whether there was an increaSe or deer mute. If figures were given at all timre ought to be some explanation about them. The CHAIRMAN: The committee have resolved to submit to the committee a quarterly comparison of the actual income and expenditure of the committee. You will then be able to compare the expenditure. 1 Mr. MAT said that in regard to the particular item under the discussion there was another strong objection to the procedure which was that the lady was not asked to explain before judgment was passed upon her. He hoped he was the friend of all the lady teachers. All his life he had been a friend to schoolmasters, and he held a degree which was conferred upon him by the general body of schoolmasters in Scotland. He hoped it would be no slur on his character to be a friend and supporter of all the headmistresses of the schools in Warrington. Whenever a case of this kind came before the committee he should do his utmost to secure a fair and a patient hearing before any judgment was passed upon any lady or gentleman connected with education. The CHAIRMAN: It seems to me that it is quite unnecessary for us to again go into the merits of this case. ,

Councillor WILKINSON said he also could not claim to have the honour of the friendship of the lady teacher in question but he had felt all along that the punishment had been too great for the crime. He felt sorry at the manner in which the lady's name had been dragged through the newspapers. He thought that the resolu- tion having been previously referred back it should bare received graver consideration at the hands of the! Finance Committee. He hoped Mr. Jolley would give some explanation of the matter other than what he (Comacillor Wilkinson) had heard. He should like to know what was behind it all, because he could not see what grivous error the lady had committed. He had been told that other schools in town were really more negligent and in face of that he began to think there was something behind the treatment of Miss Davies. 1 The CHAIRMAN said the matter had been discussed ad nanseam:.. The lady would get her increment. _

Councillor WILLEiNsoN : Let her get it. She has been tortured enough. I feel for the lady. Mr. UPSON : If the matter is to be referred back, why cannot we get an assurance to that effect? (Hear, hear).

Mr. JOLLEY said the question had been fully dis- cussed, and he should have thought the members knew the course that would be adopted. Councillor Evans had asked if the Finance Committee was going to dominate the Education Committee. Well, there was not much dominating in a committee whose minutes had been sent back twice. He felt strongly tempted to quote some remarks of Dr. Johnson. He did not see what there was in the minutes for anybody to take exception to. The mode of procedure which would probably be taken had already been indicated by the Chairman, but there was ap alternative. It Was com- petent for any member of the committee to move in the matter, but he apprehended that the ordinary course of procedure would be that the matter would be taken up by the School Management Committee. Some members seemed to have forgotten that that oommittee, sitting as the General Purposes Committee, referred this matter to the Finance Committee, and without any of the ulterior motives which had been imputed, he could assure Mr. May and any other gentlemen whose remarks ' would suggest that the Finance Committee was a sort of modern inquisition that the members of the committee were not entirely destitute of reason and commonsense. While they claimed to have the normal share of Christian virtues they did not pretend to surpass the apostles themselves. The evangelical doctrine taught that when smitten on one cheek to turn the other to the smiter, but what they had been asked to do was not only to offer the other cheek but to smite it themselves and he submitted that even the apostles did not rise to that height. (Laughter.) Councillor WILKINSON : That is the point that struck me. It was the spirit of "I won't give in" that dominated. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN : You have already spoken, Mr. Wilkinson.

Mr. JOLLEY : I should like again to eniphatically protest against the assertioni made—ntterly without foundation—and repeated over and over again, that the Finance Committee tried, for a trivial offence, to flue this person £25. It has absolutely no foundation what- ever. It! rested on a misunderstanding—l will not use a stronger term—of the circumstances of the case, and the remedy for those who were thirsting to pay this lady the increase is very simple. The minutes were then approved, the minute relating to the headmistress to be taken into further considera- tion.
THE SECONDARY SCHOOL. DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING TEACHERS.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the School Management Committee, Mr. J. UPSON said the mem- bers had done themselves the honour of re-electing the Rev. Morley Stevenson as chairman. Continuing he called attention to the fact that an assistant master at the Secondary School (Mr. Ernest Hanna) had resigned after rendering nine months'service. Since his resigna- tion had been received, another assistant master had also resigned, and the committee had had extreme diffi- culty in obtaining a sufficient number of applicants from whom they might make a suitable selection. It would be a serious matter for the committee in the regulation of the appointment of the staff as to what they should do. Apparently t -ey could not get—and he did not think they ought to expect to get—a man with a university degree and teaching experience at a salary of £l2O a year. Two years ago it was possible to get young men from the universi. ies at that figure, but since the passing of the Education Act there had been such a great demand for those teachers, owing to the establish- ment of numerous secondary schools, that the supply was almost absorbed and the market price had risen considerably. The question for the committee to decide was whether they would expect to get men who had completed their degrees and, of course, give a better salary than the present sum, or appoint men who had had teaching experience and gone so rue way towards getting their degrees. It had been suggested—and pobably that would be a wise course to adopt—that they could find among the teachers in the primary schools young men who had had experience there and were endeavouring to qualify themselves by passing degree examinations, and appoint them to vacancies in the secondary school. But they actually found that men were loath to leave the primary schools and go to secondary schools, because in the former they knew exactly where they were and had a fixed scale of salaries. They knew that the maximum salary of a teacher in a primary school was considerable higher than the amount paid to a teacher in tbe secondary school. The committee would be driven probably in the near future to increase the salary they were now offering or adopt a fixed scale for the teachers in,the secondary school. He believed each of the assistants who had resigned was going toaschool in the South of England where he would receive .£3O or £lO mors per annum than the Warrington Committee was offering. Mr. MAY said he had recently been listening to com- plaints on behalf of parents in regard to the state of the secondary school and the education given there, and they were probably owing to. the numerous changesin the staff. He wished to asit whether the work ofi'last session was fully satisfactory to the managetnent, and whether they thought the school was going on satisfactorily with the present arrangement of the joint education of boys and girls. Did not talking
and larking go on between the sexes in school hours,and was the discipline injured lay the frequent changes of masters?

Mr. H, ROBERTS said the speech of Mr. Upson raised a very important question of policy. As a new member of the committee he could not pretend to any know- ledge of an intimate character as to the manner in which the secondary school was conducted, but he said with- out hesitation that any departure from a well known policy in commercial houses of getting the very best men for important work that could be obtained would have a very serious effect upon the value of the school to this town. If towns in the South of England,which were not specially noted for commercial pioneering or enterprise, could afford to pay £2O or £3O more than the Warrington Committee were paying for the same polity of teacher, it was a reflection on them in Warrington to allow such men to go. .While he knew they were all agreed as to the extreme importance of primary education, he said unhesitatingly that the question of secondary education to the future business men of the conntry was of far greater importance than mere primary education could be. They sent to the secondary school those children who by social position and mental gifts were the most ' likely, if properly taught, to take a prominent position in the com.nerce and professions of the country. He submitted that as a matter of policy what paid business men would pay them as a community, and that was to get the best men the market could give them, and pay a fair price for good work. Mr. UPSON, in reply to Mr. May, said he was very glad to state that the committee, as managers of the secondary school, were perfectly satisfied with what was being done dere, They had no record of any want of I discipline. They had the fullest confidence in the head- master, and they had ou the staff teachers whoi were second to none in the north of England for secondary education. Of course, they had in a large staff varying degrees of ability and self-control, and no doubt they had weaknesses on the staff. The Committee were, how- ever, trying to remedy them, and be was glad to have the weight of the authority of Mr. Roberts behind the Cora- mittee when he spoke of giving reasonable inducements to able men to join the staff. They knew how care- fully and minutely the proceedings of that committee were skanned and they had to be as economical as they possibly could. The fact, however, remained that they I could not and ought not to get a University graduate with teaching experience for the miserable salary of £l2O. The committee's hands were tied because they were charged with extravagance if they gave a salary commensurate with a man's ability and work. Mr. MAY: My question was "Has the school suffered by these changes?" The CHAIRMAN: You are out of order. Mr. Upson can answar as a matter of Courtesy if he likes. The question was not replied to. TEACHERS AND HOLIDAYS.
THE CLOSING OF SCHOOLS FOR EPIDEIVIICS.

The School Management Committee had decided that notice be sent to all assistant teachers informing them that, in the event of their schools being closed by order of the local Sanitary Authority, the Committee require their services at other schools during that period. The Committee, explained Hr. Upson, thought that was a perfectly legitimate resolution to pass. Recently there had been a number of teachers out of school be- cause their schools bad been closed through epidemics, while other schools in the borough had been suffering because they were under-staffed. They thought it a ' very proper thing that those teachers.' who had their holidays in the usual course, should go into schools where the staffs were short and render services. Mr. R.T. FAIRCLOUGH said the committee had missed the point which he had in view when he originally raised,the question. Formerly all the schools had five weeks holiday during the year but the committee had now increased the vacation to ten weeks, which he I thought was extremely generous. If, in addition, some schools were closed an extra fortnight or month through epidemics, he contended that at least a fortnight should be deducted from the regular holidays. The CHIIRMAN : I think the committee really had your object in view, hut the difficulties were so great that they were not able to adopt the suggestion. Mr. Lino's said he had been a teacher for nineteen years and he never knew the time when they had only Ave weeks' holiday. It was all very well to talk about the sehoola having ton weeks' holiday,butots a matter of fact, owing to the cutting off of days and half-days,they were open more frequently now than they were before the passing of the Educatior Act. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH: I take exception to that. Mr. UPSON : You may take any exception you like, but it is a fact. _ _

Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : I have been treasurer of aschool for thirty years and I cannot take that statement stall. Mr. UPSON: 'I can give figures for many schools. Continuing, he said Mr. FaircloUgh did not quite see the danger there was in his proposal.:The medical officer of Health could close schools for measles if 3 per cent, of the children were absent through that disease. That meant that in a school of 200—which was the average infants school—only !six children need be absent for the school to be closed. If in February a teacher found there were sixcases of measles and she know that if the schools were closed then she would be deprived of say the Whitsuntide holiday, would there not be atempta- tion to her not to reveal the existence of those cases ? Then again if one sohool was open while the others ware closed they would have great difficulty in getting the children to attend. It would mean the employment of all the committee's officers for the sake of one or two departments. The proposal was impracticable. It had never been done elsewhere, and it could not be done in Warrington. SCHOOL CHILDREN AND THE BATHS.

At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter was submitted from the Town Clerk, intimating that the Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee cannot see their way to grant the free use of the second-class swimming bath to children attending the public ele- mentary schools, and forwarding copies of the terms upon which school children are admitted to the first class plunge bath for the information of the members of the committee, and it was resolved that a sub-com- mittee consisting of Mr. Alderman Bennett, Mr. Coun- cillor Craik, Mr. J. Upson, and the Chairman (the Rev. Morley Stevenson) beappointed to confer with the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee upon the subject. 'Mr. UPSON said he need not say anything as to the necessity and importance of the above work. They found that since the p issing of the Education Act there had been in other boroughs arrangements between the various committees of the Council, resulting in the baths, parks, museums, and libraries being made more readily accessible to the children in all the schools. That kind of thing ought to be done in Warrington, and there ought not to be that keen desire on the part of each committee to show a profit at the expense of other committees. Although the Education Committee's request had been refused, they did not think the pro- blem was insoluble. It was hoped the difficulty would be solved either by the payment of something towards the baths or by considerably lessening the charge to the children. They found that the small sum of one penny who tnoeeadveedr ythlea rbgaethnsummboestr, oaf p rcohhi irteinv,e and those those Mr. H. ROBERTS said he was glad to notice the Com- mittee were making an effort to get the Council to agree to making the baths free to school children. He advo- cated that policy twelve or i thirteen years ago in the Council, and on every occasion when there was an oppor- tunity of supporting t, he endeavoured to press it upon the Council. Now they had made such a great advance on the general question of the curt-191nm which was given in the schools, he thought the time had come when even if the Government had not given the Commitee nuthority for doing it the Corporation,within the range of its own powers, might, at any rate, assist the principle by giving the free use of the baths to the children under proper and suitable conditions. He felt sure that if the committee pressed the matter often and hard enough, thq Council would give way and do what would be generally approved by the whole community.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Appointment of Chairman and
Committees.

The first meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council, since the annual meeting, was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present—Messrs. C. Roylance, J. Bolshaw, H. Eyes, P. Mounfleld,G.Egerton- Warburton A. Broome, T. Baxter, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, H. lViowdeley, T. Guest, J. Woodward, W. Harrison, G. Pilling, J. L. Jones, E. Bretherton, C. Horton, R. A. Chrimes, J. Fryer,J.Snruce, J. Rutter, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, R. Billington;C. E. Linaker, jun., J. Mounfleld, W. Turner, J. B. Chadwick, A. G. Guest, T. Antwis G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk),,f.Swinton (surveyor),J.Farring- ton (inspector), and Dr. Adams (medical officer).

div.head: ELECTION OE CFIAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OE CFIAIRMAN.

Mr. Wright moved the re-election of Mr. S. Wood- ward as chairman of the Council. The unity and good feeling amongst the members of the Council was he thought in a groat measure due to the courtesy displayed by Mr. Woodward in the chair. Mr. Baxter seconded and the proposition was unani- mously carried. Mr. Woodward thanked the members of the Council for re-electing him and hoped he would be able to maintain the promptness and businesslike proceedure which had characterized the work of the Council in the past. lie moved the election of Mr. Baxter as vice-chairman of the Council.
Mr. Hallows seconded, and the proposition was heartily approved.
APPOINTMENT. OF COMMITTEES.

The committees were elected as - follow; :—Finance Committee : Messrs. Wright, Chadwick, Roylance, Baxter, Spruce, Stokes, T. Guest, Smith, A. G. Guest, Eyes, Bolshaw, and C. E. Linaker. jun. Buildings Com- mittee: Messrs. C. E. Linaker, J. Mountleld, T. Guest, A. G. Guest, Antwis, Whitley, Hallows, Wright, Chad- wick, Smith, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, Eyes, Warbur- ton, and Jones. Parliamentary Committee: Messrs. J. Moundeld, Spruce, Chadwick, Wright, Linaker, Roylance, C. E. Linaker, jun., A. H. Talbot, J. Smith, Whitley, Broome, Bolshaw, and H. M. Davies. Isolation Hospital Committee: Messrs. Woodward, Wright, Chadwick, Linaker, Pilling, Harrison, Bolshaw, Mountield, A. G. Guest, Broome, Roylance, Jones. and Billiugtnn. Small- pox Hospital Committee : Messrs. Mounfleld and Broome, Roylance, and Jones.

div.head: POLICE MORTUARIES.
div.p: POLICE MORTUARIES.
_ It was decided to accept the tender of Mr. Mort, Runcorn, for the construction, at a cost of £55 Bs. 10d. of a mortuary at Weston Point. _
The Clerk to the Frodshatu Parish Council, wrote asking the Council to ascertain the cost of a mortuary and whether the whole of the cost would have to be borne by the township. _ . .
Mr. Ashton said that if the mortuary was provided by the district Council the district council would have to pay for it If provided by the parish it would be a special charge upon Frodsham.
Mr. Linaker siiggested that &public mortuary if pro- vided should be conveniently placed for the use of both Sutton and Frodsham.

Mr. Hallows remarked that a mortuary was greatly needed at Stockton Heath. IMPROVEMENTS AT FRODSHAM. Mr. H. M. Davies, Frodsham, wrote in regard to the Church street improvement. He agreed to give £l.O and sufficient land for the purpose of widening the present footpath psovided a satisfactory wall was erected at the expense of the council. Mr. J. L. Jones wrote agree;ng to the offer of the District Council.
Mr. Woodward moved that U.-I-0.-clerk 'take such steps as were necessary for the prompt carrying out of the work. The motion was carried. HELSBY WATER SUPPLY.

QUESTION REFERRED TO A SUB;CO—MAIITTEE. The clerk reeommended the appointment of a special sub-committee to go into the question of the Helsby water supply. The matter had been gone into but it had been found impossible to come to a satis- factory arrangement.. The Clerk's suggestion was unanimously adopted the chairman, vice-chairman and Mr. C. E. Linaker jun. being elected to form the sub-committee.
STREET PAVING AT STOCKTON REATH. It was decided to proceed with the paving of Bedford- street, Cawdor-street and Birch-street, Stockton Heath.

THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL. Mr. Woodward reported that work at the isolation hospital was proceeding satisfactorily though hardly so rapidly as might have been wished. The clerk of works had received another appointment and he suggested that he be allowed to attend to the duties of his new appointment in conjunction with his present duties, at a salary to be arranged. He also suggested that a committee should visit the respective works of Messrs. Johnson, Garnett, Weaver and Greenhalgh, Warrington to inspect their goods with the view to the arranging of a contract for the furnishing of the hospital. The report was adopted.

div.head: A' VERY PORTIA.
div.p: A' VERY PORTIA.

I "And what then? " Phyllis asked, a smile trembling about her lips. "Can you ask? Why, counsel's ease on the other side would be a desperate one indeed. If he knew ! before oecepting the brief who was retained for the plaintiff, he would hesitate. Presuming he decides to proceed—as he would—what a forlorn hope! " f "It is still a mystery," she said. "Recollect, the jury is composed of men—earnest, sincere, but susceptible. men. Can you blame them? ! The plaintiff, herself a pathetic picture of hopeless grief, gives evidence in broken tones under the delicate guidance of her counsel, Iwhose lovely face, minute by minute, reflects the emotions aroused by the unfolding story, while her slender hands play restlessly with her brief. Wig and gown and all, 1 can see you quite clearly—a very I Portia-"

I "It wouldn't he like that a bit," Phyllis remon- -1 strated," and I would be quite sincere." I "Of course, and then there would be the danger_ to your learned friend. Plaintiff's evidence concluded, what is the position ? The judge, who so far has had no disputes to settle between counsel, maintains an impassive exterior. But on the face of the jnry, even so soon, is 'a suggestion of sympathy." "They wouldn't all," Phyllis said. "Some might have been in the position of the defendant once." „ . . .
• "One, perhaps; and that is a veyy high percentage. And he wciurd agree with the rest. The advocate— not to speak of the plaintiff herself—being so fair, the defendant, of course mtist be a brute.

• " Then counsel for the defendant begins his anwel- ; come task of confounding, in gentle, persuasive manner the plaintiff. She cannot tell any other story, even at his suggestion, so he brings his legal inicroscope to , bear on minute trifles, until they assume alarming proportions in his Er§ee ; he endeavours to make her ; confirm his convictions, but she, in despair of the effort, replies with tears. . "That is sufficient. Counsel for plaintiff inter- venes to save her client from this ogre. ' "-His Lordship, after a dispassionate consideration ; of the circumstances, decides in favour of counsel for I the plaintiff. Counsel for the plaintiff looks expres- sively—tenderly, that is—towards the now plainly sympathetic jury, and, with many feminine touches to adjust her hair and wig, and having daintily arranged her gown, sits down again. _ _
"The east is already won, for the rest doesn't count."

Phyllis blocked most consciously. " I'm not con- vinced," she said. " Juries are business men, not imaginative," " I agree. They would not require any i.aginntion ' —only open eyes and ears to appreciate the extraordin- ary 'conditions that would be introduced with the advent of the lady advocate in the Courts."

didn't think you would have denied women that profession," Phyllis said, reproachfully. As if woman did /not practice already ! • In the Court of Love she is the most eloquent advocate, and sole judge in the only Court of Appeal. (1'; be continued.) _ . .

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

I BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The Sun- day school anniversary in connection with the Hill Cliffe Baptist Chapel was held on Sunday. In the morn- ing there was a fair attendance of scholars and friends. The children sang several special hymns, Miss Alice Cliff° recited the 100th Psalm, Miss Tovvena Thomas, Widnes, sang "There is rest, sweet rest." Mr. J. Harrison, Liverpool, was the preacher. In the after- noon the chapel was full. Mr. William Arnold presided and delivered an address on "Roses and Lilies." The pastor, the Rev. J. S. Hughes, conducted the service and Councillor Brough gave an address. Miss Lily Hargreaves recited the 90th Psalm, and Miss Bouchier gave two well played selections on the violin. Miss T. Thomas sang very sweetly "The better land," and the choir, under the direction of Mr. J. M. Muir, rendered the anthem "Teach me, 0 Lord," and the children's choir Havergal's two hymns, "The buds and bells sweet ' April pleasure springing all around" and "The golden glow is paling, between the cloudy bars." At the even- ing service the chapel was again filled. Mr. Harrison occupied the pulpit and preached from the words "Behold He standeth at the door." Master Harold Jones recited the 551h.chapter of Isaiah, and Miss Towena Thomas sang with effect "Jerusalem" and "He knows." The children contributed two special pieces— " The stars" and "Now the light has gone away," and the choir rendered the anthem, "Breathe upon us an evening blessing." Miss Jones presided at the organ all day. Much credit is due to Mr. G. Moss who, with M the aid of Mr. Muir, trained the children, and to r. J. Moss, jun., for preparing them for the services.

Puncture-Resisting Devices Are still being experimented with, and the good results obtained in preventing both punctures and side slip by covering the tyres of Motor Cars with a leather band studded with metal studs, will probably lead to a somewhat similar device for bicycles being placed on the market. Recently 1 niet a rider using an experimental tyre protector of this kind, consisting of a narrow strip of leather
A ROADSIDE REPAII

rivetted on to the tread of the tyre, and protected at the back of the cever, so that the rivets might not damage the inner tube. The idea seemed to answer well. Most cyclists, however, will prefer to take the trouble to learn ho* to deal with punctures as they ariSe. Finding a Puncture.

During a roadside repair it is often a matter of some difficulty, owing to the lack of the necessary -bowl of water to im- fICFSC the tube in, to locate the puncture. &nue cyclists carry a collapsible drinking cup •;, made of metal rings whir h fold up one within the • Other to allow the cup to be carried in the , Pocket. I have often Wondered what useful purpose these cups could - serve, as one never sees a cyclist drinking out of . One. On a recent ride, however, a friend pro- duced one, which served t to convey a small quan- • tity of water from a neighbouring- brook, and this was carefully applied to the partly inflated tube SEARCHING With the finger till the PUNCTURE. • Puncture was located.

Tyres for Lad: Should be of easy detachability,so that ia ease of puncture a lady rider can attend to her own repairs in the event of male assistance not being forthcom- ing. The Palmer and Clincher varie- ties of tyres, held on by beaded edges, not. wires, are un- doubtedly the tyres of easiest detach- ability. Now, owing . tothelapseof thetyre Patents, these kinds of tyres are made by nearly all the Tyre Companies, and Whatever make of HERE IT Is! , tyres are used the rider can have a choice of either Wired on or beaded edges. div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
thin running-side screw ,in-off into a baulk pocket from the D.—Red ball half an inch out of baulk and one ir,ch from the end of the D. Cue ball at the end of the D.

Diagram 88 shows a stroke that is constantly mishandled by the majority of players. The ob- ject ball is half-au-inch out of baulk and one inch from the end of the D. Played from the (the strtker being in hand) .an in-off into the baulk pocket is an easy enough shot if the cue ball be placed on the D line about 15 to 13 inches from the object ball, and the stroke be made a forcing ono. Played in this way, how- ever, little control can be had over the object ball which may go almost anywhere.. The strength of the stroke doubles the ball back- wards and forwards across the table, and the chances are just about equal as to whether it come to rest in some good position or whether it find some safe position, not to mention the possibility of its falling into one of the centre, pockets. Instead at playing a forcing in-off, a good player places his ball quite close to the object ball, and plays the in-off by means of a thin screw with running side (left hand side in the diagram). Played in this way very little strength is neces- sary, for owing to the cue ball 'being so near the object ball it strikes it without loss of re- verse rotation. Though the in-off played in this 'way may, not at first be quite as easy as the forcing stroke, there is nothing difficult about it, as any player will quickly find by trying it a few times. Confidence is the chief thicg neces- sary for such a stroke, and when a player has found the pocket a few times by mer.ns of a slow thin-sorely he will abandon the forcing stroke altogether. The forcing stroke means trusting to luck for the after position, the slow thin screw almost always means good position for the next stroke, for the object ball strikes one cushion . only, and coincs. nicely away. The degree of thinness of contact will of course determine the direction that will be given the object ball, but, the intersected line on the diagram may be taken as a fair sample of this. Played as shown on the. diagram, a centre pocket in-off would be left for the ensuing stroke. Even with the object ball an inch or two farther from the end of the D the in-off can still be played as a slow screw, but the contact must be a little less thin than when the cue ball is quite close to the object ball.

SLOW SCREWS WITH RUNNING SIDE. Few ordinary players are aware of the assist- ance to be gained from running side when play- ing slow screws, but this virtue of running side is regularly made use of by professionals and good amateurs when good after-position, depends upon the stroke (whether a screw in-off or a screw ball-to-ball cannon) being played with very little strength. The reason that the cue ball can be made to screw a certain distance with less strength when running side is used than when check side is used, is because a ball spinning with -running side is, at the moment of contact with the object ball, rotating in the direction it has to travel and is consequently thrown off the object ball with extra pace much in the same way as though it had touched a cushion whereas 'when it is spinning with check side, the rotation at the moment or contact is in the reverse direc- tion to that in which the object ball is thrown. The slow running side screws most often played .by the best players, are in-offs into either of the fop pockets when the object ball is in such a position that whilst only a slow stroke can keep it out of baulk, a fast stroke will not drive it in and out of baulk.

elow-screw running-side in-offs.—Position A, red ball 261 inches from the top cushion and 181 inches from the side cushion. Cue ball 24 inches from the top cushion and 28 inches from the side cushion • very good stroke is required to get the in-off, and keep the red from going into baulk.

Diagram 89 shows such a position. If the screw in-off at Abe played at all strong thered will in- evitably go into baulk and remain thefe. In fact quite a slow stroke is required to keep the red out of baulk and herein lies the difficUlty of the stroke. Few'except really good players can play slow screws to a pocket any distance away, and only constant practice can make any player really proficient at such a stroke. In trying to screw slowly it is so easy to underserew the stroke and miss the pocket altogether. -Play,ed with running side the stroke is, however, much easier than if played with check side, for an already explained running side causes the cue ball to travel considerably faster after contact than it would were it spinning'the reverse war with check side. Many players play strokes like the ones shown on Diagram 89 with check side under the impre- *ion that the angle of reflection off the s4ie sash ion is very considerably lessened by -t-.&a son of the side transmitted to the object' ball, and Oat this alteration of the angle materially assists in keeping the ball out of baulk, whereas the side transmitted to the object ball by running

side on the cite. ball, considerably incremes its I angle of reflection off the side cushion, and i tends to send it into baulk. As explained, how- ever. in :lie chapter on Side, though side on the lifie-ball may be transmitted to an object-ball the

At Runcorn,on Monday,John William Barlow,licensee of the Rose and Shamrock, Mersey-st:eet, was sum- moned on two charges of keeping his house`opened during prohibited hlburs, and serving beer to Arthur Percival (known as Marsh). At half-past eleven on the night of the Ist inst., Detective Wollershead saw through chinks in the shutters of the kitchen the de- fendant Percival and a lodger, named Eeezley, drinking. He fetched Inspector Egerton and Police-constable Bratt,who watched until 12.40, and saw the defendant fetch beer from the cellar and serve it. The defence was that Percival had hada difference at home, and told to get a fresh place, and he had taken lodgings for the night. It was stated that Percival never had a drink after 10.45 p.m. The defendant was fined 20s.and costs, £2 19s. 6d.--Joseph Edward Jones, licensee of the Volunteer Inn, Granville-street, Runcorn, was fined ss. and costs. 10s. 6d. for being drunk on his licensed premises on the Ist. inst. ALLEGb THEFTS OF BRASS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes, on Monday, Michael M'Conville, 8, Frederick-street, Reuben Hewitt, Fzederick Timperley, and Mary E. Hewitt, Travis-street, Bartholomew Bowles, Victoria-street, and Peter Grady, Margaret-street, were remanded until Thursday, charged on suspicion with having stolen a quantity of brass belonging to some persons unknown. With the exception of Bowles and Grady, they were also charged on suspicion with receiv- ing the metal. Mrs. Hewitt and the man Timperley were allowed out on bail in one sum of £5, and the remainder were ordered to find surety for .8,10 each.

amount transmitted (which is always the reverse side to that which the cue-ball carries) is never very much, and though in the stroke under dis- cussion check-side on the cue-ball may cause the object-ball to rebound from the cushion just a shade more squarely than if the cue-ball had bees struck with running-side (the strength of the stroke and the contact being the same), the difference is far too slight to outweigh the great _advantage of being able to screw with much slower strength when using running side. In fact, in such a stroke the amount of side trans. mitted to the object-ball is even less than in ordinary strokes with side, for as the cue-ball has to be hit well below the centre in order to screw, it cannot by any means receive the maxi- mum of side which it is possible to impart to a ball. tilt This slow screw follows the rule that screw in-offs should be played with running side whenever the pocket is fairly open, and although running side is not pocket side off the ' opposing angle (the angle of the top cushion), there is pleuty of room for the ball to go straight to the pocket, and should it strike the side cushion angle the spin on the ball will generally carry it into the pocket, for owing to the ball travelling slowly it will not as a rule be thrown on to the upper angle; and even should it strike the upper angle it can still enter the pocket, provided it strike the angle close to the fall of the slate.

These running side slow-screw in-offs with the object ball some distance from the pocket, are far too difficult for the .very moderate player, but those players who occasionally make forties and fifties should assiduously practise them: Per- haps the best way to practise them is to begin with a very easy one by ,placing the balls near each other and the pocket, and then to gradually place the balls farther and farther apart and farther from the pocket, yet still forming much the same angle with each other and the pocket. The positions shown at B on Diagram 89 show a‘ series of such practice strokes. The nearer the balls are to the pocket the more slowly should the stroke be played.

div.head: rAGRAM 93.
div.p: rAGRAM 93.

Diagram 90 shows two screw-back in-offs into a top pocket. Most players would play both these strokes in exactly the same way—that is, with check side. The stroke shown at A must be played with check side, for here the pocket is very blind, and check side (left-hand in the diagram)---,,.._wi1l be pocket side off the opposing angle (the angle of the top cushion). When, however, ,the balls are situated as at B the pocket is moderately open, and therefore the strong necessity for cheek side no longer exists, so much so that a really good player often uses running side in playing this in-off, because when this side is used the stroke can be made. far more gently than with check side. In fact, no,other stroke more for- cibly sxleitionstrates how much more slowly a screw can be played with running sidAsthan with check side. If any player who can play slow screws fairly well will place the balls as shown at B, keeping to the measurements given tinder the diagram, he will find that with running side the cue ball will recoil quite briskly, but that with check side it will come back quite slowly (the strength of the stroke being. of course, the same in both eases). Played with running side the object ball can easily be kept out of baiilk, whereas with cheek side it would require a very good stroke to prevent it crossing the line. Of course, even with running side the object ball could not be kept out of baulk were it a little farther from the cue ball instead of being quite near to it as shown on the diagram.
