div.head: LEVERS TO THE EDITOR. I WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ____
div.p: LEVERS TO THE EDITOR. I WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ____

Councillor Stott and the Next Election. Sir,—May I congratulate "airplay" upo i his last letter? There is a decided improvement in the tone— even if the argument is not convincing. Let us not be unfair to the gentleman who for some weeks has headed this controversy. Councillor Stott is not yet entitled to a pedestal; nor, probably, does he desire one. As the result of the next election cannot depeal upon the actions of one individual, who can content himself with voting in one place and working for a candidate in another, there is no real cause for alarm. Let us not therefore become down-hearted. What we now understsnd is, that Councillor Stott is to be "passive" in Warrington and "active " in Newton. He in other words, will not co-operate " actively " in Warrington for the party he will support " passively." It is a peculiar position for any man to occupy and it is to be hoped that he may find it less irksome than it appears to be on the face of it. The Liberals may yet win without Councillor Stott's activity. With those few • final comments Councillor Stott passes from the con- troversy, so far as I am concerned, and will now devote our time and attention to something more easy of understanding if not quite so exciting. In the first place, let me answer" Fairplay's" question —" If a Labour 6andidate had been in the field for Warrington, would he have supported him, if not, why net ? " It's a fair question and shall have a fair answer. If a Labour candidate had been in the field against a Conservative candidate I should, providing, of course, that the candidate was an honest Labour man and had promised to support certain measures, undoubtedly give him my support—not in any ' passive ' way but in a real,' acti ve,'•whole-hearted manner. Will " rplay" answer my question as fairly and as plainly as I have answered hist "If a Liberal candidate is in the field for Warrington, and there is no Labour candidate, will he support the Liberal candidate, if not, why not ?" "Fairplay's" next question is—" Would you expect a Trades Unionist to invite his employer to become chairman of his Trade Society? I should say not. Then why expect him to send employers, capitaliets,and monopolists to Parliament to make lbws governing him and the] trade in qaestion on which he depends for his living?" " Fairplay " has, in that question, melted down Labour representation. To liken Parliament to a workshop where the people of this land are to be repre- sented by employers of labour on the one side and ern- ployeson the other is as unfair to the'employer as it is to the employ. that is class legislation with a vengeance. He cannot mean that all the "capitalists "—dreadful men—will be on one side the house and all -the Trade Unionists weak mortals —on the other, and that it is to be a continual fight between " capital " and "labour." Surely not. God forbid that we should ever contemplate such a sorry state of affairs. Things are bad enough as they are; but ono dreads to think of what would happen should the representation of the people reach such a sordid level. Is that the "practical Christianity " which" Fairplay "aspires to promulgate? He seems to go upon the principle that if you would see life as it should be you must look for it through the windows of a Trades Union Society window? I should like to ask him whether a Trades Unionist can become or ever is, a capitalist? Are there any good capitalists ? If he will answer those questions I am prepared to argue the matter further with him. I dare not trespass further on your space this week.— Yours truly, 17th April, 1905.
NUNQUALM.

A Poser for Protectionists Sir,—Coming, as it does, immediately after his secret negotiations with the Chamberlain group, and at a moment when the Protectionists propaganda seemed to have been effectually checked, a letter which has just been addressed by Mr. Balfour to the Editor of The Yorkshire Herald" has a special significance, and de- serves close consideration. It appears that the well- known and prosperous firm of Reckitt and Sons,Limited have decided to open a branch manufactory in .New York. The "tariff reformers" in Hull and the vicinity at once raised a cry that local labour wa.s being penalised and that the incident proved the advantage of a Pro- tectionist tariff. Sir James Reckitt and Mr. T. R. Ferens, directors of the firm, both convinced Free Traders, replied that no reduction of labour employed I in Hull was involved and that the profits of the American branch would be used to a large extent in developing their British business. Thus left in a quandary, the j "tariff reformers " turned to the Prime Minister, who ' replied in these two oracular sentences : "It really is beyond argument that hostile tariffs which withdraw capital and plant from this country do it a serious injury. The fact that same tariffs may also injure the country which imposes them may be true, hut is not to the point." The last phrase is a magnificent specimen of Balfourian insouciance. The Prime Minister's corres- pondent is a plain man with a plain creed. Not being a Free Trader, he is a Protectionist. He believes that the American tariff withdraws capital and plant from this country, and that our tariff or comparative lack of tariff encourages such withdrawal; and, so believing,he desires to get even with the enemy by copying his method of "retaliation " and "protection." Mr. Balfour, however, is still not ready to declare himself in any practical way; so, in one sentence he states the Chamberlainite case,and in the next, albeit under pre- I tence of irrelevance, the Free Trade reply. We are I asked to adopt a Tariff system which, he admits, may damage as much as it helps us, but this, if you please, "is not the point." Shall we ever learn, what, in Mr. Balfour's view is "the point" of the fiscal controversy?• The "Tariff Reformers," of course, ignore the second sentence and seize upon Vie first as a confirmation of their argument about the case of Reckitt .% Sons Ltd., and Mr. Balfour's words serve them well. In this muddle-headed view of the natural course of trade, every overflow of surplus wealth and energy into foreign lands becomes a "withdrawal of capital and plant from this country" which, even though there is no reduction of home employment, is supposed to be in some mysterious way injurious to us. It does not occur to , these wiseacres to cite the innumerable instances of the I establishment of French, German, or American businesses on British soil as a sign of the superiority of our tariff system and the injuriousness of their own. There is an instructive likeness and a still more instructive unlikeness between the two cases. In the direct employment of British labour the one case balances the other; we evidently gain at least as much as we lose. But indirectly we gain enormously and lose nothing. Let us imagine the transfer of two identical factories, the one from Berlin to London, the other from London to New York. The price of Reckitt's Blue, thanks to the Protectionist system, is 40 per cent. higher in New York than in London, and it is fair to suppose that profits are proportionate. While direct employment in London remains the same, then the I British proprietors of the New York factory are receiv- ing 40 per cent more profits than the German proprietors of London factory. We know the Board of Trade' returns that these profits pass not in money, but in commodities —from London to Berlin in the shape of British manufactures, and from New York to London in raw cotton, wheat, and other food an 4 raw materials. It is the extra 40 per cent of the latter, the tribute paid by the consumers of a Protectionist country to foreign Free Trade capital that has got behind the tariff wall, , that accounts for the "surplus of imports " which Mr. Seddon and other "tariff reformers" cannot understand. As British "capital and plant" has been steadily flowing abroad in this way for fifty years past, so that ; 'we own to-day thousands of manufactories in all parts of the world, it is "beyond argument "that we would I have been ruined long ago if the tariff reformers were right. Instead, the conditions of British labour have steadily if slowly improved, and the income tax on these foreign properties mounts up and up. There is, indeed I a simple test by which the Chamberlainite can be• effectually cornered. Mr. Balfour's first sentence is as applicable to the British colonies as to foreign countries. Canada, the pee of the Protectionist party, has been created by the removal of capital,plant,and labour from this country; and Mr. Chamberlain and his friends I glory in the process. Would they do so if they really I believed that it involved a "serious injury " to the Mother Country ?—Faithfully yours, G. H. PERRIS. London, April 19th, 1905.

div.head: FATAL PUSH.
div.p: A FATAL PUSH.
Singular Saturday Night Inoinent at Warrington.

The peculiar circumstances surrounding the death of Edward Kelly (-11), a painter, of 40, Stephen-street, gave rise last week-end to sensational rumours. The affair was investigated by Coroner Brighouse and a special jury at the Police Station on Tuesday and on the evidence offered, the case resolved itself into a simple one of "Accidental death. " The facts were briefly aummse up by the Coroner. At 9.30 on Saturday night. be said, Kelly was in Bewsey-street drunk. He stopped a man named William Bradshaw and asked him to give him a drink. Bradshaw declined and pushed Kelly away, saying he did not want anything to do with him. Kelly fell, his head striking the curbstone. He was picked up by Bradshaw and others and conveyed to the Infirmary, where he died without regaining consciousness. Several witnesses gave very similar versions of the incident. Bradshaw, who is a hawker, living at 7, Boardman's- yard off Haydock-street, was called. When he refused io give Kelly a drink, deceased wanted to fight him. Witness gave him a slight push and he fell backwards, and his head appeared to strike the footpath. He (witness) had been under medical Care for some time and he was so weak that he could not fight or use violence to any man. Dr. Lee, junior house surgeon at the Infirmary, sub, milted the results of the post mortem examination. There was, he said, a fracturi at the base of the skull. and death was probably due to that. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and exonerated Bradshaw from all blame. The Coroner intimated that he agreed with the verdict

div.head: Contest For the Chairmanship.
div.p: Contest For the Chairmanship.

There was a contest for the chairmanship of the War- rington Board of Guardians at the annual meeting on Wednesday. Messrs. W. Hickman and J. Biltinge were nominated for the office, and the voting resulted in the honour being conferred upon Mr. Bißinge. There were present at the meeting :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Revs. Dr. Mercer, and T. R. Matthews, Dr. Murray, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. A. Brooks, A. J. Jolley, W. Knowles, NV. Hickman, J. Billinge, J. Payton, S. Davies, T. H. Ashcroft, G. Thompson, G. Mather, E. L. Bent, W. Flannaghan,M. W. Seton,NV. Houghton, R. Forshaw, R. Bolton, 'l.'. Ritchie, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent). The clerk was elected to preside over the meeting, pending the election of chairman. Mr. SurroN observed that this was the thirty-seventh year in succession on which he had taken the chair, and sixty years had expired since he first became a iunior clerk. He had, he thought led a pretty useful life so far. (Hear hear). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

IMr. KNOWLES said he was of a very forgiving dis- posltion—(laughter)—and the gentleman win he was going to propose as chair,aan had in days gone by been one of his strongest opponents. When friends of his (Mr. Knowles) wanted to appoint him chairman or junior vice-chairman this particular member used to oust him. (Laughter), He always respected a man who could do that sort of thing. (Laughter). That gentleman's war-like tactics and perseverance were as much to the fore to-day as they were seven or eight years ago. He was alluding to Mr. Hickman. On some occasions he (Mr. Knowles) had opposed Mr. Hickman quite as strongly as he now supported him. He did not support Mr. Hickman out of any particular feelings of friendship or any motives other than public motives. He felt that if they elected Mr. Hickman that the ratepayers, at any rate as far as the Borough of Warrington was concerned, would feel gratified and pleased. Lately there was a hullabaloo in the borough about the extravagance of the Board and Mr. Hickman took up the cudgel of warfare. He must have spent a great deal of time and given much perse- verance and ability to that matter. He did not go along in the swim with the ordinary crowd of Guardians, but he took a lead of his own. Alluding to Mr. Hickman's successful oppositioa to the extension scheme, Mr. Knowles appealed to the Guardians not to bear malice or ill-will, or to say that because Mr. Hickman had beaten them on that question they would nominate someone to oppose him for the chairmanstap. Mr. Hickman had had a good many years' experience as a Guardian and some fire or six years ago he held the office of vice-chairman. He and his party, however, seemed to get out of favour but it seemed that to-day there was a strong amalgamation. It was formed at the critical moment some months ago when people found that the rates were going to be spent a little Imore lavishly than they dight to be. Mr. THOMPSON seconded. Both Mr. Hickman and , Mr. Knowles had, he said, been vice-chairmen of the Board, and they were the two gentlemen whom he con- sidered eligible for the chairmanship that day. He did not think it right, when there were gentlemen present who had served in the vice-chair, that anyone should miss that step before succeeding to the chair. Mr. Hickman had been a very useful member of the Board for ten years and he devoted a great deal of time and attention to the new Infirmary seheme. He was now retiring from business :and would be able to give the whole of his time to the duties of the Board. He (Mr. Thompson) hoped tie election would be unanimous, Air. Hickman was one of those who hit straight from the shoulder, but he was genuine in his actions. Mr. S. DAVIES said he hoped.the Board would not ' consider he was knocked down altogether after the speeches to which they had listened. He had been asked to perform what he would like to have said was an agreeable duty—to propose a gentleman for the office of chairman. Unfortunately he learned that morn- ing that there were no fewer than four or five members of the Board fired with the ambition of becoming chairman. (Laughter.) Therefore he felt in a rather awkward position because they could hardly in that case chose a man who would be agreeable to all. They must, however, try to pick out one who had the first claim upon their votes. He considered that Mr. J. Billinge, whose name he should propose, had that claim. He had length of service on his side ; he had been I chairman of the Newton Relief Committee for about five years ; he had also held the vice-chairmanship of the Assessment Committee ; and in various other ways he had rendered admirable service to the Board. Mr. HOUGHTON said he was not afraid of seconding; on the contrary he was pleased to do so. He could not bear to see a division on the election of Chairman, but he supported Mr. Billinge for the reasons mentioned by Mr. Davies—his long, continuous and valuable service to the Board. He occasionally visited the Relief Committee at Newton and the work there was very heavy. Mr. Billinge Zdirected it in an able and pains- taking way. Without a suggestion of disparagement of Mr. Hickman's claims, he felt bound to support Mr. , Billinge's nomination. Before the vote was taken. Mr. JOLLEY said it had been the practice in the past when there were two nominations for the candidates to retire while the vote was taken, The member who obtained the majority was afterwards declared unani- mously elected. Mr. lisowLus : I object strongly to that. They are entitled to vote for themselves and they might just as well see who votes for them as hear afterwards. Mr. JOLLEY : To test the feeling of the Board I pro- pose that the general practice of the Board be adhered to and that the candidates be invited to retire.
_ After further discussion the CLERK held that it was optional to the candidates whether they remained in the room during the voting or not. The candidates decided not to retire. _ .
_ On the vote being taken, Mr. Billingo was elected by 11 votes to S. _ _ _

-- In returning thanks, Mr. BELLING fr. said he valued the honour and trusted that in following the distinguished gentlemen who had occupied the chair, he would merit a continuance of the confidence the Board had reposed in him. He hoped he would be able to dischaige the duties efficiently and to the entire satisfaction of the members. He was sorry he had been put into com- petition with his esteemed colleague Mr. Hickman who Joined the Board at the same time that he (Mr.Billinge) took up the work. The Guardians had,however,learned long ago to agree to differ on little minor matters. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that during his chairmanship the country might realize a revival of trade,and that in consequence there would be a diminution of destitution, and that the Board would continue its aggressive policy for many years to come. THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.

On the motion of Mr. BENT, seconded by Mr. RITc lIIE, Mr. W. Hickman was unanimously elected to the vice-chair. Mr. HICKMAN, in returning thanks, said he thought more highly of a unanimous vote than a divided one. He was sorry Mr. Billinge and himself were placed in opposition for the chairmanship. He thanked the mem- bers sincerely for the honour conferred upon him and although he did not expect to be able to please every- body, his time and abilities would always be at their disposal. He would endeavour to work in the interests of the ratepayers, the union, and the officials, and he hoped they would have a very happy year, and that there would be no wrangling. (Laughter.) There might be differences of opinion, but he trusted that when such differences arose they would not be made a personal matter. (Hear, hear.) ....

div.head: PADGATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE PADGATE SCHOOLS.

The Superintendent of the Padgate Schools reported that on April sth Mrs. French and Miss Ivey • gave a party to the officers and an enjoyable evening was spent. On April Bth the officers of the Workhouse gave their entertainment in the schools which was much appreci- ated and enjoyed. Thirteen boys and six girls attended the confirmation service at Hollinfare. Confirmation cards had been received as a present from Miss Broadbeut.

div.head: TILE LATE ALDERMAN SUTTON.
div.p: TILE LATE ALDERMAN SUTTON.

The CLERK read a letter from Hr. Thomas A. Sutton thanking the Guardians for their letter conveying the sympathy of the members with the family of the late Alderman Sutton in the loss they had sustained by his death. He assured the Board that not only was that soothing expression of condolence highly appreciated but, aocornpanied by a kindly recognition of his father's en- deavours to serve the public of Warrington, it rendered the resolution one which his sons and relatives would often refer to with pride.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW SIDING.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW SIDING.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board consenting to the proposal of the Guardians in regard to the provision of three chutes for use in the delivery of heavy goods to the Workhouse from a siding pro- posed to he constructed adjoining the House on the Cheshire Lines Railway. A committee consisting of the Chairman, vice-Chair- man, Messrs. Jolley, Brooks, Knowles, the chairman of the House Committee, and the Master, was appointed to go _into the details of the scheme.

THE ABLE-BODIED INMATES. At a meeting of the House Committee on April 7th, a roll call of the men wa4 proceeded with and in the cases of a largo number of apparently able-bodied inmates they were directed to discharge themselves from the House on Friday. At a meeting ons April 4th, it was recommended that Miss Davies be appointed charge nurse at a salary of £32 10s. per annum, to com- mence duty on May 2nd. and to be allowed ten days holiday later in the summer. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Master and Matron (Hr. and Mrs. Awhery) and compliment try references were made to their services to the Board. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: ACTION AGAINST COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON.
div.p: ACTION AGAINST COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON.
Successful Claim for Damages for Trespass.

His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., was at the Warrington County Court on Wednesday, called upon to adjudicate in an interesting case in which Horatio Julian, 3, Myrtle Grove, Latchford, sought to recover from Councillor Pemberton, the sum of .222 for wrong- ful trespass. Plaintiff was represented by Mr. A. Browne, Mr. Madden (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) appearing on behalf of the defendant. Mr. Browne stated that the plaintiff was a cabinet maker whose wages averaged £2 per week. He lodged with his father and mother in a shop rented by his mother. His parents got into financial difficulties with the result that a distress was loved upon their goods for arrears of rent, several of the plaintiff's possessions being also seized. Plaintiff at once consulted Mr. A. J. Willett, who drew up for him a declaration under the Lodgers' Goods Protection Act, that the landlord must not sell the goods belonging to the plaintiff. The goods mentioned were a black cob, a cart and a set of brass mounted harness, a joiner's bench and tools which were the absolute property of the plaintiff. That notice was served upon the bailiff (Mr. Mainwaring) who executed the distress, but he took no notice of it ihid sold the goods by public auction. Plaintiff gave evidence bearing out Mr. Browne's statement, and produced receipts to show that the articles named were purchased by him. He bought the horse on the hire purchase system from a Mr. Hill. Cross-examined : It was arranged between 'himself and his father that he should see Mr. Hill and buy the horse from him and then allow his father to use the horse to assist him in his business. His father did rt.lt pay a single penny towards the cost of the horse. His object in bringing the action was not to recover part of the money realized by the distraint and so do Mr. Pemberton out of the rent which was owilg. Evidence was given by Mr. H. J. Pearse and Mr. S. Hall (Manchester) as to the plaintiff having purchased a joiner's bench and a pony which were sold by Mr. Mainwaring. Mrs. Julian also gave evidence to the same effect. In answer to Mr. Madden she said she was now living at Latchford. The house at Latchford was originally rented in her name but was subsequently transferred to her son.
Mr. Madden: For what purpose was the house transferred. -

Witness : Never mind the purpose. Mr. F. A. Barton, articled clerk to Mr. Willett. said he saw Mr. Mainwaring on the day of the sale and told him if he sold the plaintiff's goods an action for damages would be brought against him, Mr. Mainwar- ing replied " Oh— the action,we have had notice of this action served upon us a few days ago." Mr. Willett gave evidence as to having prepared the declaration for the plaintiff. This concluded the plaintiff's case. Councillor Pemberton stated that he gave Mr. and Mrs. Julian every opportunity to pay the rent before he distrained upon their goods. Six months before he issued the distress warrant he met Mr. Julian who told him he was purchasing a horse for which his son was going security. Mr. Mainwaring said he did not recognize the declaration given him by: the plaintiff because he did not regard the plaintiff in the light of a lodger. He did not get the declaration until two days before the sale. Mr. Madden, at the outset, took objection to the declaration, but was overruled by his Honour. Mr. Madden proceeded to argue that the plaintiff was not a lodger. The whole family were living together, and combining for their mutual protection. There was, he contended, great discrepancy between the evidence of the plaintiff and the evidence of the mother, and he asked his Honour to disbelieve the statement of both. He suggested that the horse was purchased by plaintiff's father, and that the money was paid from time to time out of the proceeds of the business which Mr. Julian, senr., carried on. The whole thing, he suggested, was a combination on the part of the members of the family to avoid their proper responsibility. His Honour said he was favourably inclined by the ' manner in which the plaintiff and his mother had given their evidence, and be could not think they were parties to any conspiracy. He thought Mr. Mainwaring had made a mistake. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed with costs.
A Newcastle man was asked on Saturday what he tbouirht of London. Doubtfully, and as if making a too generous concession, be replied, "Well, it's a change."

of a certain section of people who tried to handle him (Mr. Dunnico) rather roughly. Neither of them appeared to be much worse for it—(laughter)—and if Mr. Macidison shared his (Mr. Dunnico's) feeling he would do exactly the same thing again under the same circumstances. They in Warrington were commencing what was going to prove a strenuous and possibly a very bitter conflict. He had no doubt whatever as to the result but he appealed to them to act so that—be the result what it man—the Liberal party would emerge from the conflict with clean hands and a clean conscience. (Applause.) If they could not roll Mr. Crosfleld into Parliament excqpt on the top of a beer barrel, then they would keep him out. (Applause.) Mr. Robert Pier- point WM an honest man; he knew his own opinions and had declared himself AN OUT AND OUT CHANIBERLAINITE, so that at the next election they had a clear issue. Cobden, Bright, Gladstone. and all the great statesmen of the past were Free Traders. It might be said that , they did not know the present circumstances, but it ' should be borne in mind that every living man who had held the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer was a Free Trader. Then again great business men said that Mr. Chamberlain's policy was a wild cat policy and almost every professor of political , economy in our universities was an out and out Free Trader. The whole principle of Protection was as economically false as it was politi- cally disastrous. But he was opposed to it on the moral, ethical, and religious grounds. The kernel of true religion was the fatherhood of God andithe brother- hood of men and Protection was quite contrary to the idea of the brotherhood of men. Mr. Donnie° quoted a manifesto signed by prominent Church of England clerymen opposing Protection on the grounds above- mentioned. He proceeded to deal with the Education , question, and said they would never got a satisfactory ! national system until they said to,the priest, the parson and the minister, as such, Take your hands off it." If they (the clergy) wanted to have any part in the settlement of tho question they must come in as citizens, as fathers who had the welfare of the children at heart,;and not with the desire to promote the interests of any particular church. The Government had protected the rich brewer in the Licensing Act, and had protected the rich Jew in South Africa by the introduction of Chinese labour, and it now sought to protect tha landlords by taxing bread. At present the House of Commons was the theatre of the most despicable proceedings that had ever disgraced English public life. The last act in the farce was being played out, the curtain was about to drop, and he would nrr,'e his hearers to help to send men to the House of Commons who, whatever their failings, were sincere. He asked them to return Mr. Crosfield for Warrington because he stood as the embodiment of the only principles which would make ,! the nation truly great. (Applause.) ! Mr. JOSEPH' HOWES, in moving a vote of thanks to the speakers, said the next election would touch the cupboards of the people. Would they vote in favour of cheap) food or dear food? Mr. Howes advocated that Irish should be allowed to manage their own affairs, pointing out that Home Rule had never failed in any part of the world. (Applause). 3 Councillor CLEGG seconded and the vote was heartily accorded.
The Chairman having been thanked for presiding, the meeting concluded.

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
Latchford Branch to ha Opened.

Another record of progress was presented at the quarterly meeting of the Warrington Equitable In- dustrial Co-operative Society which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening. In the absence through illness of the president (Mr. T. Birchall) the ch.tir was taken by Mr. W. Jeffrey. There was a fair attendance. . .

The CHAIRMAN expressed regret at the illness of the president, but said they were pleased to hear that his condition showed an improvement. They trusted that that improvement would be maintained and that Mr. Birchall would be with them again in a few weeks. They had experienced another very successful quarter, in fact it was a record one. The sales and profits were increas- ing and they were able to pay the usual dividend. In about a month they hoped to have completed the extension of the Winwick-road branch and that, it was expected would increase the turnover. The committee had agreed to purchase the old Vicarage and adjoiningland at Latchford and plans for two new shops to be erected there had been, approved. With regard to the presenta- tion to Mr. Rathbone, the photograph had not yet been taken, but it was hoped that at the next meeting they would be able to rrange for the formal handing over of the testimonial.

div.head: BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: THE BALANCE SHEET.

In subraittting the 177th report and balance sheet the committee stated that the sales for the quarter amount to £37,481 10s. 2d., which showed an increase over last quarter of £252 3s. 2d., and £993 G. 10d. over the corresponding quarter of last year. The profits realised, after providing interest on capital amounting to £5Bl 13s. 9d., and meeting all liabilities, would allow a dividend of 3s. in the 2 on members' purchases with a balance of 2180 2s. Id. to be carried forward. The report was adopted. ADVICE AS TO WITHDRAWALS.

Speaking of colonial loyalty Sir Wilfred Laurier said " We are loyal because we are free." The corrolary of that was that they would not be loyal if they were not free. If we put shackles upon them, they had no longer any regard for the mother country, because the mother would be unnatural. Mr. Chamberlain told us that We ought to mike sacrifices, that we ought to IMPOSE BURDENS ON ounsrixfis AND OUR CHILDREN, but the colonies had not asked us to do anything of the sort. (Applause). Even if they had,speaking for him- self, he (Mr. Maddison) would refuse to do it. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Wycliffe Congregational Church.

The service at the above church on Sunday evening was of a special character, and was attended by a large congreption. The choir gave an able rendering of "The Cruciffxion" (Stainer), the chorus "Fling wide the gates" being well sung. The principal soloists were Mrs. R. H. Pearson, Mr. W. H. Wallington; Mr. A. Griffiths, Mr. B. Hibbert, and Mr. A. Cotterill. Without a doubt Sunday evening's interpretation—the third—of Stainer's work, ivas the finest ever given by the Wycliffe choir.

div.head: Ideal City.
div.p: The Ideal City.

The Rev. H. Dannico preached at the Parr Hall on Sunday evening on" Christ and the ideal city," salect- ing for his text the words "And when He was come near, He beheld the city, and wept over it, saying,' If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace, but now they are hid from thine eyes:" The preacher described the entry of Christ into Jerusalem and the cause of His weeping, and pointed out that probably for the first time in His life Christ was zon- fronted with the city problem. The first step He took in the solution of the problem was to enter the temple and cleanse it from corruption. The clean church ever resulted in a clean city. The preacher then pointed out that the key to the social problem lay inside the Christian churches, and said that all social reform was ever preceded by a true revival in religion.

the happiness of the working classes." At the 1895 election the Liberals were defeated and the Tory Government entered into possession of a surplus of four millions. The Government also came into office on a rising trade and the country became prosperous. Did the Government provide old age pensions? No. Acts were passed for the benefit of the English landlords, Church schools, and Irish landlords in the years 1896, 1897, and 1898, but it was only in 1899, when there was no sutplus,that the Tories awoke to the necessityof old age pensions. They suddenly became alive to the fact that something ought to be done for the working classes, and gave them an Old Age Pension Committee, (Laughter.) Mr. Maddisbn dealt with the proposals advanced by the committee and said the workers would have to watch the old age pensions business or it would degrade instead of help them. At the outset of the fiscal campaign Mr. Chamberlain said he believed old age pensions would become practicable if his policy were carried out. Now, however, they never heard him mention the pensions. They had been absolutely eliminated from his fiscal programme. He (Mr. Maddison) was a member of the committee of the working classes which advocated the treatment of pensions on the lines laid down by Mr. Charles Booth. He wanted the workers to stand firmly by the principle of that scheme, which was universal pensions to people who had reached the age of sixty-five, or sixty if possible. (Appause). Free traders were told that they had no policy. He hoped they had not • THE DECEPTIVE PROMISES

of Mr. Chamberlain. (Hear, hear.) The Government's policy of the last ten years bad made for the present a large scheme of old age pensions practically impos- sible. The Government's extravagance had cut at the very root of social reform. During the ten years from 1894 to 1904 the expenditure on the army and navy had increased by fifty millions, whilst only five millions more had been spent on education. That showed how highly civilized we were ! (Laughter.) Now the Government had flown to Protection in order to finance their pernicious Imperialism. Protection was natural to a military nation—it was all part of that ruinous imperialism which always had its eyes in the utter- most parts of the earth. The list of Protected nations I was

div.head: PARISH COUNCIL MEETINGS. Stockton Heath. THE FUTURE POSITION OF THE VILLAGE.
div.p: PARISH COUNCIL MEETINGS. Stockton Heath. THE FUTURE POSITION OF THE VILLAGE.

Perhaps the most important business done at the annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Parish Council held on Monday, was the appointment of a committee to go into the question as to whether it is advisable that the district should seek urban powers. There were present at the meeting Messrs. J. H. Clarke, J. W. Bouchier, J. Fairhurst, J. Whitley, J. Hallows, W. Mclntyre, S. F. Welsby, 'l'. Williams, H. J. Westbrook and E. .Bradshaw (clerk and assistant overseer.)

ECONOMY AND EFFICIENCY. The Clerk said he had written to the County Council and Rural District Council, as instructed, asking them to exercise the greatest economy consistent with efficiency in view of the increasing rates. He had received an acknoMedgment of the letter in each case.
APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.
The first business was the appointment of a chairman for the year and that honour was unanimously con- ferred upon Mr. J. W.Bouchier.

Mr.WE;TnnooK said he regretted that,Mr.Clarke would not again act as chairman as they all know the great in- terest he took in parish affairs, and knew, also, that the parish was indebted to him for the energy and painstaking work he had done to secure its welfare. (Hear, hear.) Ho proposed that the vacancy should be filled by Mr. Bouchier—(hear, hear)—in whom they felt, a great amount of confidence for his fairness and levelheaded- ness. He was sure they would have from him the same loyal assistance as they had had from Mr. Clarke, as well as the same zeal on behalf of the parish. Stockton Heath was fast ripening into a comely plum which the Rural Council would do its best to keep and which Warrington, with its octopus hands, would like to pluck. Midway between those two things there was the plum's own feeling that it might claim a separate existence and entity for itself. He saw that in the negotiations which would be bound to take place on that occasion there would be a call for the best men the village possessed to look after its interest, and he thought they , would be well looked after under the chairmanship of Mr. Bouchier. (Hear, hear.) IMr. Hallows seconded the motion. He said it needed a good man to fill Mr. Clarlco's place, but in Mr. Bortchier they had such a man. Mr. Clarke supported with pleasure. Regarding the eulogium which had been passed upon him personally he was afraid he did not deserve all that had been said, but he had tried during the three years he had been chair- man to perform the duties to the' best of his ability. They had always worked harmoniously together, and he hoped they would continue to do so. The motion as above stated was carried unanimously. Mr. Bouchier in returning thanks said he would not have accepted the position had it not been that Mr Clarke would still be a member of the Connell. He. endorsed all that had been said regarding Mr. Clarke's chairmanship. They had had a little trouble with the Corporation, but that was only to be expected, considering the relative positions of the two places. He thought it would not be very long before they would be called upon to consider whether they were in a position to govern themselves or not. There was, of course,greatdifficulty in regard to that question.He had a talk with a gentleman well versed in municipal matters the other day and explained the position of the village to him, and he gave his opinion that it would be better for them to try for self-government, even if the expense was a little more than they wore under now. He thanked them for the honour they had done him in electing him chairman.

THE OVERSEERS. Messrs. Whitley and Fairhurst were unanimously re- appointed overseers and thanked for their past services. A. REDUCTION IN THE R.kTES. Mr. Bouchier said the assistant overseer had got the threatened increase of rates reduced by lid. in the on the special rate. They were all very pleased, and he would like the reduction to be generally known. The Clerk reported that last year was commenced with a balance in hand of .C 4 and ended with a balance in hand of £3 4s.

ASSISTANT OVERSEER'S SALARY INCREASED. Mr. Whitley proposed an increase in the salary of Mr, Bradshaw, the assistant overseer. He said Mr. Brad- shaw had always carried out his duties in a most satis- factory manner during the seven years he had held the position, and the way the books were kept was very pleasing to the overseers. The work now had doubled in extent, and he thought Mr. Bradshaw was thoroughly deserving of an increase of salary. When Mr. Bradshaw was receiving 225 in 1998, the ratable value of Stockton Heath was £3,788, whilst since his salary was fixed at £4O the rateable value had gone up by £4,000. Mr. Whitley quoted figures to show that as compared with other assistant overseers Mr. Bradshaw was underpaid, and moved that his salary be increased to £6O. Mr. Hallows : If Mr. Bradshaw applies for an increase T think we would willingly consider it, but I have never heard of his having asked for an increase. I think we ought to have an application first. Mr. Wolsby also thought it would have been better if an application had be3n received, though there was something to be said for recognizing the fact that an increase,was deserved. Still, he thought £2O was a big increase, even although Mr. Bradshaw deserved it. Mr. Whitley said Mr. Bradshaw had asked the over- seers to bring the question of his salary forward instead of his formally applying for an increase. He thought they might give him the £2O increase with an under- standing that he would not apply again for five years. Mr. Fairhurst seconded Mr. Whitley's motion. Mr. Westbrook moved as an amendment that the salary be increased to £5O instead of £6O. He thought the ratepayers would object to a 50 per cent. increase. Mr. Hallows seconded. He said if Mr. Whitley had stated that Mr. Bradshaw had approached him regarding the salary he would not have made the remarks be did. , Mr. Clarke, Mr. Welsby, and Mr. Bouchier supported the amendment, which was approved. Mr. Bradshaw, after having been informed of the Council's decision, said he made it a rule not to apply for increases, and the present' application did not I emanate from him. THE QUESTION OF UREAN POWERS. Mr. Clarke said ho thought they might appoint a corn mitteo to consider the position of Stockton Heath and whether or not it would be advisable to seek urban powers. (Hear, hear). He must say at once personally he felt that the time had not arrived for that—(hear, hear)—but he made the suggestion because there were others in the parish—who he thought were a minority— who held the opposite view. The committee could go into the finaneal aspect of the question. Mr. Westbrook said that matter was one for serious consideration. If they did apply, the County Council, the Rural Council and a section of the inhabitants would probably object, so that the question of expense was a serious one.

The Chairman also thought if the matter was inquired, into it would relieve the people's minds. The proposition was carried and Messrs. Ilouchier Welsby, Warburton, Clarke, Pearson and H. J. West- brook were appointed the committee to go into the question.
PENKETH.

The annual meeting of the Ponketh Parish Council was held in the Wesleyan schools on Monday evening when there were present, Dr. Murray (presiding), Messrs. J. J. Withinshaw, Isaac Ashcroft, James Ditchtleld, Richard Routledge, William Hodgkinson, David Houghton and Mr. E. Foster (clerk).
OFFICIALS ELECTED.

On the motion of Mr. Withinshavv, seconded by Mr. Ashcroft, Dr. Murray was re-appointed chairman for the ensuing year.—Dr. Murray, Messrs. J. B. Aitken, and J. Ditchtield were re-appointed overseers.—Mr. Withinshaw was re-appointed vica-chairman. The Chairman said the County Council had arranged that the representatives on the local sub-committee of education should be appointed at that meeting, and they would come into power at the end of May. On the motion of Mr. Routledge, seconded by Mr. Ashcroft, Dr. Murray was appointed the representative for the Infants' School and Mr. Withinshaw for the Wesleyan School.
(num r.usfsEss.

It was decided to approach the Home Wee with a view to the appointment of an additional magistrate for the district. Mr. Hobson referred to the state of certain footpaths in the district, and upon his motion it was decided to ask the County Council to place concrete cement flags along the main road from the Lion Inn ta the Co-opem- tiveStores, and also on the other side from the Lion to the corner of Stocks-lane. The proposal was carried. Mr. Madeley remarked that in the time of the late Mrs. Worrall of the Lion Inn, parish records were kept in a chest which he believed dated back to 300 years ago. He thought they should be examined and the interesting items preserved. These antiquarian relics might be of some interest to the residents of the village. He moved that a committee be appointed to consider the matter. Mr. Hobson observed that the matter had been in his mind for some time, and he thought if a committee was appointed, the residents would have a history of the past. The resolution was carried. It was decided to consider the advisability of re- introducing the old custom of walking the boundary. A long discussion ensued, regarding gymnastic appli- ances being fixed on the recreation ground for the chil- dren. . _
—The Chairman said the Parish Council slid not intend to spend any more money on the recreation ground, and it was decided that the money should come out of the ates.

GRAPPENFIALL. The annual meeting of the Grappenhall Parish Council was held the schools on Tuesday evening. There were present :—Messrs. J. C. Parr, A. Lister-Kaye, P. N. Avery, T. Smith, Jos. Warburton, F. W. Waring. S. H. Jenkins, F. Ellison, John Bradford, F. T. Spence,and S. J. Woodcock (clerk). / MR. PARR RE-ELECTED CHAIRMAN. Mr. Avery proposed that Mr. Parr be re-elected chair- man.
Smith seconded, and the motion was unanimously carried. Mr. Parr said he could only thank them for the con- fidence they reposed in him. He would continue to do

div.p: his best for the good of the parish and hoped the meet- ings of the Council would be as harmonious as in the past. (blear, hear). Messrs. Avery and Bradford were elected overseers, and the Clerk (Mr. Woodcock) assistant overseer. INCREASE IN THE RATES. The Clerk said he had been informed by Mr. Ashton (clerk to the Rural District Council) that the estimated calls for the present half-year amounted to £758, as against £B3l, which meant an increase in the rates of fourpence in the pound. Mr. Jenkins sail he would have been rather pleased if the advance in the rates had been 4s. instead of four- pence. He would willingly bear that for once or twice beeause it would help to bring about the crisis which was certainly gradually coming on. He noticed front that day's papers that the County Council required for education purposes during the coming year,Zl9,ooo more than last year, and, of course, the ratepayers would have to meet that. Their county, and county Glamorgan, were the two counties holding the unenviable position of having spent the maximum amount—% twopenny rate —on higher education. He thought they ought to exercise more consideration for the poorer classes who had to struggle enough to make ends meet. The Chairman agreed with Mr. Jenkins, and thought the increased expenditure was rather alarming,espeeially in regard to education. Ho hoped there would be a re- action, and that the authorities would begin to see that they had been too extravagant and draw in their horns. Mr. Lister-Kaye also regretted the great increase to county expenditure. GREAT SANKEY. THE DANGERS OF THE STATION. The annual meeting of the Sankey Parish Council was held on Monday at the Council schools. Mr. G. Thomp- son presided and there were also present—Messrs. \V. Taylor, W. Fairclough, H. Fairclough, A. Birch, and J. Smith (clerk). Mr. Furness proposed the re-election of Mr. George Thompson as chairman for the ensuing year. He said they could not do better than re-elect him, as he had served them well during the past twelve months. Mr.Fairclough seconded and the resolution was passed unanimously. Mr. Thompson thanked the meeting and said he would do his best for the township. He had attended every meeting of the Council during the past year. On the motion of Mr. Furness, seconded by the Chair- man, Mr. W.Taylor was re-appointed vice-chairman. Mr. Thompson and Mr. Fairclough wore elected over- seers and the following officers were also appointed:— Messrs. Thompson and Birch, representative managers for Sankey school; Mr. H. Fairclough, trustee of the Dole Charity; the vicar (Rev. J. R. Jones) representa- tive on the Education Committee. The Clerk read the following letter from Mr. E. J. Dignum :—To the Parish Council of Great Sankey. Sirs,—" On behalf of my sister and the other members of the family, I beg to thank your honourable body for the kind letter of condolence and expression of sympathy at the great loss we have sustained by the sudden death of our revered father." The Clerk reported that he had written to Mr. Pinion the manager of the Cheshire Lines Committee, with reference to Sankey Station, and informing him that unless something be done, the Board of Trade would be communicated with. He had received no reply from Mr. Pinion. Mr. Furness did not think they would get a reply from Mr. Pinion, because their letter was practically an ultimatum. If, however, they did not follow up their letter with any further action, they would be wanting in their duty to the ratepayers. There was no doubt about the dangerous character of the crossing, and the risk people ran in having to book and then to re-crsss the line,anl he certainly thought further action should be taken. The Chairman thought it would be best to get through all the correspondence together and send it to the Board of Trade. Mr. Furness snagestecl that before the letter was dis- patched, the Clerk should get all the information possible as to the accidents which had taken place and a photograph of the place, and then a letter numerously signed by residents could be sent up. He proposed that this course be taken. Mr. Taylor seconded and said that at the time the- line was laid the Company had a difficulty in getting it passed. The resolution was passed and it was decided that a • sub-committee consisting of the Chairman and Mr. Furness be appointed to assist thc Clerk. A precept for £5 was ordered to be laid upon the overseers for Parish Council work.

SECTION 8 (1) and (3) of the EDUCATION ACT, 1902. PROVIDES as FOL.,OWS "(1) Where the Local Education Authority or any other persons propose to provide a new public elementary schoolthey shall give public notice of their Intention to do so, and the Managers of arty existing school, or the Local Education Authority (where they are not them- selves the persons proposing to provide the school)or any ten ratepayer' in the area for which it is proposed to provide the schooLms7 within three months, a,ter the notice is given, appeal to the Board of Education on the 'round that the proposed school is not required, or that a school provided by the Local Education Authority, or not so provided, as the case may be, is better suited to meet the wants of the district titan the scheol proposed to be provided, and any school built in contravention of the decision of the Board of Education on such appeal shall be treated as unneces- sary." "(3) Any transfer of a public elementary school to or from a Local Reification Authority shall for the purposes of this section be treated as the provision of a new school."

LANCASHIRE HEROES. The Warrington Sewer Fatality At its monthly meeting in London on Monday, the Royal Humane Society made the following awards in cases sent from Lancashire : Testimonial to William S. Mycock, Chorley-road, Swinton, for his gallant attempt to save James Side- bottom, who was drowned in the canal at Clifton Junc- tion on March 27. Testimonial to George D. D. Williamson, Poole- stree, Hulme, for his gallant rescue of John Daymond, an old man of 65, who threw himself into the Bridge- water Canal at the Pomona Docks, Old Trafford on March 14. Testimonial to Joseph Smith, Ney-street, Ashton, for his pluck in saving Emma Flowers from Bft of water in the canal at Bardsley on the 2nd inst. Silver medal to John Stockton, Helsby-street, War- rington, for his splendid pluck on March 6th, in saving ' men named Donoghue. Mitchell, and Baxter, who had been struck down by foul gas in a sewer at Warrington.
